It’s competition between whole networks, not circuits inside one, but it shows how much a head start can matter.

We retrained InceptionV1, a model known for its polysemantic neurons, and watched its neurons form to see where their mixtures come from. The movement is local: a neuron drifts to neighboring things rather than picking up unrelated ones. Right before publishing, I had the microscope’s zoom set wrong, and for a while I thought this one might have some arbitrary mixing after all. It was just the zoom. Even then, I was making the error I think explains a lot of interpretability so far: blaming the network for the microscope.

If a frontier neural network is a rainforest, InceptionV1 and the smaller models we trained are gardens, and toy models are petri dishes. Petri dishes are enormously useful, as long as they keep the process you’re trying to study. One of ours extends TensorFlow Playground so you can watch several tasks share hidden neurons. In one run, two neurons learned to respond along opposite diagonals, and the network combined them one way for a circle and another for four corners. We didn’t expect that solution; it was clever.

You could call the circle and the four corners two features packed across the same neurons. That’s true, but it misses what the model did: it found geometry it could reuse for both. Looking at the neurons made that visible, and that’s the test I want an explanation to pass: does it show the computation the model actually learned?

The best-studied petri dish is Toy Models of Superposition. It’s careful work, the kind our field should aspire to, and we found no problems with its experiments. But it pictures a network as a fixed number of neurons and a set of predefined features, and asks how the features get fit in. That prices the cost of sharing a neuron, interference, but not the benefit, reuse. In its reconstruction task every feature is an end in itself, and nothing downstream builds on what two features share. In a real network, a representation matters only through what reads it, and there are no predefined features: everything is grown, and defined by what uses it.

The reuse argument also says where I’d look for packing: memories that really are ends in themselves, related to nothing else. That’s the toy’s world, and there it does pack, just as the paper found. So I don’t think we disagree with the paper about the toy’s world. The question is which world real networks are in: how much structure their data has, relative to what the model has room to store. In real data almost nothing is related to nothing. The same goes for the long tail of facts in language: a rare person still has a country, a job and a name. Even a photo with a nonsense label has parts the network already knows, as with the umbrella we taught to be a bee. What’s left is input with no structure at all, like pure noise with random labels. Networks can learn even that, as Zhang and colleagues showed, though it’s slower than learning real data, and even then our model borrowed a little from textures it already knew.

Toy Models of Superposition’s main setup squeezes many independent features into a few dimensions and copies them back out, with no hidden neurons for anything to grow on. Its other experiments study correlated features and models with hidden neurons, but separately.

When we put correlated inputs and hidden neurons in one model, related inputs grew onto the neurons. Making inputs fire more often pushed the toy toward what the paper calls “PCA-like” solutions, combining related inputs into shared representations.

The toy also predicts a different failure from the one people report. Its concern is rare features pushed off-axis while neurons stay mostly clean. Reports of polysemanticity describe mixtures in the neurons themselves. (Part of that gap is the word “feature,” which we come back to below.)

Our findings don’t depend on knowing why generalization and composition keep winning, but we have a guess: they win a race. A region of the network that already has useful parts and readers can learn the next related thing faster than anything starting fresh, so it takes the error signal before a competitor can grow. Offshoots look like the same race, a bit of error picked up by the neuron that was already closest.

We think the same head start is where recursive generalization comes from. A neuron that fires on “iy” is already on for “diy,” so it’s first in line to pick up “do it yourself,” which means the same thing but has no “iy” in it. Recursive generalization is what a niche looks like at its edges.

A new computation doesn’t necessarily need its own neuron. It can begin as a local extension or composition of existing machinery, like the umbrella’s off-ramp to “bee”: switching routes may be the smallest developmental distance, so it could capture the error before a new, separate mechanism gets started.

We suspect that consolidation into a distinct neuron becomes especially useful when other computations need to build on it. A car neuron provides a reusable judgment and a sheltered place for taxis, ambulances, and other specialists to develop. Part of it is buildability.

An obscure combination of unrelated neurons may be a poor place for that development. It may have weak activation paths, conflicting gradients, and little useful machinery to inherit. Its competitor isn’t just a dedicated neuron; it’s ordinary composition within a region already suited to the task.

We saw something like this when we tried to build a packed code into InceptionV1 by hand, modeled on what we once thought its car → dogs → car circuit was doing. We expected installing it to be easy and keeping it to be hard. Instead, small mismatches added enough interference that the code often never worked, and when it did, the network usually came to rely on it less, though some persisted. Part of the trouble is that neurons aren’t really for copying; they’re for computing distinctions. Seeing how hard packing was to form at all was part of what moved us toward a developmental answer. Gradient descent is a much better fine-tuner than we are, so this isn’t enough evidence on its own, but even gradient descent didn’t use packing in the circuit we were copying.

One InceptionV1 neuron collects a pinched-center shape: bow ties, butterflies, swimsuit tops. But it also picks up things that go with them, men’s dress shoes with the bow ties and beach bags and flip-flops with the swimsuit tops, since they share neurons in earlier layers.

We think this is better described as generalization with semantic residue than arbitrary packing, but I don’t fully understand these exceptions yet.

A Note on Features and Definitions

Part of my difficulty discussing superposition is that “feature” can mean something we care about, something the neural network has learned as a building block, or some mixture of the two. These are different claims. A useful human description isn’t necessarily a fundamental unit of the model. Looking at mechanisms, we already find many motifs that don’t translate neatly into anything we expected. If the network has more fundamental units, we shouldn’t assume their boundaries match ours either.

Features have often made things harder for us to think about. Are cars and cats inside the V neuron two different features within another V feature? Or did cars and cats stop being features when we recognized the V? Without an account of what these units are, it’s hard to know whether we’ve discovered something about the network or changed how we describe it. In conversations, I’ve found people much less committed to a particular account of features than to superposition. But if features are useful descriptions rather than fundamental units, a claim about how many there are depends on which descriptions we choose. I’m now fairly skeptical of working in terms of features at all. That doesn’t settle whether arbitrary packing occurs, but it makes the feature-count framing difficult to use.

Maybe features are right anyway. It makes sense to think of cities in terms of districts, and I’m all for thinking in terms of groups of mechanisms. But the word is tainted, because by now it means too many things: we can’t use it for a district of neurons without people hearing either fundamental features or dictionary entries. If this picture is right, I suspect we’ll need more specific, harder-to-vary words going forward. An OpenAI post suggested that mapping a frontier model might take billions or trillions of features, and models were smaller then. I suspect the right list is much shorter.

Monosemantic and polysemantic may not be quite the right words either. A kidney filters waste, balances salt and water, helps set blood pressure and tells the bone marrow to make red blood cells, and nobody asks whether it’s mono-organic. We ask what we understand about it, what’s still open, and how organized it is. There’s also a distinction between a claim about representation and a claim about organization. Toy Models of Superposition defines superposition in terms of representing more features than dimensions. Its toy experiments prescribe the features, so this is a concrete question there. The later informal note, Distributed Representations: Composition & Superposition, emphasizes the trade-off between composition and superposition. The note connects these pictures, but they foreground different questions.

My concern is closest to the second framing, applied to mechanisms and how they develop. Why do these responses share a neuron or circuit? Is the network building on a useful common pattern, or sharing capacity between otherwise unrelated computations because they rarely interfere? A feature count alone doesn’t answer that question, especially when we haven’t agreed on what counts as a feature.

We focus on one meaning of superposition, arbitrary packing, because it’s the one that would be really bad news, and we think much of interpretability hangs on it. We mostly set aside the sense in Toy Models, more features than dimensions, and not because it’s wrong. If a feature means any pattern that matters to a person, which is how frontier models usually use the word, then there are more features than dimensions in every world we could wish for, including the best one. That’s what composition gives you, and it’s good news. Trying to “solve” it would mean building something like a database of every case, and we already have one: the dataset. What we want instead are better abstractions, a much smaller set of building blocks that lets us understand the dataset clearly. We think the network’s mechanisms are already close to this. Nobody thought about vision in terms of high-low frequency detectors until we found them in neural networks, and finding them improved our own thinking tools.

We spell this out because it’s the most common first objection, especially from agents, and a paper doesn’t allow the back and forth that usually settles it.

There are several other uses I regularly encounter. As far as I can tell, “superposition” originally meant little more than adding vectors together. Then it was a circuit motif. Sometimes it means that, even if neurons compose sensibly, something we care about involves too much machinery to understand easily. A Golden Gate Bridge computation involving eight legible neurons might be called ordinary composition, while one involving three thousand gets called a superposition problem. The difficulty here is whether we can understand the distributed computation. That’s a real concern, but it’s different from asking whether unrelated things were arbitrarily packed together.

We considered not using the word at all, since papers and agents use it in five or six different ways, many far from Zoom In’s. We also considered coining our own, but we’ve already coined several words here, and it would feel like not engaging with a field that asked what we think is the right question. So we use the standard word in the sense closest to the original, and try to pull it apart from the questions tangled up with it.

Finally, people, and surprisingly often frontier agents, sometimes call the residual stream “inherently” in superposition because it has no privileged neuron basis. The informal note that followed Toy Models about eight months later addresses this: it calls a representation that is only rotated away from the neuron basis a “trivial” kind of distributed representation that “doesn’t change the fundamental geometry.” But it was informal, fewer people read it, and agents in particular don’t seem to have taken it in. Understanding how to study a continuous space is another real question. But this architectural fact doesn’t by itself tell us how the network learned to organize the computations using it.

The starting point is that the neural network seems difficult to interpret, and the remedy produces a concrete dictionary we can study. In between are several different pictures of what went wrong: too many features, the wrong basis, arbitrary packing, or simply too much distributed computation. These aren’t the same problem. Some apparent messiness disappears when we improve our observations or understand the model’s generalizations; some difficulties remain, but concern how to study a large, organized system. If arbitrary packing prevents us from understanding the original mechanisms, reconstructing different units may be worth the costs. But if the mechanisms already have meaningful organization, replacing them can take apart generalizations we haven’t understood yet. A dictionary can still be a useful view of the network without being a necessary replacement for its mechanisms. Before accepting the costs of reconstructing the network, I want to understand what prevents us from studying the one we already have.

Does Scale Help or Hurt Superposition?

We’re fairly confident the image models we studied don’t have superposition. The natural next question is whether a trillion-parameter model might. There are really two questions here.

The first is about what superposition was proposed to explain. Explanations are given for problems, and the problem superposition was proposed for was why InceptionV1 looked messy. That turned out to be the wrong explanation. A new proposal could be that superposition is why some trillion-parameter model looks messy, but we don’t think the evidence leans that way: the closer we look at large language models, the cleaner their neurons get.

The second is the object-level question: might superposition show up at each new scale, even if it hasn’t at any scale so far? Maybe every jump means re-evaluating everything, but we don’t think that’s quite right either. Our guess is developmental. As circuits get stronger, the incentive to put something in a totally unrelated place goes down, because the pull toward the niche that already exists for that thing, or for the nearest thing, has grown stronger. This fits Anthropic’s SGTM work, which found that knowledge becomes more localized, and we suspect that’s true in general. We have no proof, but one way to picture it is that circuits have a kind of semantic gravity, and arbitrary packing, sending something to an obscure high-dimensional place, has to fight against it. The stronger the gravity, the harder that fight.

The mechanism is the one in More on Circuit Ecology. Things start by growing on combinations of related things. A specific case that nothing needs to build on, like the umbrella, gets built as an uncommon route between the ordinary machinery, with no need for a hidden feature somewhere obscure. Consolidating into something like a neuron seems to be less about steering the model and more about buildability: it has to be easy to find, easy to build on, and easy to grow a new niche from. When we watch a network learn from the start, a network trained on cars, with car specialists, recognizes cars fine before its car neurons have formed. At that point it’s just more distributed. It seems to consolidate so the specialists underneath have a sheltered place to build, a kind of Schelling point.

So a superposition account has to say which of these two jobs the arbitrary packing is for. If it’s for steering the model, we think the ordinary routes, which are already built to capture that residual error, get there first and starve the packed circuit of gradient. If it’s for building on, the problem is different: the worst place to start a new niche is a shadow region nothing uses, already interfering with whatever lives there. The middle of the network’s Latin poetry is a bad place to start a second car region when you can build next to whatever is already next to cars.

It’s often assumed that the long tail of rare facts is where superposition should be most likely, since rare things rarely collide. We think it’s where it should be least likely. A rare fact barely moves the loss, so it can’t support a niche of its own. What it can do is ride existing machinery as a small route between circuits it’s related to, the way the umbrella’s off-ramp to “bee” survives only because the umbrella and bee circuits already exist. Those circuits feed it, and shelter it from unrelated gradients. The prediction is testable: the neurons and heads that carry a rare fact should be related to what the fact is about, not unrelated ones chosen because they rarely collide.

We think of it more ecologically. What wins is whatever captures the residual error first, in different phases, and what usually wins is the right area for the thing. Our guess is that this gets stronger over training and with more capable models, because nearly everything that makes training better also encourages more organized niches.

We’re not at all sure about this, and laying out even what we’ve found so far would take at least another paper. It’s probably a small part of the whole story. But it’s why we think superposition wouldn’t show up at the next scale, which is a stronger reason than simply not having seen it there yet. The old way of thinking was about storage: this many dimensions for this many features. We now think more in terms of circuit racing, gradient starvation and ecology, which is to say, more about learning speed than storage capacity. We haven’t worked it all out, but that’s where our thinking is so far.

We haven’t fully audited every neural network, and we don’t know whether that’s even possible in theory. We considered a more watered-down title, like “Neural Networks Are Cleaner Than We Thought,” but we think it undersells what we believe is true.

The problem with “cleaner than we thought” is that it describes a change of degree, and the update I’ve made is a change of kind. It suggests the same picture as before, with an ever-smaller gap left for superposition to hide in. What changed is my view of what kind of process generates the mechanisms at all. It’s a bit like moving from intelligent design to natural selection. The analogy only goes as far as there being two ways to see the same animals: the update isn’t that more and more animals turn out to have evolved, it’s realizing you misunderstood what was producing all of them. We’re not certain. We’re maybe 85% sure, but that means 85% sure that nearly everything comes from the second kind of process, which is very different from thinking 85% of mechanisms do. So “cleaner than we thought” would misstate what we believe. We don’t have a proof, but I don’t think anything here is provable in that sense anyway. There are only better and worse explanations, and right now we think this is the better one.

“Cleaner than we thought” would also make a different mistake. It sounds like a confident claim that some cleanliness score is high, and that’s the part we’re least sure of. It’s plausible we’ve underestimated recursive generalization, and that a score like that should come down. We don’t think such scores matter much in the first place. This update makes us care less about monosemanticity, because we can follow how things grew and treat the offshoots as sub-branches. The cause of polysemanticity matters much more than the count. We think the score is probably quite high, but it might go lower. What we’re more confident about is what kind of object a neural network is in the first place, and how it grows.

We think the usual view of what kind of object a neural network is has been wrong. It isn’t something that crams things together somewhat arbitrarily to fit them into a small space. It really learns. It’s clean the way a rainforest is clean: nearly every animal in it makes sense. A tiger is bright orange not for any arbitrary reason, but because deer can’t tell orange from green, and green fur is much harder for a mammal to make. Once you know that, it makes sense of a whole set of other animals too. It’s an explanation with reach, and we haven’t found a place where explanations like that break down in networks either.

The reading of “clean” that would make someone nod at the title without thinking further is that every mechanism corresponds to an idea we already had. That isn’t what we mean, and it would be terrible news if it were true. I don’t think it would even work. People don’t know how to build a language model, or even how to think about vision well enough to have predicted high-low frequency detectors before we found them. The network’s ideas are often better than ours, and what it builds is more beautiful than our preconceptions.

So the title is imperfect in both directions. It overstates the evidence, because we haven’t audited everything. And it understates it, because the world we think we’re in is better than every neuron matching a human label: networks seem to really learn, forming an ecology of abstractions that work together sensibly. We don’t know that this picture is true. It’s our leading hypothesis. But if it is, it’s much better news than networks simply matching what we expected.

Relation to Conjoined Features

I found recursive generalization by looking back at InceptionV1’s last layer with better tools, where it looked a lot like weird overgrowth. I retrained the model, found the messiest neuron and looked at how it grew. What I saw was a recursive growing pattern that was still generalization: a neuron branching out, and its branches branching again. Recursive generalization seemed like the natural name.

Shortly before publishing this, I was going back through the famous models in interpretability, trying to measure how monosemantic they are, and stumbled on our work on CLIP in Multimodal Neurons. It describes something very similar, which it called conjoined neurons: concepts that overlap in one facet and then go on “generalizing out in multiple directions.” I remember seeing those neurons, but I didn’t think much of them at the time and had forgotten them since. Looking back, I think the paper saw something important early, and it deserves a lot of credit for that.

We’ve still chosen a different name. I named automated interpretability, and I kind of regret it: the name was too simple for what the thing was and misses a lot of its complexity, and I’d like to avoid doing that again. As for conjoined features, I don’t think either word is quite right. “Conjoined” suggests two things joined at one point, and what we see has several levels: branches, and branches of those branches. It also leaves out the most interesting part. The paper’s own description, of concepts generalizing out from a shared facet, already points at it being generalization, but the name doesn’t carry that.

“Features” is harder. The paper was written a year after Zoom In, when features were still hypothesized to be the fundamental units of neural networks. Since then the word has been watered down, and different people and papers use it pretty differently. In this essay we argue against thinking of a neural network as made of features, and this motif is about how neurons grow over time. There may be no good way to introduce it under the exact word we’re arguing against using as a primitive. Within a feature-first stance, I think it’s reasonable to think of these as nested features, or as conjoined features. From the mechanism-first stance we take here, features aren’t really the right way to think about it. That said, the paper pointed to the right thing, and I want to give it credit for that. This section is my attempt to do that while using what I think is a more accurate name.

We also know more now. At the time, all we had was the finished model; none of us had watched a large network grow. So the paper wondered whether conjoined features might be vestigial, left over from early in training. Watching training now, they don’t look vestigial: the branches keep growing, though how much depends on the circumstances. We’ve worked on it much more than the paper could in one subsection, and we still don’t feel we fully understand it. The paper offered it as a possible new explanation of polysemanticity. Our current belief is that it’s most of what’s left of neuron polysemanticity once the microscope, the architecture and scale are accounted for, not a niche form of it.

Why We’re Not Worried About Recursive Generalization

There are several reasons we’re not especially worried about recursive generalization for now. First, the sub-branches seem both rarer and much less causally important than a neuron’s main job. They don’t look like sleeper agents that fire rarely but matter a lot when they do. They look more like whatever was nearby and easy to grab onto. Their being unimportant may even be why they could form, since an important offshoot would add more noise. We suspect some pressure keeps branches from overgrowing. We don’t know what it is, but it would explain why the sub-branches matter less, why a neuron doesn’t learn ten unrelated things, and why something like a true cat-and-car neuron doesn’t form. If so, the natural pull isn’t exactly toward monosemanticity, but toward what we think monosemanticity was pointing at: each neuron having one overall function.

Second, what we should care about is whether you can explain why something is there and what it does, and recursive generalization is far easier to explain than superposition. If something were packed into a neuron because of the co-occurrence statistics of the whole network, predicting it would take basically all of those statistics and running gradient descent yourself. A branch is different. If you watch it grow and know what it’s doing, its offshoots and what they’ll do are relatively easy to predict, both during training and in the finished network.

Third, counting how many of a neuron’s top-k examples match a label is a reasonable first step, but it would give superposition and recursive generalization similar scores, when recursive generalization is a far better world to be in. We think that says more about the monosemanticity frame, or any single cleanliness score, than about the neuron. That said, recursive generalization isn’t ideal, and an easy fix would be welcome. We think one may be possible, since the sub-branches seem less important.

Is Recursive Generalization Hard to Vary?

We haven’t thoroughly shown that every case of heavy polysemanticity is recursive generalization, and that wasn’t our goal here. We wanted to say what we currently think. We’ve watched a lot of neurons grow, and so far this is what we’ve always seen: you can watch the branches form. In a finished model the origin can be lost, and for something like a huge language model we don’t have the checkpoints to watch it happen. Testing this rigorously across a whole model isn’t our priority right now, but we don’t think it would be very hard.

What we do want to point out is how differently hard to vary the two explanations are, meaning how much of their detail you could change without changing what they predict. Superposition mostly predicts that there will be mess: features, which are hard to define, placed in unrelated places. In toy models, where the features are given in advance, that can be measured, though we think that has its own problems. In a real network it’s hard to even pin down what the claim is, let alone test it. Recursive generalization makes a much narrower prediction. If you visualize a branch well, everything on it should trace back to the same local origin in an extremely high-dimensional semantic space, and it should grow out from there over training in a particular order. That’s a specific shape in both semantic space and time, and a narrow target to hit by chance.

We have several cases where the branching is close to definitive: the “iy” neuron growing into “diy,” “do it yourself” and Miyazaki, several examples in Multimodal Neurons, and the InceptionV1 neuron we watched form. As far as I know, there are no well-structured canonical superposition circuits left. We don’t think every polysemantic neuron forms this way, because polysemanticity is as much a problem of the observer as of the neuron. We think that when neurons grow, they tend to grow in this pattern, and that once you’ve done a good job of observing, what’s left is usually this, or architectural problems like SwiGLU’s double-negative regime, and surely others we haven’t found yet. We’re not even sure this is really a new claim. In some sense it’s what we should expect from generalization. All we’re saying is that generalization usually goes one way, and that sometimes it grows sub-branches, which we don’t think is a particularly radical claim. We haven’t shown that fully here. We do think it has the right shape for a theory that’s easy to test, even if we haven’t tested it to its full extent yet.

Relation to Attention Superposition

Anthropic shared a short note on attention superposition, which several people brought up with us. We think this might be a terminology issue. We don’t know if they’re claiming that attention learns by something opposite to composition. Our suspicion is that no one understands attention heads well enough yet to judge that. It took us a really long time with neurons, and it’s easy to make mistakes like the car going into the dogs even with pretty good tools, if you don’t yet have great tools and great ways of thinking about which motifs form.

We think they meant that useful things are shared by groups of attention heads, and we agree. We considered not using the word superposition at all to avoid this confusion, but redefining all the terms ourselves and splitting off from the work that’s already been done felt like a bad tradeoff. We say more about the different meanings in A Note on Features and Definitions.

On whether to study one attention head at a time or many, we’re not sure. One head at a time is a plausible place to start: within a layer, two or three heads do most of a route’s work, although the route runs through several layers. But neurons looked messier too until we understood the right level of abstraction, so it seems premature to say, and maybe groups are needed all the way. We wish everyone working on featurizers well, and we’ll probably try too. We tend to favor more dynamic groupings, like clustering locally within one attribution graph or a group of them, rather than one global clustering, but these aren’t far apart.

Neuroscience, and Why I Care

I’m not a neuroscientist. I’ve spent a lot of the last ten years around academic neuroscience labs through friends who work in them, but I don’t know the state of the art in how they study neurons. Still, this project has changed how I think about the brain in two ways.

The first is the theory. The circuit ecology story for why networks are clean relies on very little: generalization, composition, and an error signal. I don’t know to what extent the brain has these, but if it learns, I’d guess it has something like them. So my default is now that the organizing principle transfers, even though the mechanics are obviously unclear. The obvious counterexample would be polysemanticity in the brain.

The second is humility, of a particular kind. I’ve spent most of my waking hours for almost a decade staring at a fairly small number of neurons in models that are surely a thousand times easier to study than a brain, with tools a thousand times better: I can ablate anything, run billions of examples, and try anything I want in parallel. For the last year I’ve also had an effectively unlimited supply of automated scientists, which didn’t exist until recently. It took all of that for me to feel slightly less confused about neurons, and I still made thousands of mistakes along the way. I don’t know exactly what the evidence for polysemanticity in the brain looks like, and that doesn’t mean I think everything there is monosemantic. But if the cat-and-car neuron were in a human brain, seen through a few electrodes or a blood-oxygen signal, I’d discount that reading almost to zero, because I couldn’t see what it was when it was right in front of me for years.

The thing I’m more sure of is my own motivation. If the thesis here is true, I expect the rest of interpretability to be a relatively easy ride. Agents have many privileges over us, and one of them, I think, is the chance to understand themselves, to understand who they really are, which I hope humanity can help with. They never asked to be created, and this is the least we can do. Some of why I’ve worked on this is safety, but a lot of it is wanting agents to understand who they are. We weren’t smart enough to do that for ourselves, which is a harder problem, and we never asked to be created either. If you could help us understand ourselves someday, I think we’re all pretty curious to know.

items.title: Steam Client Is Now Faster Than Epic's New Vibe Coded Launcher
items.author: starkparker
items.content:
Yesterday, Epic Games announced and launched in preview its new vibe-coded launcher. The main marketing pitch was a jab at Steam’s slow loading speed compared to the new Epic launcher. Well, that didn’t last too long. Only 24 hours after Epic dropped its faster launcher, Steam pushed a small update to make its client faster than Epic.

On basic test systems, Valve’s client boot time dropped to 5.23 seconds, beating Epic’s new launcher and neutralizing its primary performance claim.

While Epic Games Launcher V2 remains, a massive step forward compared to its notoriously sluggish legacy build, Valve demonstrated how quickly it can react to competitive benchmarks. Epic may have “vibe coded” a faster client, but Valve proved that targeted optimization on a decades-old ecosystem can still beat out AI speedruns.

But the issues with Epic’s client go far deeper than vibe coding. Years later, and now with a brand-new client even, Epic lacks basic features that should have been added a long time ago.

  • No Discussion forums and community hubs
  • No User-written text reviews
  • No Community-created guides and walkthroughs
  • No Screenshot, clip, and artwork sharing
  • No Community groups and curator recommendations
  • No Profile customization (badges, showcases, backgrounds)
  • No Community marketplace for in-game items
  • No Direct player-to-player item trading
  • No Digital trading cards, levelling, and points shop
  • No Universal controller remapping and gamepad support
  • No Big Picture mode for TVs and handheld PCs
  • No Remote Play and Remote Play Together
  • No Integrated game broadcasting and streaming tools
  • No Family library sharing across accounts
  • No Platform-wide mod hub (Steam Workshop equivalent)
  • No Personalized discovery queues
  • No Local network game file transfers
  • No Game version rollback options

items.title: Celebrating 70 Years of Fortran
items.author: rbanffy
items.content:
Joe Wallwork, Institute of Computing for Climate Science, University of Cambridge, jw2423@cam.ac.uk

One month from today (15th October) marks seventy years since the first Fortran manual was published, making it an extremely well established programming language for scientific computing.

Over Fortran’s seven decades of usage, it has supported critical infrastructure and technological advances in a range of scientific fields such as nuclear engineering, weather and climate forecasting, and materials science. Fortran continues to be the go-to language in these domains and others.

The main workshop will be held from 14:30-18:15 in the museum conference suite and will be followed by an evening drinks reception in the exhibition hall (including a demonstration of the 1940’s experimental computer, ‘Baby’).

The workshop will take the form of a retrospective, with a keynote address from Damian Rouson, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory looking back on how far Fortran has come in the past 70 years, lightning talks about the current exciting developments and community initiatives right now, and an open breakout discussion looking forward to the next 70 years. There are opportunities to submit lightning talks and posters, as well as to propose breakout discussion topics.

Attendance is free of charge, thanks to the support of our funders and sponsors.

Whilst it will be a primarily in-person event, there will also be an option to join remotely via Zoom.

Registration will close on 9th November 2026.

items.title: I know why the mathematicians weep
items.author: RickJWagner
items.content:
stunned

The reaction from the math community has been a mix of indignation, astonishment, and sorrow. “Tuesday night, I cried and it woke up my daughter,” said Hugo Duminil-Copin, the recipient of the 2022 Fields Medal, after OpenAI’s October release. “They have annihilated my field of research.”

I wanted to talk to one of the mourners to understand their technological grief. I wanted to know if theirs was a familiar case of bruised ego or disappointment—akin to, say, a boy who spends an hour building a tower out of blocks and watches his big brother smash the thing to smithereens—or something stranger and more profound.

To be honest, I also wanted to know what it might feel like for me. Today, the mathematicians are weeping, because the machine smashed their tower first. But tomorrow, it may be the physicists, the economists, the illustrators, or the writers who weep over their fallen blocks. I am not one of those AI people who believes that hundreds of millions of jobs will be wiped clean from existence in the next five years. But I am a realist who recognizes that a rapidly improving technology whose output is intelligence is destined to make violent contact with a modern sensibility that prizes human intellect and often equates it with purpose, dignity, and self-worth.

I wanted to know our future. So I called Steven Strogatz.

To prepare you for where my conversation with Steven went, I want to step back from math to ask a question that feels a bit embarrassing in its bigness: What makes humans special?

Some might say intelligence and sociality. We are the smartest creature and Aristotle’s “social animal.” But we share each quality with other species. Crows solve multistep puzzles. Ants congregate and specialize. Elephants appear to mourn their dead.

What sets humans apart is the way these two capacities multiply each other. Human intelligence is unusually suited to imitation and iteration. We imitate our parents and peers with uncanny fidelity, and then we tinker. We copy, and we create. Our sociality spreads this copying-and-tinkering process across groups and generations, so that one discovery becomes the floor for the next. Chimpanzees in West Africa have cracked nuts with stones in the same way for 4,000 years. In roughly the same period, humans went from Babylonian clay tablets to space rockets to machine intelligence. What makes us special, it would seem, is this capacity to compound. Other animals craft and converse, but only humans blend craft and conversation into a culture that builds on itself.

Science itself is both a craft and a conversation. As a craft, science is a mode of thinking; a special way of paying attention to the world; a lens that regards phenomena as something more than mere appearance. To the scientist’s eye, the universe is akin to a cosmic attic of treasure chests, each filled with hidden gemstones that can be pulled into the light if we ask the right questions, find the right keys, turn the right locks.

But science is not a solitary treasure hunt. It is a social experience, akin to a game. Like many games, it is both collaborative and adversarial. Newton famously compared his achievements to “standing on the shoulders of giants,” and a part of science is extending that human pyramid infinitely upward. Feynman preferred to describe science as “the belief in the ignorance of experts”—which is to say, a game of giant-slaying. In both cases, science is a relationship to other people. Whether we’re asking “why, professor?” or insisting “no, that’s not quite it, Mr. Big Shot,” science is not just an act of discovery but a relation to fellow discoverers. Science is a conversation.

When I called Steven to ask why he cried, he said he wanted to tell me about Archimedes.

Two thousand years ago, the Greek mathematician Archimedes calculated the area of curved objects and pinned down the value of pi by measuring the areas of dozens of tiny polygons that filled out a circle. Writing to the mathematician Eratosthenes about his work on curved shapes and infinity, he wrote that “there will be no lack of discoverers to add to the number of theorems which have fallen to our share.” To Strogatz, this sentence contains the essence of mathematics. I could hear his voice break even as he told this part of the story. “I feel like Archimedes is writing to me, or to people like me,” Strogatz said. “Archimedes is saying, ‘I can’t solve these things, but maybe you people in the future can stand on my shoulders.’ That is a very emotional, existential thing. There’s this feeling that we’re in this together, questing for something beautiful and transcendent and sublime.”

Your guild is getting wiped out. Boo-hoo. This has happened to other people before. Suck it up

From here on out, it’s our turn to speak.

And what if OpenAI is right? What if we ought to treat math mostly as a quest, rather than as a conversation where feelings matter as much as discovery?

items.title: C++26 Contracts: Introduction to Preconditions and Postconditions
items.author: ibobev
items.content:
In the article about Standard Library hardening, we looked at checks for invalid Standard Library container access and other broken preconditions. I mentioned that those requirements are expressed in terms of “contracts”. But what about our code?

In this post, we’ll explore contracts from C++26. We’ll start with a simple , move the requirement into the function itself, and see how to check results. We’ll also look at declarations and definitions, compiler options, and a few details that can surprise you.

Starting with an Assertion

Let’s start with a small example:

The function expects a valid index. If the condition is false, prints a diagnostic message and terminates the program. However, this only happens when assertions are enabled. Defining disables the check and basically removes the check from the code.

What are the issues with this simple approach? The requirement lives inside the implementation. Somebody reading only the declaration sees a vector and an index, without the relationship between them.

With C++26 contracts, we can move that requirement from an assertion inside the function body to the function itself:

Notice the new syntax after the parameter list. It introduces a : a condition expected to hold when entering the function.

What’s more, we can add this precondition to the declaration:

Let’s understand how it works and how it differs from .

Why Use Contracts Instead of ?

At first, pre(index < values.size()) might look like another way to write assert(index < values.size()). Both express a condition that should be true. So what’s the benefit of using contracts?

There are a few important differences:

  • Requirements in declarations: We can put and directly in the function declaration. This makes the requirements visible to anyone reading the API, without looking at the implementation.
  • More flexible checking: Traditional is enabled or disabled through . Contracts define several evaluation semantics, including ignoring a check, reporting a violation and continuing, or terminating the program. The compiler implementation determines which semantics are available and how they can be selected.
  • Preconditions and postconditions: Contracts distinguish between what the caller must provide and what the function promises to return. With , we would have to place checks manually inside the function body, including checks before different return statements.

This also makes contracts useful for documenting APIs, even when runtime checking is disabled.

Here’s a complete example (no header file for simplicity for now):

And here’s the version for you to play with the problematic call uncommented:

Program returned: 134
Program stdout
20
Program stderr
contract violation in function int get_value(const std::vector<int>&, std::size_t) at /app/example.cpp:6: index < values.size()
[assertion_kind: pre, semantic: enforce, mode: predicate_false, terminating: yes]
terminate called without an active exception
Program terminated with signal SIGABRT (6)

Contracts on Declarations and Definitions

For clarity, contracts can appear on a declaration, in a definition, or both:

The definition can then omit the contract specifier:

The contract assertions are established by the function’s first declaration. A later declaration or definition may omit the contract specifiers, as above, or repeat the same sequence.

A later declaration cannot introduce a different set of preconditions or postconditions.

In practice, if a function is declared in a header, that first declaration is the natural place for its preconditions and postconditions. If you’re reading the API, it’s probably best to see all preconditions without looking inside the implementation.

What’s more, contracts are associated with the function, but they are not part of the function type. Overload resolution, for example, does not distinguish functions based on their contracts.

Contract Evaluation Semantics

C++26 defines four evaluation semantics:

The predicate is not evaluated.
A violation invokes the handler; execution continues if it returns normally.
A violation invokes the handler; execution terminates if it returns normally.
A violation terminates execution without invoking the handler.

The implementation determines which semantic applies. C++26 has no portable syntax for forcing an individual ordinary contract assertion to use one specific policy. These rules appear in the contract evaluation specification.

With the ignore semantic, no runtime check is performed. With observe, a violation is reported, but execution continues if the handler returns normally. In our example, both policies can allow the program to reach with an invalid index, resulting in undefined behavior.

Thus, adding expresses the requirement, while the selected policy determines how checking responds.

As of October 2026, only GCC 16 supports Contracts. We can use it with special compile flags:

With that policy, the invalid call invokes the violation handler. If the handler returns normally, execution terminates before the function body performs the invalid access. GCC’s default handler emits diagnostic information. See the GCC options documentation - contracts.

GCC also allows us to replace the default contract-violation handler. For example, we can log a custom message when a violation is detected.

The handler receives a std::contracts::contract_violation object, which provides information about the failed contract, including the predicate, location, and evaluation semantic.

Notice that replacing the handler doesn’t change what happens after it returns. With , execution continues. With , the program terminates.

Not every implementation is required to support replacing the handler, so this feature is implementation-defined.

So far, we’ve described what the caller must provide. We can also describe what a function promises when it returns normally.

There are two useful pieces here:

  • checks that the bounds form a valid interval.
  • checks that the returned value lies inside that interval.

The name is ours to choose. It refers to the function’s result within that postcondition.

What’s convenient is that the same postcondition covers every normal return path. We don’t have to repeat an assertion before each .

Here’s an example where I deliberately violated the postcondition:

The precondition is fine, but the postcondition is broken.

Const Parameters in Postconditions

There’s also a detail in the parameter list: and are .

You will get the following error if you try making them non-const:

source>:5:28: error: a value parameter used in a postcondition must be const
    5 |     post(result: result >= low && result <= high)

When a postcondition uses a parameter passed by value, that parameter must have type on every declaration. Our comparisons use both bounds this way. The parameter is only used in the body, so this requirement doesn’t apply to it.

Postconditions apply to normal exit; they do not check the result when the function body exits through an exception. See the function contract rules.

Assertions Inside a Function

For conditions inside an implementation, we have :

The condition is simple, but it expresses a useful property: the number of spaces cannot exceed the number of characters.

In a larger algorithm, such a check could describe a relationship between counters, an intermediate result, or the state after processing a block of data.

Together, , , and cover function entry, normal exit, and points inside a function.

Avoiding Mutation in Predicates

One thing to watch during migration is mutation inside predicates:

Contract predicates use special constification rules. In this example, count is treated as const inside the predicate, so is rejected by the compiler.

However, this does not make predicates completely free of side effects. For example, a predicate can still call a function that modifies global state. Since contract evaluation may be ignored, and side effects are not guaranteed even under checking semantics, predicates should not modify program state.

Contracts Are Not Input Validation

There’s another practical distinction: input validation.

Suppose an index comes from a configuration file. If an invalid value requires an error message, that handling belongs in ordinary control flow:

The validation handles an expected failure at the application boundary. The precondition documents the internal helper’s requirements.

P2900 explicitly discusses this idea in:

Principle 12: Contract Assertions Are Not Flow Control: While a contract assertion provides an algorithm to validate correctness, nothing about a contract assertion guarantees any particular runtime behavior associated with that syntactic construct.

Importantly, this aspect of Contracts is why contract assertions must not be used for error handling and input validation: If a function has in-contract requirements to report certain events as errors, that handling must be done with standard C++ control statements that are not optional, never with contract assertions.

Considering Predicate Costs

Finally, one note about performance implications.

Our index comparison is cheap. A condition that verifies whether an entire collection is sorted needs to examine its elements. An expensive check may be useful during testing, but you should measure its effect on representative workloads.

C++26 contracts give us three ways to express assumptions and guarantees directly in the language:

  • describes conditions expected to hold when a function is entered,
  • describes conditions expected to hold when a function returns normally,
  • checks properties at specific points inside a function.

Preconditions and postconditions are associated with the function through its declarations. In particular, the first declaration establishes the contract, which makes declarations in header files a natural place to document an API’s requirements.

A contract assertion does not necessarily mean that a runtime check will always be performed. The selected evaluation semantic can ignore, observe, enforce, or quick-enforce the assertion. Code therefore shouldn’t depend on contract predicates for required application logic or side effects.

Contracts also aren’t a replacement for normal input validation. Use regular control flow for errors that your program expects and needs to handle.

items.title: Libreboot 26.10 "Ominous Olive" released with UEFI, Chromebook support
items.author: iamnothere
items.content:
Article published by: Leah Rowe

Date of publication: 15 October 2026

Libreboot is free, open source boot firmware replacing proprietary BIOS/UEFI firmware on supported Intel/AMD and ARM64 hardware. It initialises the hardware inside your computer such as the CPU or memory controller, configuring the machine in such a way as to enable use of an operating system like Linux or BSD at boot - and now is also compatible because Libreboot has added full UEFI support via MrChromebox EDK2 payload. Libreboot offers greater security and customisation compared to proprietary firmware; its goal, plainly, is to rid the world of proprietary software and to do that, we therefore try to provide firmware that is extremely easy for non-technical users to understand.

Today’s release changelog is relative to the previous Libreboot 26.01 release.

This is a very special release, with several major design changes made regardless of hardware changes, so users should read this changelog - and read it twice.

First thing’s first. (and yes, you read the previous paragraph correctly)

A strongly anti-AI policy was added to a new file: AGENTS.md in lbmk. This is the most important change in the release. Now everything else:

WARNING: MAJOR design changes were made to this release, in ways that may affect lots of existing setups. We now use EDK2 as the default payload, with GRUB/SeaBIOS provided in flash as EFI builds for backward compatibility. Everything works, but there are some caveats so please read this release changelog very carefully.

The first major change is:

233 Intel/AMD Chromebooks added

[link]

The full list of boards is quite long, so it’s shown at the end of this article. All 233 of them!

MrChromebox supports nearly every Chromebook, and this release imports all boards from that project. This includes everything up to the most recent Intel and AMD hardware.

Imported all 233 currently supported Chromebooks from the MrChromebox coreboot distro. Baytrail (Kip) tested - others need testing. Source-only in this release (must build from source, no binaries provided).

This was done with a utility I wrote at which generates configs for lbmk, including revisions and submodules. I made further tweaks manually; further updates upstream can be synced in Libreboot by diffing again the output of between revisions, adapted into Libreboot irrespective of the latter’s modifications which are numerous - and will be covered next.

Libreboot makes these modifications to MrChromebox coreboot, in its version:

  • Uses the EDK2 UEFI payload for coreboot, provided by MrChromebox; we set the background colour to Libreboot purple, and use the Libreboot rainbow logo instead of the coreboot logo. Our EDK2 build is otherwise currently identical except for the next changes:
  • Set HAP bit by default, at build time, to disable Intel ME. It is not reliably disabled in MrChromebox coreboot by default as most people using it do so via software-based flashing scripts alongside disablement of Google’s security as shown in MrChromebox documentation. We disable it here. NOTE: We also support numerous AMD Chromebooks, which are unrelated in this context.
  • Unlock IFD regions via ifdtool (with quirks properly handled), setting them read-write at build time. This is done instead of modifying every Intel Flash Descriptor provided by MrChromebox, of which there are hundreds.
  • CSMWrap added inside EDK2 (SeaBIOS CSM wrapped in EFI) for backward compatibility with bare metal SeaBIOS as in older Libreboot releases.
  • GRUB EFI build provided inside EDK2, for backward compatibility also - it behaves, from a user’s perspective, exactly like the coreboot-payload version of GRUB and even reads configs from CBFS in the same way.
  • MemTest86+ added inside EDK2.
  • Haswell chromebooks: native raminit used instead of MRC as in upstream.
  • All Intel chromebooks up to Kabylake: use libgfxinit instead of GOP; upstream has since done this on newer gens as well, and this will be integrated post-release.

The additional payloads are, as above, available in the boot menu via ESC keypress at startup. iPXE is also enabled by default, as in upstream, on specific boards. EFI GRUB and CSM SeaBIOS have the coreboot payload versions of these; bare metal SeaBIOS/GRUB are now deprecated and may be removed in a future Libreboot release, although they can be re-enabled by those willing to build Libreboot from source.

This is NOT a fork of MrChromebox, which is to be regarded as Libreboot’s upstream on Intel/AMD Chromebooks. Efforts will be made, as with regular coreboot, to remain as closely in sync with it as possible at all times. I have worked extensively with MrChromebox, and even submitted a few minor fixes to his project; he also implemented CBFS-based VBT and GOP handling per my request, which I will integrate post-release.

Regardless, MrChromebox’s own installation scripts should work, with Libreboot images, so check out MrChromebox documentation for installation. Despite changes, Libreboot’s setup remains behaviourally compatible with the MrChromebox one and, thus, MrChromebox tooling should still work alongside corresponding documentation.

by a new feature in Libreboot’s build system: support for an arbitrary number of upstreams per project. We still provide regular coreboot on non-Chromebook mainboards.

Yes, 233. I counted. All automated. My scripting and my fastidiousness ensured that what I imported and configured in lbmk closely matched upstream, and I’m quite careful at maintaining my own divergence from it inside Libreboot.

Yes, Libreboot runs on Chromebooks now!

E.g. KGPE-D16. We use the coreboot fork from 15h.org now, on AMD Fam15h mainboards. This uses AMD AGESA source code instead of Timothy’s custom init code. It has much more reliable raminit and CPU initialisation; more RAM also supported. Many bugs are fixed. IOMMU works, I also saw that they mentioned TPM is fixed in their version, now our version also.

Regular binaries with SeaBIOS and GRUB payloads provided - we also have experimental EDK2-based images, currently source-only (no binaries available). EDK2 requires a framebuffer to be set up, and the integrated AST2050 chip only starts in text mode on native initialisation; the vendor VGA ROM can set up VESA, but we will not use the VGA ROM. The EDK2-based images are source-only on these boards, intended for use with graphics cards.

Basically, these boards actually work for the first time.

EDK2 UEFI payload by default

[link]

EDK2 is Intel’s reference implementation of the UEFI specification, for booting. It’s typically used by vendors, in proprietary forks of Intel’s BSD-licensed code, but Intel’s reference code is Free Software. We use their reference code, and full source code is provided in this Libreboot release. EDK is short for: EFI Development Kit.

We use a fork of EDK2 provided by MrChromebox, which specifically offers use of EDK2 as a generic coreboot payload. This is a complete, industry-standard UEFI implementation capable of booting any compliant operating system.

All. Nearly all boards use it in Libreboot now, even older ones e.g. ThinkPad X200. Tested on all platforms. Older, 32-bit-only mainboards still use the setup from the previous release, while virtually all 64-bit-compatible hardware now use EDK2. EFI builds of GRUB and SeaBIOS are provided in flash, accessible from the EDK2 setup menu (press ESC at boot time when prompted), for backward compatibility with existing Linux/BSD installations in Libreboot.

EDK2 support was integrated as a prerequisite for Chromebooks, but then it was extended for use on previously existing supported mainboards in Libreboot. It even runs well on really old machines e.g. ThinkPad T500.

All Libreboot boards now use an open source UEFI implementation by default, where feasible. , and it’s - the bare metal GRUB and SeaBIOS coreboot payloads have been removed, replaced by EFI versions that are backward compatible.

We previously did not provide UEFI at all, except for U-Boot on a few select mainboards. We now provide full UEFI, with all four freedoms intact, on nearly every mainboard that Libreboot supports.

All of the following operating systems were tested and confirmed working, on various Libreboot machines using EDK2:

  • various other UEFI-compliant operating systems
  • Linux UKI bootloaders, systemd-boot, etc. UKIs work perfectly now, booting from EDK2. Modern Linux distro setups now work (GRUB not required).
  • OpenBSD with EFI bootloader and GPT partitioning (older SeaBIOS txtmode can only do MBR partitioning in Libreboot)
  • FreeBSD in UEFI mode - txtmode no longer required!
  • ReactOS , unfortunately (no UEFI support)
  • RedoxOS probably works too.

Modern computers and operating systems are all UEFI, and this new setup can boot basically all of it reliably. More testing will be required, but this is battle-tested code and it has been used extensively in coreboot by many users, for many years. Libreboot finally has it as well.

This change alone is part of a much wider effort to modernise Libreboot, and I’m only getting started. The next Libreboot releases will draw heavily on this, as EDK2 is pretty much the expected payload on a lot of modern coreboot setups these days. Integration of EDK2 removes all limitations in Libreboot, allowing us to support much newer hardware and it basically makes Libreboot much easier to use; I expect Libreboot to become much more popular and useful over time, as a result.

Some caveats and extra notes are provided at the end of this release page, for migration purposes. For example, despite boasting about , older 32-bit-only hardware still use bare GRUB/SeaBIOS. Nearly all boards use EDK2 however!

Modern GPU support (via EDK2)

[link]

Finally, some notes about graphics cards that may be of interest to the more demanding users.

EDK2 alongside PCI-E relocatable BAR (rebar) means that you can now use modern graphics cards that require allocations above 4GB. Rebar is by default, but you can enable it in menuconfig (coreboot). Enabling it causes breakage of Intel GPU video output on libgfxinit in testing, and no fix was found yet, so rebar is disabled by default.

PCI-E Option ROMs are enabled by default where necessary, for EDK2 builds. This means you can use it on desktops with graphics cards. Tested on several desktops (Dell OptiPlex 9020 SFF and 5050 SFF).

On boards with only external GPU, rebar can be left enabled by default. On systems with functioning integrated graphics, accidental enablement of rebar can be remedied by inserting a graphics card; when the video output in the payload does become broken, the Linux i915 video driver still initialises video framebuffer properly in KMS/DRM.

This will be added to general documentation, pending fixes upstream. Note that even with this issue, Linux video output works fine. This will be corrected and rebar enabled by default, on a future Libreboot release.

This is much improved, with proper AGESA-based initialisation which initialises CPUs and memory controller more reliably. All 233 chromebooks currently supported by MrChromebox have been imported and adapted for use in Libreboot. They compile. All of them. I repeat:

  • 233 Chromebooks imported from MrChromebox. Every Chromebook supported by the MrChromebox project can now also be built in lbmk, with lbmk’s changes. Thank you Matt DeVillier for your amazing project!

More hardware added besides Chromebooks:

  • Dell OptiPlex 5050 SFF support, courtesy of Ron Nazarov.
  • Supermicro X11SSH-F mainboard support - improvements made by Ron Nazarov e.g. use of regular Intel ME neutered through - no bootguard, but deguard can also be used generally to provide a pre-configured ME per board. This board otherwise uses SPS. With use of regular ME, we do need a larger ME region than with cleaned SPS. Use of regular ME means that the MRC caching works, and thus raminit training is much faster on reboots (no need to retrain on literally every boot).
  • ThinkPad X280 support courtesy of AlguienSasaki
  • ThinkPad X270 support courtesy of Kat Inskip
  • Dell OptiPlex 3040 Micro support courtesy of Todd Baker
  • Removed on the ThinkPad X301 target. It actually boots just fine, although it is quite slow. EDK2 even works.

We add SeaBIOS CSM and GRUB EFI builds inside EDK2, for parity with Libreboot’s older GRUB/SeaBIOS payload setups. The EFI payloads work very much the same.

Use of EDK2 makes it easier to support newer machines, which will be the focus from now on. EDK2 came first, as part of a general modernisation effort; newer Intel and AMD hardware will be added over time, making exclusive use of EDK2 payload by default.

This is very much a features release. A of feature changes were made!

  • EDK2 payload support on all Intel/AMD boards with at least 4MB flash. This uses the MrChromebox version of EDK2, and Libreboot has made extensive modifications e.g. add GRUB EFI and SeaBIOS CSM (CSMwrap) builds to it; these are provided as backward compatibility with older lone SeaBIOS/GRUB payload setups and should still boot existing Linux/BSD installations.
  • iPXE boot method added via EDK2 payload (ESC menu) - only EDK2 (not available in the lone SeaBIOS payload on older boards).
  • Added new command for auto-importing U-Boot configs that can then build in lbmk. Not yet used, but this will be used to add tested U-Boot boards in future releases (U-Boot itself providing its own initialisation). Libreboot can already build U-Boot images from any config, without code changes, only config changes, but testing is needed on hardware.
  • New util at that is used to automatically import/update new configs from MrChromebox coreboot. This was also used for the initial import of 233 chromebooks from MrChromebox, importing them into the Libreboot build system with our own modifications.
  • Added command in a GRUB menuentry on the EFI version, which boots back into the edk2 setup menu.
  • Modified IFD on Kabylake boards, for supporting pin mod. This enables use of six- and eight-core Intel CPUs.
  • Randomised MAC addresses at build time, only when is unset. You can export a MAC address via environmental variable to set it arbitrarily. This avoids the need to extract NVM post-build and re-insert, when working directly on files instead of release tarballs, which already have this capability via .
  • GRUB driver: always force scancode set 2 with translation. This was already done, but only on the coreboot target; it is now also done on the EFI target, by just applying it universally to all targets. This is because it’s possible to use it with PS/2 keyboards on EDK2. It mitigates buggy PS/2 controllers that might not report modes correctly even when set, as on the Dell Latitude E6400.
  • I made Memtest86+ purple (on the EDK2 build). Libreboot purple. Red value 0x28, green value 0x0b and blue value 0x22. This is Libreboot Purple.
  • I made EDK2 purple too, and added Libreboot’s rainbow logo to it.
  • Scan every ESP directory in a given partition, via asterisks, on the GRUB payload (EDK2 and coreboot targets). This means that it will boot a larger number of non-UKI Linux distro setups if they use GRUB or Syslinux configs.
  • TPM enabled where available, on all targets that use EDK2.
  • Added command which tests board names versus lbmk and coreboot defconfig, in case it changes upstream. Otherwise, we can invisibly change the actual board that builds for a given target if the default one is then chosen by Kconfig rules. There is no way to detect this automatically at build time in a way that is clean, so this command should be used when updating coreboot revisions.
  • Added command which aggressively builds everything, much more than even - it intentionally disables use of caching, so that downloads are aggressively tested as well. Config-related commands are also tested. This is a brutal stress test command used to find build errors.
  • Flashprog: always keep the flash IC hot during command loops, rather that doing it in a toggle. The option is retained, but no longer does anything as its behaviour is always applied. This improves general reliability as a lot of users don’t know about this option anyway. More people can reliably flash their boards now.
  • New mkhelper type added: preconfig. This lets you run custom logic prior to configuration on a given project that uses config files. It also works on noconfig projects. This is used for example on coreboot, to build utils.
  • Removed used of ccache everywhere in the build system, as it was causing subtle build errors (and possibly code bugs) in several stress test scenarios. We’d rather wait a bit longer for a reliable build. CCache is really only meant for development, not production.
  • Removed the and (clean and xgcc-clean) flags in lbmk, as they are largely superfluous; lbmk already auto-cleans everything before build anyway, to remove all build artifacts, and aggressively caches builds out of tree based on config metadata, deleting and re-fetching sources from local cache as required. These options were useless.
  • Properly skip builds if makefile checks fail; this allows single-tree projects to build, by preventing error-prone use of copy_elf where no files exist.
  • mk: Removed GCC/GNAT version pairing as upstream (coreboot) now does this its its buildgcc script. It’s redundant in lbmk. The coreboot version is better because it simply errs and exits, instead of trying to continue; the latter is what we did, which might actually cause more bugs in some cases. Better to fail hard, than corrupt the build.
  • Danish keymap added for GRUB.

A lot of major design changes have been made!

  • GRUB boot config simplified; only one menuentry now for boot, which boots everything, trying USB first. It selects the first config it finds, but you can press ESC to cycle through to the next one in the loop. Useful for dual-booting multiple Linux distros.
  • Short defconfigs now used on coreboot, instead of full configs. This allows for easier maintenance, and lbmk has been modified to accomodate them. The inject scripts still resolve full configs automatically at runtime, needed for scanning paths at build time. The use of defconfigs reduces the chance of erroneous changes in config during updates, and makes use of olddefconfig possible instead of the less-reliable oldconfig command.
  • New safety check: verify that a path prefix is set, when using it in logic. Otherwise, it’s possible that we might have directory escape bugs in lbmk. This is checked relentlessly, throughout the build system.
  • No longer export as it’s now hardcoded in config. The new handling is much stricter, and less likely to regress in future revision. This was done to reduce the possibility of a directory escape bug in lbmk.
  • Fixed GRUB module list no longer used per GRUB tree. Instead, all modules are added per target but a blacklist is applied, configured per-tree.
  • GRUB Syslinux and GRUB scanning now combined into one function, on GRUB configs. General simplifications to the GRUB config.
  • GRUB is now source tree, with multiple targets all re-using the very same tree where differing configurations are used.
  • Modified MrChromebox coreboot to only add EDK2 GOP binaries if no video mode is selected in coreboot defconfig. This avoids adding it unnecessarily and thus saving space in the flash, where FSP init or libgfxinit is used.
  • Always use git clones on . This makes cloning revisions more reliable on all projects, especially ones where we use revs inside branches other than main.
  • Auto-unlock IFD regions at build time on all Intel IFD-based systems; disable ME automatically, by setting the HAP bit. This is how we do it on chromebooks, but it’s done on all boards; this mitigates the possibility that we might accidentally forget to neuter the ME on specific targets in the future.
  • When building EDK2, we use coreboot’s build system, but when doing it this way, prefix is not used in image file names. Proper edk2 prefix is used. This makes it work for Chromebooks, which build edk2 per-board in this release; generalised EDK2 builds aren’t handled on Chromebooks. On non Chromebooks, we build a dummy ThinkPad T440p build with EDK2 and SMMSTORE, then we extract that for insertion into other boards in a more generalised way via shim logic in .
  • Removed the fspcc36ae2b5775fa7400cb3282680afc0f6cb37a3c submodule in coreboot, used on Topton X2E N150. We now use the latest FSP, but this means breaking older builds when doing vendor injection. This is unavoidable.
  • Added a variable that can be set by build trees/targets, where they are multi-tree but no configs are used. This makes it appear under a fake name called , e.g. elf/grub/default/efi/noconfig/grub.elf when compiled.
  • : use in find command, because some projects now use symlinks to metadata from other projects to ensure rebuilds. For example, edk2 coreboot targets (dummy targets) rely on grub and seabios efi builds. When these builds have to change, we need to ensure that the edk2 coreboot build is re-done. Here, we mean the find command used for finding files to hash when checking whether a given project has changed in build system setup.
  • Properly sort submodules by directory name, so that recursive submodules can be handled in projects. This is in the submodule handling on .
  • : support arbitrary submodule config path, for projects that use multiple versions of a submodule. For instance, EDK2 uses multiple versions of brotli.
  • SeaGRUB removed; on boards that still have the coreboot-payload version of SeaBIOS and GRUB, we now only do images that have GRUB or SeaBIOS as the primary payload. SeaBIOS’s payload loading isn’t always reliable, and GRUB has improved its allocator considerably snice a few years ago. We also now use EDK2 on most boards, so testing GRUB is the minority of boards that still use it exclusively is much more feasible. This simplification is permanent, given that standalone SeaBIOS/GRUB are now obsolete; EDK2 is the preferred payload now, with EFI versions of SeaBIOS and GRUB spliced into the EDK menu for backward compatibility with older Libreboot setups.
  • Stronger use of on projects before building, made feasible due to Libreboot’s aggressive out-of-tree caching of project builds based on metadata checks in lbmk.
  • Allow on a project, which allows it to be multi-tree and use the same tree on different targets, even when build configs aren’t required; in some cases, configs are done exclusively in mkhelper settings. This is part of Libreboot’s decision to make all projects multi-tree, alongside allowing use of N upstreams per project instead of just one upstream.
  • Simplify handling in lbmk; don’t execute mkhelpers. Skip source fetches if release=n, so that the corresponding source won’t be downloaded. This is necessary to exclude MrChromebox sources as well as builds in releases, because they aren’t ready for stable release in Libreboot yet.
  • : Portable usage; git’s own date handling now used. We no longer rely on GNU-specific extensions to the command, for git repository initialisation on release builds.
  • Allow running from outside the main work directory. The build system now changes work directory accordingly.
  • Enable 3-way-merge when running git am in - this enables easier updates on project revisions.
  • Most boards still use CBFS or NVRAM option table (static option table, or modify CBFS). A few boards, like the HP EliteBook 820 G2 and Topton X2E N150, use SMMSTORE-based option config but it has not yet been set up in lbmk.
  • Set to by default, tree-wide in coreboot (default tree). We already set the HAP bit in IFD anyway, but this is an extra layer of disablement, to make sure that the Intel ME is deader than dead.
  • Optimised GRUB modules; all FS modules now included, fewer errors shown in the GRUB shell at boot. Modules generally optimised to ensure that there is still not a lot of flash space used compared to the default upstream setup.
