  • Fix offline GRUB builds. The build system caches sources and repos, but GRUB had custom logic in it for downloading unversioned PO files from translationproject.org - so when I did my FOSDEM talk, my demo failed because the internet was down, while I wrongly believed I had everything cached. GRUB was modified to not download the files, and lbmk caches them instead. They are also now version-checked, by virtue of checksum; no versioning is actually provided upstream, but their contents were checked and further updates will inspect the diffs between them. Basically, whatever is on translationproject.org pertains to the current HEAD in GRUB. It’s fine because the way gettext works is that if a literal string is not defined, it defaults back to original language. In this context then, use of the wrong PO files will just result in some sentences not being translated. Still, a bug in the way the files are handled might allow for a… buffer overflow, on unversioned files that GRUB was downloading without checking hashes. Yes. Libreboot fixed this reproducibility problem by forking the repository containing the files, keeping it static. Next time I do a talk, my demo won’t fail. I fixed this literally a few hours after my talk.

A lot of changes were made to to the extent that it deserves its own release log:

  • Generally safer use of macros (use brackets).
  • Removed errno-based error handling. Just return zero or one, based on logical errors, but do not rely on the status of errno for error exits. Only use return values as appropriate to POSIX in libc functions. However, errno reset is handled more reliably accordingly, after return from libc functions; not required but also not counterindicated by POSIX. - dell-flash-unlock errno handling also fixed in the same way. We previously relied heavily on errno for exit, in ways that were not portable. Not all libc will properly reset it, and may set it randomly even when a given function logically returns with success. Any number of things could set it, so it’s not a reliable mechanism for general error handling.
  • Don’t use flag - also remove this on . Reduces the chance of pedantic build errors based on warnings.
  • General correctness fixes; bound checks, proper handling of word alignment, use of uintptr when converting pointers, etc. The code is generally much safer, in terms of memory management, as a result of extensive auditing.
  • EINTR-safe wrappers for various functions; loop until EINTR clears, where error occurs, otherwise err-exist on non-EINTR errors. Properly ignore EINTR on if function returns with error (EINTR on close is not an error condition in POSIX, and the descriptor should be disregarded in such scenario).
  • More testing and fixes for OpenBSD, especially on memory management (much stricter libc in OpenBSD).
  • Generalised I/O functions for libc functions like , writepreadpwrite` - EINTR-safe, with stricter (than libc) checks against incomplete writes and such.

NOTE: This applies to the standalone version of nvmutil. There was an attempt to rewrite it in a much larger utility, mentioned in the following section about canceled changes for this release (see notes below about libreboot-utils).

A few changes were worked on, but did not land in this release. They pertain to two major projects:

This was an extension of nvmutil that later became a generalised set of utilities alongside a library for handling things like atomic writes, and userspace mitigation against various types of TOCTOU attacks. Not really critical for nvmutil itself, but…

An attempt was made to implement a hardened version of mktemp called mkhtemp. It implemented several mitigations in userspace against TOCTOU attacks e.g. directory replacement and symlink attacks.

Check lbmk git log for to see more (might have been .

Mkhtemp was started when implementing atomic writes for nvmutil, but then I naturally made use of tmpfiles for that, and that led to me auditing every implementation of mktemp. I concluded that I could do better - and I did.

Examples of how mkhtemp innovated:

  • Still provided libc-like behaviour when requested, but:
  • Stricter checks against use of world-writeable non-sticky directories.
  • Generally stricter error-exit handling.
  • Relentless checks against changes to files during operation/check, inode changes and so on. Checking that a file wasn’t operated on by another program - basically, openat2-like security was attempted to implement in userspace, though openat2 was also enabled as a fast method on Linux.
  • Own implementation of rand, wrapping around Linux getrandom and BSD arc4random. It provided various functions for rand, including one that matched the semantics of arc4random_buf (rset function in libreboot-utils).
  • Descriptorless operation in general, on files and directories.
  • Pathless operation where possible - including userspace directory walking and sandboxing.
  • Unveil-like restrictions in userspace (and pledge/unveil usage in OpenBSD).
  • Use of symlinks disabled by default.

…it was an over-engineered piece of crap, and had several memory issues related to stack memory usage, which tripped up a lot on BSD. The could could be tidied up and finished, but I came to a conclusion:

Distros would never accept it. Mkhtemp worked fine on Linux, but it had much stricter operation that would trip up most build systems that use it. I tried it in lbmk to replace mkhtemp, symlinking it in PATH, but for example GRUB had virtually no error checking on mktemp. Most programs that use mktemp wrongly assume that it can never fail, so it doesn’t; implementations try to mitigate errors and continue operation, in ways that are extremely complex. Mkhtemp was a clean attempt at stricter TMPDIR usage.

Because I decided it was a waste of time, I don’t think I care to write more about it in this changelog. Check lbmk git log if you’re interested.

Miscallaneous canceled work

[link]
  • Updated U-Boot to a late 2026 revision on ARM64 chromebooks, but the bootflow menu looks ugly now and barely works. Upstream completely broke it. Therefore, we still use the early 2025 revision of U-Boot that was there in the Libreboot 26.01 (January 2026) release.
  • GRUB keymap support via parsing of in CBFS when booting with EDK2. This was canceled because a better method will be implemented post release; use of HiiDatabase and a graphical config menu in EDK2 to change the keyboard layout and locale. This will be written to SMMSTORE and also used by payloads. For example, the GRUB EFI payload could read from SMMSTORE to know locale and then change its language accordingly, using its existing gettext integration (GRUB already supports internationalisation).

Hidden third cancelation, because there always is one:

Linuxboot. Now with EFI support, we can easily use any number of UKIs added to flash if we want to - and we will, in a future release. The term Linuxboot refers to any flash-based Linux distro that can boot other Linux kernels via Kexec - my preference is ZFSBootMenu, or at least something inspired by it as ZFSBootMenu’s build system is thoroughly incompatible with Libreboot’s strict design principles.

(which is a polite way of saying that I hate podman/docker with a passion)

Linux UKIs are common now, for boot, and Libreboot EDK2 can easily integrate it.

U-Boot x86 payload REMOVED

[link]

The ARM64 payload is still present, but EDK2 has replaced U-Boot on x86.

This deserves its own section, in this release, as it is a major design change. EDK2 was not merely added as an option; it has U-Boot on x86. I could make this its own article. It deserves one. It deserves my judgement, publicly as I’m now about to articulate in no uncertain terms:

U-Boot was used for lightweight UEFI implementation on Intel/AMD boards, but the person chiefly in charge of the x86 coreboot payload for U-Boot has largely forked U-Boot into a newly vibe-coded project; Libreboot opposes heavily the use of AI, as per new policy. AI is no good, and upstream x86 U-Boot support has largely bitrotted although several interesting patches were merged.

U-Boot is thus a liability on x86. EDK2 is more fully functional already, so this is used instead. Think AI makes you a super hacker? Think again:

U-Boot was always buggy on x86 anyway. It’s really just not ready at all. It is better used on RISCV and ARM64(where we continue to use it).

U-Boot upstream itself is staunchly anti-AI, at least at the time of this release, and much discussion of the above was had on their mailing list. It would not be productive to re-ligitate that on this release page, but it should suffice to say that the Libreboot project considers U-Boot to be effectively dead on x86. The ARM-based development is still ongoing strongly, upstream, and we will continue to use U-Boot for UEFI on ARM64 (chromebooks for example).

I will not say his name, or the name of his fork, because I don’t want to promote him or his U-Boot fork. If you know his name or his project, you should not say it or promote it either. AI is bad, very bad, for reasons here:

The fork in question, of U-Boot, is heavily AI vibe-coded and thus useless to Libreboot. This is not mere conjecture; in said aforementioned U-Boot mailing list thread, the author stated thus. We will not, in any way, encourage or facilitate use of AI. It has been made clear that several projects Libreboot uses also have some AI-assisted commits; GCC, GRUB, etc. This is not our fault, but it is my intention that I and others will audit these projects in the future, de-slopping them and possibly even forking them entirely for that very reason. The author of the fork basically went insane with it, proposing to the U-Boot upstream that his work be “custodian”, and merged slowly into the upstream U-Boot tree. He was basically pressuring them to accept AI code against their wills. I say in my capacity as leader of the Libreboot project that U-Boot should never allow AI to taint its project. When you accept AI, you become deskilled and you erode the trust that exists between you and your users. You remove the human connection between maintainers and users, and your project will start to become dependent on what is - yes - proprietary technology, paid for in blood. AI is one of the single biggest consumers of electricity and water on the planet, leading to resource shortages all over the world and its increasing control over what information people see in the news is even a threat to democracy worldwide. This is before even arguing about unclear licensing, copyright violations and so on. It was decided that Libreboot would join the crusade against all artificial intelligence. The countries chiefly in charge of AI training and infrastructure are the United States (led by several companies currently attacking democracy worldwide) and the People’s Republic of China; even if all the other problems with AI didn’t exist, it would be a very bad idea to give these countries even more power over our computing.

NO. Libreboot says no to AI. Thus, we will continue using upstream U-Boot as they say no also, and we will not use any vibecoded forks of it. Even if that causes me to have to spend weeks integrating a totally new system to replace it. That is precisely, exactly and indubitably how far I will go to prove my point.

That is why I went to such extreme effort integrating EDK2. Rather than replace U-Boot with yet another incomplete UEFI implementation, I simply added EDK2 which is already feature-complete as it is the reference, industry-standard implementation of the UEFI spec.

CrabEFI was what I initially considered, to replace U-Boot. This is a new payload written by Arthur Heymans, and the project itself is excellent, but rustc/cargo is inherently unreliable for several reasons:

  • Unpredictable toolchain setup. Most people use e.g. rustup and they set up all sorts of custom environments. Much less predictive than e.g. LLVM/GCC provided in distros. Libraries and such are provided by Cargo, instead of distros, and users often leave everything out of date, leading to breakage.
  • Rust is not standardised; the specification is implementation-defined, and code written today may still compile in the future when the spec changes, but code behaviour would naturally change as a result of the latter.
  • Given the above, we would have to bootstrap rustc/cargo ourselves, and we would have to do it from source (from a compiler like GCC which already has source bootstrapping courtesy of the Guix project and others).

Rust is awesome, but in my opinion not production-ready yet. Give it another ten years. EDK2 is infinitely more complex, but the size of the code is not a concern as it is generally stable, and written in C (some small bits of it are in C++). It has the most amount of eyes on it, and regularly receives security audits. It’s one of the most battle-tested codebases on the internet, and works well.

CrabEFI will likely be merged in Libreboot at some time in the future, when Rust tooling has stabilised across distros (including BSDs). It has a much better design, even if it’s not yet feature-complete, and use of Rust means that it will have fewer memory bugs. For now, Libreboot uses EDK2 to replace U-Boot and it has been enabled by default on all boards.

On memory safety, we can say contrarily that EDK2 is at least stable; bugs are also stable. That’s the point. We have stable C/C++ compilers, properly tested according to formalised standards (not really, because GCC and LLVM do all sorts of whacky things too, but they also try to be compatible with each other behaviourally). You want your code, when compiled, to behave exactly the same, bugs included. This is more strongly guaranteed with projects written in C and C++ (especially pure C projects, and most of EDK2 is in fact pure C).

It was originally intended that U-Boot would become Libreboot’s primary payload on x86, but alas. I bit the Intel-flavoured bullet and went with EDK2.

Say no to AI. AI makes you stupid. AI is the reason we can’t have nice things.

No ability to change the keyboard layout yet - a graphical menu option can be added for this later in EDK2, saved to SMMSTORE. The EFI build of GRUB uses only, and input is thus handled by the EDK2 input drivers (ditto USB mass storage and other storage devices); GRUB’s nativedisk driver is removed for example, and its native NVMe/xHCI drivers are no longer needed as in previous Libreboot releases.

EDK2 input drivers work with both USB and PS/2 keyboards in Libreboot. GRUB is made to use input instead of as it otherwise lacks USB keyboard support in the EFI build. Thus, layouts must be handled by EDK2. There is code for this in EDK2, not currently handled by either Libreboot or MrChromebox so it all defaults to UK QWERTY in this release. Upstream (MrChromebox) uses US QWERTY by default, but Libreboot is a British project, so EDK2 was patched accordingly. Work will be done post-release.

Keymapped images no longer provided. There is now only one ROM image per config on each mainboard. This simplifies builds, and users can insert a file inside CBFS from if they wish; if you add a grub.cfg to flash with set to , this will work on devices with PS/2 keyboards if wanting to use the GRUB EFI payload (a command in grub.cfg to load the keymap is also needed, specifically keymap (cbfsdisk)/keymap.gkb.

EDK2 has been tested extensively on all Intel hardware from GM45 e.g. ThinkPad X200/T400, all the way to Intel Kabylake hardware supported by Libreboot e.g. ThinkPad T480, X280, Dell Optiplex 3050/5050.

Want old GRUB/SeaBIOS back?

[link]

The new compatibility modules in EDK2 should more than suffice for most users, who may still want GRUB/SeaBIOS for booting their existing Linux and BSD setups. It is recommended that you convert these to EFI or just reinstall them - use of UEFI is strongly encouraged as the default from now on, but Libreboot must (will) continue supporting older setups.

FreeBSD users booting with SeaBIOS text mode may be interested in this, as BIOS-mode FreeBSD bootloaders do not boot with anything else. A UEFI-based FreeBSD installation will work just fine in EDK2 though, so new FreeBSD installations are best recommended via EDK2 (do not use the compatibility modules of GRUB/SeaBIOS).

Some users might want it. Here are some brief notes. They won’t be added to the main documentation as they pertain to a configuration that Libreboot now regards as obsolete, but some users may nonetheless find it useful in the short term:

Older mainboards that are 32-bit only or with limited flash space still use the standalone GRUB/SeaBIOS payloads without EDK2; some newer ones with weird graphics setups also still use lone SeaBIOS/GRUB e.g. HP EliteBook 8560w.

To re-enable use of standalone GRUB/SeaBIOS (without edk2), modify as follows for your board: remove , and variables. Then add these lines:

payload_grub="y"
payload_seabios="y"
payload_memtest="y"

This is obsolete now in Libreboot and may even be removed in a future release. EDK2 is much better as it boots nearly everything, and supports more hardware setups. It is simply much more versatile than Libreboot’s old setup as in the previous release.

Then you can just re-build. NOTE: In the above guidance, is assumed to be grub/default seabios/build memtest86plus/default by default. You may want to set them explicitly:

build_depend="seabios/build grub/default memtest86plus/default"

You may also wish to set the GRUB tree explicitly:

Example config: config/module/coreboot/t480_vfsp_16mb/target.cfg

Just do this and re-build if you want these old setups back. This will be supported for as long as feasible, but will probably be removed at some point, maybe years from now, maybe a week from now. Use it while it’s there. The xHCI patches are still in there, and everything is configured as it should be.

In setups with EDK2, please note: txtmode not provided. If wanting e.g. SeaBIOS txtmode, look at e.g.:

  • config/module/coreboot/t480_vfsp_16mb/config/libgfxinit_corebootfb

Renamed it to in this example and do:

./mk -m coreboot t480_vfsp_16mb
./mk -s coreboot t480_vfsp_16mb

In the menu that appears, go into Devices -> Display -> Framebuffer mode and select - this is not recommended for any new setups, but the FreeBSD bootloader starts in text mode and the framebuffer modes in coreboot can’t switch back to it. Booting in text mode is recommended when booting the FreeBSD BIOS-mode bootloader, and then FreeBSD can be set up for KMS in Xorg/Wayland. Otherwise, new installations should be done in EFI mode directly via EDK2 (no compatibility modules). More information about this is available in Libreboot’s BSD documentation.

List of Chromebooks added

[link]

    CSMWrap is the SeaBIOS CSM build provided inside EDK2. It hogs an entire CPU core at boot, so e.g. quad-core will show up as three-core inside Linux. It’s a known limitation that will be corrected in a future release, due to the design of CSMWrap. If you need backward compatibility, it’s better to use the GRUB EFI build instead which does not have this problem. Both GRUB EFI and SeaBIOS CSM are available in the EDK2 menu via ESC keypress at boot time.

    Users are best served just switching to native UEFI boot with ESP, using Libreboot’s EDK2 payload.

items.title: Zero-Click Spyware Delivered via Targeted Ads: AdFection
items.author: jcomp
items.content:
• Devices at international news network Al Jazeera were infected with mercenary spyware from Candiru (rebranded as “Integrity Labs”) via targeted online advertisements. We provide the first public technical confirmation of a zero-click mercenary spyware attack delivered via targeted advertising, which we call AdFection.
  • The malicious advertisements were purchased by Discover-Tech, an Israeli company that presents itself as a legitimate advertising company, but which we found operates as a facilitator for multiple mercenary spyware partners.
  • Discover-Tech operates a platform called that enables its mercenary partners to de-anonymize, fingerprint, and automatically infect devices the moment an advertisement is rendered — a form of zero-click attack.
  • Analysis of four billion Discover-Tech bidding records shows that during a four-month period, the company’s ads were shown on almost 200,000 unique websites and Android/iOS apps in dozens of countries.
  • Discover-Tech’s ads also covertly directed millions of devices to contact Candiru’s servers, likely for large-scale tracking and reconnaissance. Discover-Tech is linked to mercenary spyware and intelligence threat actors beyond Candiru, including Intelos and Bindecy. 
  • A separate threat actor we call is using Discover-Tech’s infrastructure to exploit vulnerabilities across numerous mobile carriers to link device advertising IDs with phone numbers, mass-deanonymizing internet users. We will detail our findings concerning this threat actor in a separate forthcoming report.
  • Discover-Tech has appeared on lists of “certified” and “approved” vendors maintained by Google and advertising industry association IAB Europe, and has served ads via major networks such as Google, Yandex, and Beeswax. Discover-Tech has also leveraged the European General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) consent frameworks to target users within the European Union.
  • Discover-Tech’s mass abuse, privacy invasion, and facilitation for mercenary spyware attacks illustrates structural flaws with the online advertising system, which failed to detect or prevent the abuse documented in this report.
  • We call on regulators to investigate whether Discover-Tech and Candiru/Integrity Labs violated applicable laws, and make recommendations to lawmakers, defenders, and the advertising industry on how to stop AdFection-style attacks and espionage. 
  • We disclosed our findings to ad vendors and industry organizations. Google, IAB Europe, Beeswax, Vungle (Liftoff), and Eskimi took action to disconnect Discover-Tech’s access to the digital advertising ecosystem. Other ad vendors we found to be involved in Discover-Tech’s operations did not respond to our request for comment within the timeline provided. We are also actively working with vendors to mitigate ’s mass-deanonymization attack.

This section provides an overview of the online advertising ecosystem, and summarizes our findings about Discover-Tech.

The Online Advertising Ecosystem is Ripe for Abuse

When a user sees an ad on an app or a website, it is likely the result of a real-time auction, where advertisers bid on the chance to show that specific user that specific ad. So-called Real-Time Bidding (RTB) auctions, which are hosted on ad exchanges operated by companies including Google, take place hundreds of billions of times a day. In less than a second, the user’s device initiates a bid request, advertisers submit their bids, and the ad exchange determines the winner of the auction and pushes the ad to the user. Besides an image or video, an online ad can also contain code that runs within the app or browser that shows the ad.

Both advertisers and publishers of apps and websites use ad vendors that act as their intermediaries in these auctions. Advertisers typically buy ads via a so-called Demand-Side Platform (DSP), and a Supply-Side Platform (SSP) sells ad inventory on websites and apps.

Malicious actors make use of two interrelated facets of the online advertising ecosystem:

The advertising ecosystem collects a lot of data and enables individual-level targeting: When a publisher of an app or website wishes to show ads, they add code from an SSP to their app or site. This code collects and shares granular information about the user and their device with ad exchanges to solicit for the ad slots. This information can include device identifiers and characteristics, precise location, and IP address data, as well as data about the app or website, and specifications about the ad slot. The DSP or advertiser then examines this information and decides whether they wish to bid on the impression in order to show an ad. The auction system isdesigned to enable targeting single individuals based on their mobile advertising ID, cookie ID, IP address, and other identifiers.

The advertising ecosystem allows many different third parties to run code in apps and websites: It is tempting to think of an online ad as, simply, a video or image. However, ads themselves maycontaincode from the advertiser, DSP, and other parties, and run it in the app or browser while the ad is shown to the user, for example to track users, ad impressions, and clicks. Code run by advertisers, DSPs, SSPs, and other third parties within apps and websites is often referredto as “tags”, “pixels”, “SDKs”, or “third-party tracking” more generally.

Exploiting Advertising Tech for Surveillance

The totality of information gleaned from ad auctions is quite valuable. A company with access to auction data cantrack users without their knowledge as they move around in physical space, or switch between cellular, Wi-Fi, and VPNs, by observing how bid requests tied to a specific identifier change location or IP address over time. In fact, the surveillance industry sells access to so-called ad intelligence (ADINT) platforms that leverage this sort of data, often combined with third-party tracking data. In recent years, several investigations and media reports haveuncoveredvendors that sell ADINT to defense, intelligence, and law enforcement agencies.

Zero-Click Spyware Delivered via Targeted Ads: AdFection

Beyond passive data harvesting, malicious parties can also exploit this infrastructure to target certain individuals based on user data included in ad auctions and then run malicious code on their devices. Advertisers or DSPs may run HTML and JavaScript code when an ad is shown to the user. That code retrieves additional JavaScript code, which may, in turn, load further code, such as a browser exploit to install spyware. Since the code can contain identifiers for the user or their device, arbitrary JavaScript code can be sent precisely to a single user’s device. Our research in this report indicates that this architecture is indeed abused to facilitate the delivery of zero-click targeted spyware, and that the simple display of a targeted ad is enough for infection.

There hasbeen some reporting about the intersection between spyware and the advertising ecosystem. However, the specific ways mercenary spyware companies plug into the ads ecosystem to target particular users have remained largely secret. This report exposes zero-click spyware delivered via targeted ads, which we call, and is the first technical demonstration that mercenary spyware is being distributed via targeted advertisements.

Discover-Tech is a Bridge Between Mercenary Spyware Companies and the Advertising Ecosystem

We present technical evidence that the Israel-based company Discover-Tech, while purporting to be a legitimate advertising company, appears to be a front for large-scale ad espionage abuse, including the automatic delivery of mercenary spyware when ads are displayed to a target and the mass profiling and deanonymization of users.

The company serves as a bridge between ad vendors and the mercenary spyware ecosystem. In fact, it appears that serving as this bridge is Discover-Tech’s primary purpose. Its platform, Controlium, allows malicious actors to precisely profile and de-anonymize millions of individuals, fingerprint their devices, and target them with a form of zero-click hacking, where their devices can be automatically infected when an ad is displayed to them.

Discover-Tech appears to work with multiple mercenary spyware, hacking, and advertising vendors, connecting the spyware industry to the online advertising ecosystem. As we detail in this report, Discover-Tech ads are used to infect and profile on behalf of mercenary spyware vendor Candiru. We also detail connections between Discover-Tech and another mercenary hacking company, Bindecy, as well as connections with Intelos, a mercenary ADINT firm.

What is Discover-Tech and How Does It Operate?

Discover-Tech is led by its CEO Dekel Boni, who has a background in digital advertising. Eric Banoun, whom Haaretz describes as “one of the pioneers of offensive cyber in Israel”, joined the company’s board of directors soon after it was founded in 2020 and remained there until 2025. Between 2020 and March 2026, Discover-Tech’s shareholders included a company linked to Sara Hamou, who has managed the corporate network of the spyware group Intellexa.

Discover-Tech appears to place advertisements using several techniques. Firstly, the company operates a platform called which interfaces with online ad vendors including Google, Yandex, Vungle (Liftoff), and Sunteng. Secondly, separately from MyDSP, it purchases ads via the ad vendors Eskimi and Comcast-owned Beeswax (Freewheel).

A large number of ads placed by Discover-Tech contain a tag pointing back to what the company refers to as a “” (also called a “getAd server”). This tag causes the ad, when rendered, to connect back to Discover-Tech, submit advertising identifiers for the user (either a cookie ID or a mobile ad ID), and automatically execute any JavaScript code returned. The NOAS server decides, apparently based on a combination of the source IP address and the advertising identifiers, whether the target is eligible to receive any JavaScript. If so, then code is returned. If not, a 0-byte response is returned. The NOAS server is a key part of Discover-Tech’s strategy, allowing Discover-Tech to avoid directly sharing malicious code, or even pointers to malicious code, with the companies who serve and display the ads.

As detailed in , Discover-Tech appeared on several lists of “certified” and “approved” ad vendors maintained by Google and the advertising industry association IAB Europe from the year 2020 until 2026. These listings helped make Discover-Tech appear to be a legitimate ad vendor and facilitate its participation in the digital advertising ecosystem at scale.

As a result of this investigation, both Google and IAB Europe removed Discover-Tech from their ad vendor registries in early October 2026. Google, which collaborated in the investigation, terminated Discover-Tech’s access to its ad exchange platforms.  Beeswax removed Discover-Tech from its ad buying platform, Vungle (Liftoff) paused Discover-Tech’s access while conducting a review, and Eskimi blocked Discover-Tech’s accounts and domains.

Report Overview: Exposing Discover-Tech’s AdFection Pipeline 

In this report we provide an overview of the different types of ad abuse facilitated by Discover-Tech, the company’s ad targeting systems and practices, as well as its partners and corporate network.

In , we show how Candiru works with Discover-Tech to conduct AdFection attacks, and describe one such attack: the targeting and infection of devices at the international media network Al Jazeera with Candiru’s mercenary spyware.

In , we examine Controlium, a Discover-Tech platform that provides a control-panel style interface enabling mercenary spyware customers to target specific users with “controlled ads.”

In , we examine links between Discover-Tech and mercenary spyware companies Candiru/Integrity Labs and Bindecy. We then outline their relationships with other mercenary surveillance companies, including advertising intelligence (ADINT) vendor Intelos, and an ADINT vendor we refer to as , which is building databases linking users’ mobile advertising identifiers to their phone numbers.

In , we analyze Discover-Tech’s malicious advertisements land. We identified a Discover-Tech server that published almost four billion ad bidding records. These records show that Discover-Tech ads were served in almost 200,000 different Android apps, iOS apps, and websites in many countries. We also highlight specific countries and government networks where Discover-Tech’s advertisements had impressions.

In , we use technical analysis to examine how Discover-Tech deploys ads, tracks users and exchanges user identifiers with other ad vendors, including with Beeswax, Yandex, and Microsoft’s ad system Xandr.

In , we present our research on Discover-Tech Ltd, its corporate network, key persons linked to the company, the origins of its MyDSP advertising technology, and its connection to the wider advertising ecosystem.

In , we summarize what is known about the mercenary surveillance firms Candiru, Bindecy, and Intelos, and we further examine their activities and corporate networks in the context of the findings presented in our report.

In , we explore how major industry organizations and ad vendors helped enable Discover-Tech’s ad operations, including Google, IAB Europe, Beeswax (FreeWheel/Comcast), Vungle (Liftoff), Eskimi, Sunteng, and Xandr (Microsoft).

In , we discuss the implications of AdFection for user security and human rights.

In , we provide recommendations to lawmakers, regulators, defenders, and the advertising industry on how to mitigate and block threats from AdFection-style attacks.

The Citizen Lab sent requests for comment to 13 companies; their responses are included in full in the ‘Correspondence with Companies’ section.

2. How Discover-Tech’s AdFection Zero-Click Works

This section provides the first public technical confirmation of a zero-click spyware attack via targeted ads in the wild: the targeting and infection of devices at the international media network Al Jazeera with mercenary spyware. We refer to this type of attack as. Using network analysis, infrastructure fingerprinting, and analysis of implant behaviour, we connect Discover-Tech’s infrastructure with the distribution of Candiru’s mercenary spyware.

What AdFection Looks Like

The instances of Candiru AdFection via Discover-Tech ads all share similar characteristics. First, Discover-Tech wins a bid, and one of their ads is pushed to a website or app that is open on a user’s device. The user may see this ad, such as in , though in some cases the ad may render in the background.

When the website or app receives the ad, it renders it, requesting JavaScript from a Discover-Tech server embedded within the ad. In most cases, the user who sees the ad is selected for targeting, and the server will JavaScript to be executed.  Nevertheless, the ad will still gather data from the user’s browser and submit it back to Discover-Tech, which can include cookies set on the webpage including the ad, as well as the device’s public IPv6 address.

Confirming the Targeting of Al Jazeera with Candiru Spyware via Discover-Tech Ads

In 2024 and 2025, international news network was targeted in a series of zero-click attacks that we link with high confidence to Candiru’s spyware delivered via Discover-Tech’s ads. At least 45 devices within Al Jazeera were targeted in these attacks.

Analysis of network logs provided to the Citizen Lab by Al Jazeera collected during the attack period provides a clear temporal signature of how the attack was executed. Infected devices first show contact with domains from Discover-Tech infrastructure, indicating an ad impression. Next, the devices show connections with a Candiru validator server. The validator server performs an initial check of the device before it is further profiled and infected. Ultimately, an infected device communicates with a Candiru Command and Control (C&C) server. This temporal signature is illustrated by .

Fingerprinting Candiru Servers

We developed a fingerprint for Candiru validator servers. Both and returned banners that matched the following regular expression on Censys.  We refer to this as :

We found hosts on Censys matching between August 2022 through July 2026, though we note that in May and June 2026, this behaviour gradually began being retired. In all, we found 305 distinct domain names on 319 IP addresses, though to save query costs we only searched one historical Censys snapshot per month. The set of 305 validator server domains we found includes ones publicly attributed to Candiru by Sekoia, as well as Recorded Future.

We also identified a separate fingerprint for the C&C servers used in the attack, . Four of the servers matched it (, insightenterprisells[.]com, , ). We could not locate a response in Internet scanning data for the other three.

Attribution of the Attack to Candiru

Al Jazeera isolated a Windows DLL file from one of the compromised devices which contains hardcoded Command & Control servers matching Fingerprint C1. The sample is available on VirusTotal.

Candiru spyware sample SHA256: 255869de85e2a171993fc5eb8a556d873a1b8966e040f6f55926f2fa2d595cc8

This sample hard-codes two C&C servers that match : and . The functionality broadly overlaps with the functionality of the Candiru chain from our 2021 report. For example:

  • Both samples use a COM hijack for persistence, though make use of different DLLs.
  • Both samples obfuscate strings using a 48-byte repeating XOR key, though the samples have different keys. Both samples also have an interesting quirk where obfuscated strings contain a “dummy” null-terminator character that is not deobfuscated (the deobfuscation with the key would be nonsensical), and is instead silently discarded. The only function of this dummy null-terminator appears to be to ensure that the right-size chunk of memory is allocated to hold the XOR-decrypted output.
  • The configuration within both samples hardcodes the same ordered list of domain names to fetch to check network connectivity: http://www.google.com and http://www.microsoft.com.

The combination of the COM persistence hijack, the use of a distinctive 48-byte repeating XOR obfuscation technique with a “dummy” null terminator, and the specific hardcoded network connectivity check leads us to conclude with high confidence that this sample is a newer version of the Candiru attack chain that we captured in 2021.

3. Exposing Discover-Tech’s Controlium: Malicious Ad Targeting Platform

This section examines Controlium, a platform that provides a control-panel style interface allowing mercenary spyware customers to target specific users with “controlled ads” that deliver malware. Discover-Tech published the full source code for Controlium’s frontend on the app’s login page, which allowed us to review and reconstruct the user interface.

Discover-Tech provides its customers with access to a platform called that appears to be specifically designed to allow them to push malicious content to individual targeted users alongside advertisements. Customers can use Controlium to select a user for infection or profiling based on their mobile advertising identifier (iOS or Android), browser identifier (MyDSP or Beeswax cookie ID), and/or IP address. Discover-Tech’s malicious ads (referred to as “controlled ads”) sometimes also contain branding of companies that are closely linked to Discover-Tech, or branding from apparently unwitting third-party companies, including Amazon and AliExpress. We have no evidence that these ads were purchased by Amazon or AliExpress.

As is standard for many web apps, the entirety of the source code for the Controlium frontend is included on the app’s login page. We visited the login page in a web browser and saved the page to disk to obtain a copy of the frontend. We modified our copy of the code to remove any communication with any external servers, and to reveal all available screens in the UI. We then opened this version in a web browser to explore the app’s user interface.  

In our analysis of Controlium, we downloaded only publicly accessible resources without circumventing any access controls. Most data associated with Controlium, such as information about Discover-Tech’s customers and their operations, is intentionally protected with an authorization token. However, we were able to obtain data on Controlium user logins from an unauthenticated API endpoint (see below: ‘Unauthenticated Endpoint’). We also assess that it would have been possible for a hacker to spoof a valid authorization (see below: ‘Authentication Vulnerability’), although we did not test this.

Attribution to Discover-Tech

We found the Controlium platform available on the following websites:

Additionally, several strings in the Controlium code directly reference Discover-Tech:

An account designated as an “admin” on the Controlium platform can configure a number of different parameters for customers of the platform. Authentication Vulnerability

While the data associated with Controlium’s customers and their operations are nominally protected with an authorization token, it appears that it would be easy for a hacker to spoof a valid token. We did not attempt to exploit this issue, as we believe doing so would have constituted unauthorized access to Discover-Tech’s systems.

The underlying issue stems from Discover-Tech’s improper use of Okta’s product. When a Controlium customer authenticates with , a JWT is returned to their browser. This token is digitally signed by , and contains information about scopes and expiry that the backend server should validate. However, Controlium ignores this token and instead passes a separate object as a token to the backend server. The object simply contains unauthenticated metadata about the user, such as their name and email address. Controlium encrypts this information with a secret key published in the Controlium platform.

Interestingly, the code to use the JWT as an authorization token was present within the Controlium platform, but was commented out in lieu of the vulnerable code.

During our analysis of the Controlium platform, we observed that the source code mentioned an endpoint called “/csv-download”, which accepted start and end date parameters.  When we sent normal HTTP GET requests to this endpoint without any password, special headers, or authentication token, we received logs showing which users had logged in to Controlium, and from which IP addresses.  We successfully exported authentication logs for 128 days and identified 120 distinct usernames logging into the Controlium instances on and . We further delve into this data in Section 4.

DARK CARTOGRAPHER: Mass-Deanonymization With Ads

We identified Discover-Tech ads that sought to exploit the well-known “WebRTC IP Leak” issue, which can potentially reveal the IP address of VPN and proxy users. The same ads also attempted to unmask the phone number (MSISDN) of mobile users who were served the impression. The MSISDN leaks exploit various issues, including widespread problems with so-called “zero-click login” technologies, which aim to facilitate frictionless authentication and purchases for users on their mobile devices.

One way “zero-click login” operates is that mobile providers select certain websites for “HTTP header enrichment,” so that when plaintext HTTP requests pass through the provider’s mobile gateway, an HTTP header (like X-MSISDN) is added to the request that provides the user’s phone number to the website. As an alternative to HTTP header enrichment, third-party services may work directly with the telco to facilitate this “zero-click login”. There appear to be widespread bugs with this allowlist matching, as well as bugs or security issues in third-party enrichment providers. While mainstream web browsers such as Chrome are moving towards blocking any non-HTTPS requests, it is likely that the app ecosystem will still embed webviews that permit non-HTTPS content.

We taxonomized the issues into five types, exploited by attackers across numerous mobile providers in more than 30 countries in North America, South America, Europe, Africa, and Asia, and disclosure to companies is in progress. Once the disclosure process is complete, we will release our subsequent report delving into technical analysis and attribution of these attacks.

Notably, ’s infrastructure links to both a mercenary adtech vendor and a U.S. government contractor. It is rare to see such direct overlaps between mercenary vendors and U.S. government or intelligence contractors. We assess that this attacker has been exploiting MSISDN leak issues since at least 2019, fronted by a variety of mercenary adtech companies. Our investigation into this threat actor is ongoing.

We found a number of Controlium users that we could not conclusively attribute to a specific company: the user primarily logged in from India, and occasionally Israel; the user exclusively logged in from Italy, primarily a static IP in Milan; the user exclusively logged in from Pakistan.

5. Uncovering Discover-Tech’s Billion-Bid Scale Ad Targeting

To understand the scope of Discover-Tech’s activity, we analyzed nearly four billion ad bidding records that were publicly exposed on a Discover-Tech website. We found that Discover-Tech ads were displayed in over 70,000 mobile apps, and over 120,000 websites between March and June 2026.

We found two world-readable Apache Druid instances running on Discover-Tech’s website . The endpoint contains bidding data for Discover-Tech’s MyDSP platform, which is connected to several upstream ad providers including Google, Yandex, Vungle, and Sunteng. The endpoint appeared to contain additional bidding data for Discover-Tech’s use of Sunteng. These instances did not contain any information about Discover-Tech’s use of Beeswax or Eskimi DSPs. Discover-Tech appeared to shut down both instances in August 2026.

There were no instances of cookie IDs, advertising IDs, or GPS coordinates recorded in the Druid data. However, the data includes IP addresses or /24s, presumably provided by SSPs, as well as city-level geolocation information. The provenance of the location data is unclear.

No Good Evidence of Legitimate Ads

We reviewed bidding data for MyDSP for four months (March through June 2026). In this period, Discover-Tech’s MyDSP bid on 3,770,286,576 impressions, and appeared to win 441,954,291 (11.7%). About 76.7% of the bids were for ad impressions in mobile apps, and 23.3% for impressions in the web browser.

The database shows a total of three advertisers, with nine total combinations between advertiser and an advertiser domain name. Most of the advertisers seem to be directly attributable to Discover-Tech itself, or to entities we consider to be linked to it, like Akedo, MyIPInfo, and Volasim’s RemindMeWhere app.

The database records that MyDSP spent approximately in this period, assuming the cost is recorded in micros of USD. The database appears to be set up to record information about the revenues and profits generated by MyDSP for each ad, including fields like , , and , but these are always set to zero except for a three-day period in June where is nonzero for impressions shown for the MyIpInfo advertiser. The database also contains fields to record conversions, though these are always set to zero. A “conversion” typically refers to a purchase, app install or other action taken by a person who was exposed to an ad. It is highly unusual for an ad vendor that not a single ad leads to such an action, although it is conceivable that the bidding records might not track and record this information.

We reviewed ads for the major advertiser on this list that could hypothetically be a real external advertiser, “AliExpress.” The ads all appear to be a generic image that says “SALE” and shows a picture of miscellaneous products from Ugreen, a Chinese consumer electronics company.

We note that the landing page of some of the AliExpress ads is an AliExpress affiliate link.

We have no evidence of a business relationship between Discover-Tech and AliExpress and/or Ugreen, and we think the generic nature of the advertising content, the lack of any revenue recorded, and the lack of any conversion data recorded suggest these ads were likely not purchased on behalf of AliExpress or Ugreen.

Normally, a DSP would aim to earn money by selling ads to entities seeking to advertise goods and services. In this case, there is no good evidence that Discover-Tech’s MyDSP is earning money in this way.

Evidence of Ads With Attacker Script Tags

The MyDSP data shows that at least 718,748,885 of the bids (about ), were to show ads that apparently contained a tag pointing to a NOAS server. We believe that the NOAS server is, generally, tasked to return some JavaScript exactly once to specific mobile ad ID and/or browser/cookie ID values, and subsequent visits return nothing until re-tasking.

We assessed whether an ad was likely to contain such a tag by searching for ads whose name included the strings “infi” (a reference to Controlium’s “Infinite FIFO” feature), “NOAS”, “ppv2”, and “pqv2”. The “ppv2” and “pqv2” strings appear to be references to a newer version of the “Infinite FIFO” feature exposed as “Authenticator Manager” in the Controlium UI. We suspect that “pqv2” is for testing and/or QA, whereas “ppv2” is for production.

MyDSP submitted bids to show these NOAS ads to users with IP addresses that geolocate to 161 countries. It is important to note that IP geolocation can be inaccurate due to the use of satellite providers, VPNs, or other reasons. 

Looking at the full bidding data, without considering whether ad auctions were won, MyDSP also made a significant number of bids (> 10 million) on ad impressions geolocated to Russia, Indonesia, United Arab Emirates, Australia, United States, Sweden, Norway, Netherlands, Germany, Malaysia, and Cuba. However, we note that the Netherlands, Germany, and United States geolocation appeared to primarily be from VPNs or server IPs in these countries.

Ads with attacker script tags were shown to users of 75,373 different Android and iOS apps and to visitors of 120,768 different websites in mobile and desktop browsers. These numbers refer to ads actually displayed to users of apps and websites rather than raw bids.

Ad Impression Data Highlights Systemic Risk

Our review of the ad bidding data indicates that Discover-Tech ads were shown on devices in national-security-sensitive networks around the world. These include the networks of various ministries of defense, armed forces, national cyber agencies, intergovernmental organizations and multilateral security organizations including NATO, and networks associated with critical infrastructure. The data also show impressions from the networks of media organizations around the world. At minimum, we assess that these ad impressions would have resulted in profiling by Discover-Tech. In some cases, the impressions could have resulted in code from Candiru or other entities running on the user’s device. 

A Discover-Tech ad impression does not in and of itself confirm targeting or infection with spyware.  However, the fact that Discover-Tech was able to bid on and show ads on these networks highlights the systemic risk posed by AdFection and the advertising ecosystem, and warrants urgent investigation to determine whether any users on these networks were infected with spyware. We also note that our visibility into Discover-Tech’s impressions is confined to the data on Discover-Tech’s MyDSP platform.  This data does include data from Beeswax and Eskimi, and covers a limited time period. This incompleteness further reinforces the need for follow-up investigation.

    6. How Discover-Tech Deploys Ads in the Browser

    In this section we show how, beyond targeting users of mobile apps, Discover-Tech deploys a range of techniques to deliver ads and track users while they browse across websites. This involves Discover-Tech running its own code in the user’s web browser, both while deploying ads to users and independently of showing them ads. We explore Discover-Tech’s “Banner Tester” tool to show how the company generates tracking tags and pixels attached to ads, including code that connects to a NOAS server, which we identified as a vector for spyware delivery. We also document how Discover-Tech engages in “ID syncing” with other ad vendors, and how it leverages IAB Europe’s “Transparency and Consent Framework” to appear GDPR-compliant, even while facilitating unwanted and malicious activity.

    An ad displayed to a website visitor consists of an image or video to be shown and a link to be clicked, but canalsocarry HTML and JavaScript code that connects to one or more domains in order to track users, ad impressions, clicks, and other activities. This code is typically referred to as an ad tag. A related concept, a so-called tracking pixel, also describes code running in the web browser that connects to third-party ad vendors. Ad vendors use additional tracking code for user ID syncing by exchanging user identifiers with each other in order to identify, profile, and target website visitors across sites and vendors.

    Our analysis of ad tags, tracking pixels, and ID syncing activities associated with Discover-Tech’s ad delivery is based on an analysis of publicly available code, browser testing and ad transactions archived by the web investigation tool urlscan. While ads displayed in mobile apps similarly carry code that connects to ad vendors, this section focuses on Discover-Tech ads displayed in the web browser.

    Discover-Tech’s Ad and Tracking Tags

    User ID Syncing with Other Ad Vendors

    Unlike apps on mobile devices, web browsers do not allow websites to access a universal device identifier. The process of “ID syncing”, often also referred to as “cookie syncing”, addresses this lack of a universal user identifier. Research shows that digital advertising firms and data brokers use sophisticated forms of ID syncing to identify, profile and target web users across vendors. They achieve this by constantly exchanging user identifiers with each other, storing them in the browser and retrieving them again while users visit different websites that embed third-party tracking code.

    We found evidence showing how Discover-Tech engages in ID syncing with Comcast’s ad system Beeswax, Yandex, and Microsoft’s ad platform Xandr.

    Discover-Tech appears to use its domain for ID syncing with Yandex. This domain is highly prevalent as a tracking domain on a large number of websites. Starting in May 2025, urlscan archived more than 10,000 records that include third-party requests to the domain , most of them occurring during visits to Russian websites.

    A recent urlscan record shows an example of a typical request chain that involves ID syncing across Discover-Tech’s domain and the following Yandex endpoint:

    The URL component “discovertechis” indicates some kind of business relationship between Discover-Tech and Yandex.

    Discover-Tech appears to use another domain, , which is associated with via DNS links and which is also highly prevalent as a tracking domain on a large number of websites, for ID syncing with Beeswax. Starting in July 2025, urlscan archived more than 10,000 records that include third-party requests to , many of them occurring during visits to popular websites including IMDb and New York Times.

    A recent urlscan record shows an example request chain that was initiated during a visit to the website of The Guardian, which involves ID syncing across Discover-Tech’s domain and Beeswax’ tracking domain . The requests contain the parameter “bee_sync_partners=dtech”, which indicates some kind of business relationship between Discover-Tech and Beeswax.

    These ID syncing activities typically take place during website visits even when a user was not served a Discover-Tech ad. We are unsure how exactly Discover-Tech uses its browser ID syncing capabilities. Generally, being able to synchronize and correlate user identities across vendors is considered a precondition for individual-level ad targeting in the web browser. The Controlium platform, as examined in , offers to upload lists of Beeswax identifiers for ad targeting in its “cTargeting” module, among mobile advertising IDs, IP addresses, and other identifiers, based on our analysis of the source code.

    We conclude that many websites make constant requests to Discover-Tech’s domains and in the background. These requests serve the purpose of ID syncing with Beeswax and Yandex, and Discover-Tech’s domains receive, in addition to user identifiers, at least the website visitor’s IP address and information about their browser and operating system.

    Discover-Tech’s Tracking Pixel

    Separately from Discover-Tech’s large-scale ID syncing on many websites, we found JavaScript code for a “tracking pixel” that was loaded during recent visits to only a few sites including , , and Discover-Tech’s corporate website, (all three archivedonurlscan).

Once loaded on a website, the code stores user identifiers associated with Discover-Tech, Beeswax, and Xandr in the user’s web browser in order to retrieve them again during subsequent visits to websites that load the same code.

    7. Discover-Tech and Its Corporate Network

    Discover-Tech has been deeply embedded and interconnected with the digital advertising industry for years. In this section, we further investigate Discover-Tech, key persons affiliated with the company, related companies, and the origins of its MyDSP advertising technology.

    Adtech with a Background in Spytech

    Discover-Tech purports to be a typical digital advertising firm, offering a so-called Demand-Side Platform (DSP), which facilitates the delivery of targeted ads. On its website, it claims to have “unrestricted access to top-ranking apps with 1+ billion daily active users” via a “worldwide ad exchange”. In addition to its DSP, Discover-Tech offers “monetization” solutions to mobile network operators and mobile device manufacturers, which we discuss further below.

    Israeli company records we reviewed link Discover-Tech’s website, , to the company Discover-Tech Ltd registered in March 2020, with Dekel Boni listed as its initial director and sole shareholder. In the two months after its incorporation, Eric Banoun, who is a major figure in the Israeli surveillance technology industry, joined Discover-Tech’s board of directors, and the shareholder base was expanded. From April 2020, the company’s shareholders included Dekel Boni, Guy Lants, Yaniv Basil, Zfanya Leib, Sergei Bartashevich, and Chaia Services Ltd, a company registered in the British Virgin Islands. Eric Banoun left the company’s board of directors in January 2025 and Chaia Services Ltd ceased to be a shareholder in March 2026. As of July 2026, Discover-Tech is directed by Dekel Boni and owned by Boni, Basil, and Lants.

    Eric Banoun co-founded the cyberespionage firm Circles, a close NSO Group affiliate, and Senpai Technologies, which is part of the Intellexa consortium. We could not access corporate registration information on Discover-Tech’s shareholder Chaia Services Ltd. However, a Haaretz investigation reported that one of Chaia’s directors was Sara Hamou. Hamou managed Intellexa’s corporate network and was sentenced to eight years in prison (pending appeal) by a Greek court for her role in the Predatorgate scandal. Eric Banoun was listed as a director of a similarly named U.S.-based company, Chaia Services Tech LLC, which was dissolved in 2025.

    Based on the links to Eric Banoun and Chaia Services Ltd., we conclude that Discover-Tech was linked to the spyware industry for almost six years, according to Israeli company records and other publicly available information.

    Discover-Tech’s other shareholders, including Dekel Boni who is now the company’s sole director, have a background in digital advertising, previously working for adtech firms like Digital Turbine and Taptica, accordingtotheirLinkedInprofiles. Boni lists himself as Discover-Tech’s CEO, Guy Lants as its “Director of Product”. Yaniv Basil lists himself as the company’s “Chief Technology Officer” between 2020 and 2023.

    Discover-Tech Mercenary Spyware Partner: Candiru/Integrity Labs

    Candiru is an Israeli-founded mercenary spyware company that draws its original name from the parasitic Candiru fish, and has operated under a wide range of names throughout the years, including Saito Tech.     Candiru: Prior Investigations, Abuses, and Discoveries

    Candiru is a mercenary spyware threat actor known by multiple names, including SOURGUM and Carmel Tsunami by Microsoft.

    First Candiru Abuse Discoveries: 2021

    On July 15, 2021, the Citizen Lab published the first report exposing Candiru. That investigation included identifying a Candiru victim and recovering a copy of Candiru’s Windows spyware. We then worked with Microsoft’s Threat Intelligence Center (MSTIC) to analyze the spyware, which led to the identification of two zero-day vulnerabilities (CVE-2021-31979 and CVE-2021-33771). We also identified over 750 websites linked to Candiru’s infection infrastructure that masqueraded as a wide range of civil society entities ranging from media organizations to Amnesty International.

    Microsoft’s own investigation into Candiru, published simultaneously with our report on July 15, 2021, identified at least 100 spyware victims across ten countries. Microsoft reported that the victims included journalists, opposition politicians, dissidents, and activists. 

    On November 16, 2021, ESET reported on a series of watering hole attacks observed in 2020 and 2021 targeting websites in the Middle East with what they described as a “strong focus on Yemen.” They attributed the attacks to Candiru.

    Further Investigations and Abuses: 2022-2025

    In 2022, the Citizen Lab again found Candiru spyware targeting victims among Catalan civil society groups in Spain. In that investigation, we identified signs of a live Candiru infection on a Catalan university network, and successfully worked with system administrators to identify the victim, isolate the device, and extract the active spyware. The targeting we observed as part of this campaign included emails masquerading as official Spanish governmental messages about COVID.

    On July 21, 2022, Avast published a report revealing that Candiru was using a Chrome zero-day exploiting WebRTC (CVE-2022-2294), and found evidence of targeting of users in multiple countries in the Middle East.

    On December 22, 2022, Meta disclosed that it disrupted around 130 Facebook and Instagram accounts used by Candiru to send infection links amongst themselves to “test phishing capabilities.”

    In the summer of 2024, during the parliamentary election campaign, Member of the European Parliament (MEP) Daniel Freund was targeted with Candiru’s mercenary spyware, according to the European Parliament’s security services. 

    On August 5, 2025, Recorded Future’s Insikt Group investigated Candiru infrastructure and identified multiple Candiru clusters linked to Hungary, Saudi Arabia, Indonesia, and Azerbaijan, among others. 

    On September 2, 2025, Sekoia published an investigation into Candiru’s spyware, highlighting how Candiru and similar companies leverage complex jurisdictional structures to avoid discovery.

    On November 3, 2021, Candiru was added to the United States Commerce Department’s Entity List for malicious cyber activities. The entity listing noted that Candiru was added because “they developed and supplied spyware to foreign governments that used this tool to maliciously target government officials, journalists, businesspeople, activists, academics, and embassy workers.” 

    Legal Actions Against Candiru and Users

    In October 2024, Daniel Freund filed a criminal complaint with the assistance of German digital rights NGO GFF against Viktor Orbán and unnamed persons over his targeting with Candiru.

    On April 30, 2025, the NGO Sentinel Alliance filed a caseagainst multiple Spanish governmental entities, NSO Group, and Candiru over the mercenary spyware attacks targeting Catalan civil society.

    Candiru’s 2025 Acquisition by Integrity Partners 

    In April 2025, Israeli media reported that U.S.-based Integrity Partners acquired the operations of Candiru for $30 million in a bid to bypass the U.S. Entity Listing. Research by Recorded Future’s Insikt Group identified Candiru as having been rebranded to “Integrity Labs”  (אינטגריטי לאבס בע~מ) in December 2024. The current status of the acquisition is unclear.

    Candiru/Integrity Labs did not respond to our request for comment within the timeline provided.

    9. Discover-Tech’s Relationship to the Digital Advertising Industry

    This section explores how major industry organizations and ad vendors helped enable Discover-Tech’s ad operations, and notes that Discover-Tech achieved “certified” and “approved” status by Google and the major advertising industry association IAB Europe.

    Our analysis indicates that Discover-Tech deployed ads via Google, Yandex, and other ad vendors including Beeswax (FreeWheel/Comcast), Vungle (Liftoff), Eskimi, and Sunteng. In addition, both Google and the advertising association IAB Europe have listed Discover-Tech as a “certified” and “approved” ad vendor since the year 2020, which helped make the company appear to be a legitimate advertising firm and facilitate its participation in the advertising ecosystem at scale.

    As a result of this investigation, both Google and IAB Europe removed Discover-Tech from their ad vendor registries in early October 2026. Google, which collaborated in the investigation, terminated Discover-Tech’s access to its ad exchange platforms. Beeswax removed Discover-Tech from its ad buying platform. Vungle (Liftoff) paused Discover-Tech’s access while conducting a review. Eskimi blocked Discover-Tech’s accounts and domains.

    The ad vendors identified in this section are distinct from mercenary spyware or ADINT vendors insofar as they are not necessarily aware of potential misuses of their infrastructure for non-advertising purposes.

The GVL contains roughly 1,000 vendors that are “registered and approved” by IAB Europe. The TCF is the basis for passing user “consent” signals for personal data processing across the digital advertising supply chain, from users to publishers to intermediaries (like SSPs, DSPs, and ad exchanges) to advertisers, including in bid requests and tracking pixels. Most ad tags and tracking pixels that connect to third-party vendors require “consent” signals, including in some jurisdictions outside Europe and the U.K. like California. Google, Xandr, and most larger ad platforms require TCF compliance. While severalstudiesfoundthat vendors are too often ignoring “consent” signals, an ad vendor that is not listed in the GVL, and thus cannot pass any signal, can hardly interface with other ad vendors in reliable ways.

    While the vendor lists maintained by Google and the IAB Europe help a company appear to be a legitimate ad vendor and are the basis to participate in the digital advertising ecosystem in a reliable way at scale, they appear to be largely based on self-attestation by vendors. They are also the basis for most of the “consent” popups shown to European web and app users every day. Discover-Tech Ltd’s inclusion in those lists potentially means that, for almost six years, hundreds of millions of Europeans were presented with a consent request that, if the recipient clicked “Agree,” could be construed as authorizing Discover-Tech to process their data under the GDPR.
