items.title: Virtual Oxide Labs: Emulating a Full Oxide Rack
items.author: tosh
items.content:
This is the bit I mentioned a moment ago. A big part of what makes our racks unique is the embedded RoT and SP in every sled. We’ve long had an construct that served as a stub for the service processor and would return the right info at the right times. But that’s simulation, not emulation. It’s always going to be happy path, and that’s just not enough fidelity for real testing cases.

As such, we built actual emulated Cortex-M7 and Cortex-M33 devices for illumos and Linux (x86 and ARM). The repo for this tool (sp-emu) is open source. Each of the two devices runs in a single thread, and (mostly) faithfully emulates the three main requirements: instructions, time, and interrupts.

From there, you can flash our Hubris firmware directly to these emulated devices, and then communicate by way of an ordinary socket. The Voxel lab can speak with these virtual devices via the Management Gateway Service (MGS) and Inter-Processor Communication Channel (IPCC). You can learn everything you want and more about these concepts in the Management Gateway Service repo and Hubris docs.

There really is no "run real microcontrollers as virtual devices with this one neat trick!" I can think of. But the real challenge of sp-emu’s job is time. Remember all of the code we’re running there is meant for silicon. Hubris schedules off a 1ms SysTick and the emulator doesn’t use wall time; as such, we had to invent a clock. That said, emulated hardware is also than the real thing. So there’s…​ well, less time per time. So instead of trying to get all temporal about it, time became instructions. For example, I give you :

In this case, we count instructions against the kernel’s own reload value and fire exceptions anywhere the single-priority design makes it safe to take it — in thread mode, interrupts unmasked. By the same token, peripheral access costs one tick of our clock (an instruction), whereas on silicon it might stall for dozens of cycles on the bus.

You may have noticed which is defined elsewhere in the code:

fn exception_entry(&mut self, vecnum: u32, bus: &mut Bus)

In short, this function models everything the hardware does on a Cortex-M core taking an exception, all the way between "exception becomes active" to the first handler instruction. here is an ARMv7-M exception number (also the vector table index for that exception’s handler). is the memory system which is used to actually push the frame and read the table.

Hubris has a non-preemptible kernel, though it schedules tasks preemptively. SVCall, PendSV, SysTick and all IRQs run at the same priority level, while faults keep a higher priority. As such, the emulator doesn’t have to nest handlers. It processes pending IRQs based on the PRIMASK, FAULTMASK, and BASEPRI settings. If one of them pended PendSV, that will perform the deferred context switch for the kernel. For more details on how it works internally, you can check this lovely bit of documentation.

There’s a lot more we can talk about here, but to sum it all up you can look at this pseudo-ish loop:

Note: yes I’m aware I said there’s no cycles then have a field named cycles. That’s the "fake it till you make it" part of emulation.

That’s the overall heartbeat of sp-emu, and it runs ad infinitum. Everything else exists to make those calls seem real.

items.title: America didn't lose its rare earth industry, it sold it
items.author: speckx
items.content:
In October 2025, Beijing imposed sweeping controls on its rare earth exports. Since then, those controls have been suspended one short reprieve at a time, in the latest instance until Nov. 10, with a broader trade truce through Jan. 10, 2027. The reprieves have repeatedly come only after American concessions, demonstrating China’s leverage in the export fight.

Yet China has constricted sales even during the truce, as buyers have few options but to take what they can get. In June, with the suspension in force, Beijing placed MP Materials and USA Rare Earth, the two companies the U.S. is counting on to build an alternative supply to China, on an export control list.

Washington’s effort to rebuild the supply chain, meanwhile, has not yet reached the scale or durability the problem requires. With up to $100 billion in loan authority specifically earmarked for critical minerals in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, the capital undoubtedly exists. What is missing is alignment of interests among the parties that would supply and benefit from it, and a political system patient enough to hold a course for the decade or more that rebuilding a supply chain takes.

This article’s authors work at the intersection of finance and national security. Between the three of us, we have watched the same on-again, off-again rhythm play out in both Chinese statecraft and U.S. budget fights. A consistent pattern plays out: Capital markets are good at financing efficient supply but are not good at financing a binary outcome, such as insurance against a monopoly state seller that can manipulate both price and availability. And subsidies alone will not close that gap. We have seen firsthand that what the U.S. government has to offer right now insufficiently incentivizes private investors, because its tools are market tools deployed in an environment of market failure. Instead, we propose a financing instrument that could clear both economic and political hurdles: a contingent convertible security that converts into ownership if Beijing weaponizes supply.

Rare Earths Are a Market Failure

The history of how we got here is well known, but worth retelling briefly. The Chinese Communist Party inherited its strategic focus on building industrial capacity from the Soviet Union. In 1964, Deng Xiaoping inspected an iron ore mine near the Mongolian border holding the world’s largest rare earth deposit. He ordered the engineers to develop steel and rare earths alike. Since then, as technologies have increasingly relied on specialized materials, the Chinese Communist Party under successive leaders has deliberately invested in and consolidated control over the rare earths industry. China refines more than 90 percent of the world’s rare earths and close to 99 percent of heavy rare earths today. It processes nearly all the heavy elements that go into precision-guided weapons and advanced chips.

When Beijing tightened export controls in October 2025, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent characterized it as “pointing a bazooka at the supply chains and industrial base of the entire free world.” Remarkably, the entire market for rare earth oxides is worth less than $10 billion. That a $10 billion market can grind to a halt trillions in global gross domestic product is the definition of a chokepoint. Beijing controls this chokepoint today by design. Decades of state policy work laid the groundwork for the Chinese Communist Party to enact an international licensing system by 2025. General Secretary Xi Jinping himself openly speaks about the importance of maintaining global dependency on China’s industrial supply chains.

Hindsight treats this as neglect, something policymakers lost sight of and let slip during the U.S.’s unipolar moment. That is a necessary, but only partial, explanation. The truth is the United States did not lose its rare earth industry due to carelessness. Private American companies willingly sold it, for reasons that made perfect economic sense at the time and still do. China bought it for reasons that were never purely economic. That mismatch explains why, after years of investment and policy attention, the dependency remains.

Until the late 1980s, the United States was the world’s leading producer and refiner of rare earths. But it was a dirty business: The Mountain Pass mine in California leaked roughly 600,000 gallons of radioactive and other waste into the Mojave. As cleanup and regulatory costs mounted and profits fell, the mine shut down in stages starting in the 1990s until it was fully idle by 2002. Meanwhile, the work moved to China, where the state subsidized unprofitable operations, tolerated pollution, and sold the processed oxides back to the U.S. at rock-bottom prices.

The same thing happened to the magnets: In 1995, General Motors sold Magnequench, its magnet unit, to a Chinese-backed consortium. By 2006, the last U.S. plant had closed, and the machine tools and equipment had been shipped to China. Economists would say this was the right move for a free market economy. Comparative advantage did what it was supposed to do, and a dirty, low-margin business left a wealthy country for a developing one. There was even a strategic rationale: Drawing China into the trading system, the wishful thinking went, would also make it a responsible stakeholder rather than a rival.

The category error was to conceive rare earths as a market, rather than recognizing it as a geostrategic industry. A market solves for the lowest cost. To be sure, Chinese producers competed on cost, and they rode a tech boom with surging demand for their product. But a state will pay almost any price to control a chokepoint, because tolerating a money-losing business pales in comparison to the geopolitical leverage that it brings. Over time, China has become less market driven, not more. Meanwhile, the U.S. continued to treat as a market what the Chinese Communist Party came to appreciate as a strategic program.

Control over the chokepoint gives Beijing a switch. When it lets the material flow, no private interest will build alternative supply chains at scale, because Chinese state-funded producers can sell at or below cost indefinitely, and no rational private investor will willingly sign up to lose money. When China cuts off the flow, the incentives reverse overnight, but capacity cannot follow overnight, because standing up the full supply chain and rebuilding the lost know-how can take a decade or longer.

This is classic market failure in which the same critical material can become worthless or priceless on command. In 2010, during a maritime dispute with Japan, Beijing reportedly halted rare earth shipments, and Tokyo quickly conceded. The short-term truces of the past year, each struck around contentious but episodic trade disputes, further entrench that market failure. Each successive loosening and tightening seems designed to keep the United States and its allies off balance and frustrate any long-term plan to reduce Beijing’s leverage.

Government Money Has to Survive Politics

If the market will not rebuild the rare earths supply chain, the government must do so.

Administrations under both parties have tried, and their attempts have run into a predictable morass of misaligned interests. The parties to government financing all want different things. Private investors want attractive returns in fat years, while having the government carry losses in lean ones. Commercial lenders want years of fully contracted offtake to guarantee interest payments, while Congress typically appropriates money for the next year. Markets want flexibility while Congress wants tight oversight and guardrails. Washington often wants to be the last (and lightest) money in, which signals to investors that the government is hedging. And cheap, open-ended financing is exactly the wrong signal to send to management teams.

The Pentagon’s latest playbook acknowledges that the market, left to its own devices, simply will not finance uneconomic redundancy. As a result, the July 2025 deal with MP Materials includes $400 million in convertible preferred stock, loans, equity warrants, a 10-year guaranteed price floor, and a 10-year offtake commitment. The deal was right for its moment, as it gets the producer going and sustains it while Beijing floods the market. But the deal blurs two different roles: In ordinary years, the government is a lender, financing capacity the market will not; in a crisis, it has insured against a geopolitical event. These two roles call for two different return profiles. Because the deal does not separate them, it puts the government in the unenviable position of simultaneously absorbing losses and inviting the charge of nationalization, all without a clear exit strategy.

Without some structure to navigate potentially painful political costs, these financing arrangements will come under pressure during budget cycles and electoral turnover. And that is simply untenable, because when it comes to the decade-plus timeline to stand up a rare earths supply chain, whatever Washington builds must outlast the administration that built it.

A Financial Instrument That Responds to Beijing’s Behavior

Our proposal is a financial instrument that aligns these interests. In financial parlance, the instrument is called a contingent convertible security, also known as a CoCo bond, issued by the producer to the government and any private lenders who wish to join, paired with guaranteed offtake at a price floor. Its form changes with two externally observable conditions: the producer’s capacity build-out and Beijing’s behavior.

Here’s how it works. In its starting form (and in quiet years), a CoCo bond is a simple loan paying interest. Two triggers change its form. The first is capacity. The producer must cross a defined capacity threshold by a fixed date. Capacity can be measured as units of output in mining, refining, or manufacturing critical minerals. Management’s immediate incentives should be tied to the build-out itself.

The second trigger is either a sustained breach of an agreed price band or an externally observed exercise of the chokepoint. This could be denial of export licenses, a bureaucratic delay beyond a specified period, or another form of “constructive denial” that materially interrupts supply to the United States or allied countries. Importantly, no part of this trigger should rely on Beijing’s confirmation, because it is not incentivized to admit to a cutoff. The trigger should be narrow enough that it cannot be declared for political convenience, but broad enough that an adversary cannot game it simply by changing the form of the restriction.

When the first trigger fires, the lender receives a pro rata share of the producer’s free cash flow, in effect, a dividend. The lender paid to build the capacity, so it shares in what that capacity earns. When both triggers fire, the lender also gains the right to convert into common equity. The conversion event does not create new capacity—the financing has already done that work—but rather matches the payoff to the risk. If lenders financed years of otherwise uneconomic capacity because a cutoff might someday make it necessary, they share in the upside if and when the cutoff comes. The cash participation matters too: In a crisis, the market may treat a price spike as temporary and event-driven and not value the equity, but the spike still flows through the producer’s cash flow, which benefits the lender either way.

Why would a producer agree to this? Because it gets something unique that the market will not otherwise provide. In effect, the producer buys a put—the price floor that carries it through Beijing’s dumping—and pays for it by selling a call—the cash share and the conversion right. It trades some of the windfall in a crisis for the protection of surviving quiet years. Either way, the taxpayer is paid for the risk actually borne, when it is borne, rather than for a risk merely feared.

Nor does the government have to finance the entire CoCo bond. Pre-vetted private co-investors, including foreign co-investors subject to Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States (CFIUS) screening, can offset government money dollar-for-dollar. Ideally, co-investors should be firms that fear a cutoff the most, such as defense contractors and automakers. Private co-investors would receive a pro rata right to offtake as a further incentive and could potentially even trade the bond with its associated offtake rights with other investors. Japan’s JARE consortium did something similar when it financed Australia’s Lynas in return for supply. Finally, private holders also give the program a constituency that outlasts any single administration.

Neither Nationalization nor Welfare

This instrument compensates for the asymmetric risk a lender (whether taxpayer or private) assumes when countering an adversary-controlled chokepoint, by providing an asymmetric reward if that chokepoint is ever exercised.

The risk here is not from a natural shortage or an ordinary price cycle, but from the Chinese Communist Party’s policy decisions. The same logic reaches other chokepoint materials such as pharmaceutical precursors. Rare earths are the clearest case and, at under $10 billion in market size, the cheapest place for the U.S. government to start. And it can start under existing authorities. For example, the Pentagon has leaned on Title III of the Defense Production Act for its recent mineral deals involving equity. The Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital can lend, but its equity authority remains unclear. The Senate is currently revising the National Defense Authorization Act for 2027 to clarify those authorities. Its language should cover instruments like this CoCo bond.

Our CoCo bond proposal does not replace stockpiles, price floors, or offtake agreements. These instruments solve significant but different problems. Stockpiles buy time in a crisis, price floors protect producers against predatory pricing, and offtake agreements guarantee demand. The CoCo bond, in contrast, distributes risk and reward to investors in a binary, geopolitical event outside the producer’s control. It also enables the government to lend as a portfolio—some developers will fail, but the winners, and any crisis, can carry the portfolio as a whole. And it may have some deterrent effect as well: If this instrument makes capacity more likely to get built, and that prospect enters Beijing’s risk calculus, so much the better.

Economically, the conversion right works like the equity warrants the Pentagon took in MP Materials. The difference lies in the quiet years, when under this structure the government holds no equity. Outright equity stakes invite the charge of nationalization; cheap financing with no upside smacks of corporate welfare. We believe a structure that is intentionally designed to avoid both at the outset—but flexible enough to change form in response to an adversary’s actions, not domestic political developments—has the best chance of surviving enough political cycles to complete a decade-plus build-out.

Translating this concept into reality raises important implementation questions about statutory authority, precise trigger definitions, CFIUS integration, and corporate governance. We offer the CoCo bond model to stimulate discussions around aligning interests in a market failure and national security context, and we invite the legal, policy, and financial communities to help refine the “plumbing” necessary to make asymmetric financing a workable pillar of U.S. statecraft.

A market will always sell a chokepoint to whoever runs it cheapest, and by market logic, it would be the right thing to do. Subsidies alone cannot win it back, because they only affect price; Beijing prices for geopolitical leverage, not profit. Neutralizing a chokepoint created through market failure requires capital willing to absorb years of subpar returns or even losses against an extraordinary geopolitical crisis. In quiet years, the government should earn like a lender, with the price floor protecting against Beijing’s dumping. When capacity is built, it should share in what it financed. And if Beijing ever reaches for the switch, the taxpayers and private investors who paid to insure against that moment should participate in the value their capital created. The risk is asymmetric. The financing should be too.

items.title: Containment and monitoring failures are to blame for AI hacking reports: experts
items.author: latexr
items.content:
SANS Lee says, “That’s where the traceability for both liability and insurance comes into play, because if one of these agents is detected, and they’re able to trace it back to the person that initiated it, liability’s going to kick in and say, ‘Hey, you, you broke the law, ergo, we need to prosecute.’”

What security leaders should do now

Even as evidence mounts that frontier labs are not implementing sound cybersecurity practices, and the debate over liability remains unsolved, CISOs and other security leaders can take steps to protect themselves from AI model misfires.

First, when it comes to assessing tools based on frontier lab models, “I would always get an external entity to help with that,” McGraw says. “AI is extremely powerful and extremely useful, but it comes with very serious grown-up risks that do impact the enterprise. Identify those risks, put in the right controls, make sure that AI adoption is not just arbitrary and willy-nilly and all over the enterprise, but has some centralized authority that is looking at the problem, and then get ready for the next big thing, which is swarms of agents.”

Introducing Design Creativity Bench, a new benchmark evaluating AI models’ creativity on UI design tasks.

Despite rapid advances in their ability to generate functional websites and product UIs, leading AI models still struggle to make creative design decisions.

We evaluated 16 frontier models across 80 open-ended UI tasks, each adapted to two distinct product domains alongside human designer references.

Existing UI benchmarks often measure a single output quality metric. Instead, we measure three dimensions of design creativity:

  • – Originality: How distinct a model's designs are from other models' outputs for the same brief.
  • – Creative Range: How much a model adapts its design decisions when the product domain changes.
  • – Appropriateness: How well the generated UI satisfies the functional requirements of the brief.

The results reveal a substantial gap in overall creativity: The best model, GPT-6 Astra, scores 65.5 against a human reference of 92.3.

items.title: Better HTTP/1 connection reuse in Go 1.27
items.author: allddd
items.content:
Take a look at the following function:

func getStatus(url string) (int, error) {
    resp, err := http.Get(url)
    if err != nil {
        return 0, err
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    return resp.StatusCode, nil
}

It sends a request to and returns the HTTP status code.

Using HTTP/1 (), calling this function 100 times against index.golang.org takes ~710 milliseconds on Go 1.26 on my machine. On Go 1.27, the same program takes ~150 milliseconds.

That is almost 5 times faster! How is such a drastic performance difference possible?

The cost of establishing HTTP connections

To understand the difference, consider what happens on the network when we make an HTTP request.

Go’s package supports HTTP/1.0, HTTP/1.1, and HTTP/2. All three run over TCP, and usually over TLS when talking to HTTPS endpoints. Making a request over a new connection looks something like this:

  1. : the client sends a packet, the server replies with , and the client replies with . Because the client can send the first TLS message alongside that final , establishing the TCP connection takes 1 round-trip time (RTT).
  2. : next, a TLS handshake exchanges encryption keys and verifies the server’s identity; using TLS 1.2, this takes 2 RTT.
  3. : with the keys exchanged, HTTP requests can finally be sent after a total of 3 RTT.

These round trips (plus some CPU time spent on TLS handshakes) add up quickly. In cross-region communications, one-way latencies often reach or exceed the 50 ms (100 ms RTT) shown in the diagram above. Compared to the 300 ms spent just setting up the connection, the HTTP request itself can be cheap to serve, taking only a little over 1 RTT when bandwidth is plentiful or the HTTP response is small.

Even in more favorable conditions, opening a new connection can still be expensive. Our opening benchmark queries index.golang.org, which is distributed worldwide and supports TLS 1.3. This means that latency is relatively low, and the TLS handshake can actually finish in just 1 RTT. Even so, the performance difference is still very noticeable.

To avoid paying this setup cost on every request, HTTP clients and servers try to reuse existing connections across multiple requests when possible. The mechanics of this differ based on the HTTP version:

  • : while not part of the official specification, clients and servers often opt into connection reuse by sending a header. Reuse continues until either endpoint omits the header or sends a header.
  • : connections are persistent by default, and can be reused for subsequent requests and responses unless either side declares otherwise by sending a header.
  • : multiple requests and responses can be multiplexed over a single TCP connection.

When connection reuse fails

In HTTP/1 (both HTTP/1.0 and HTTP/1.1), multiple requests and responses on the same connection are sent sequentially on the wire. If two requests are sent to index.golang.org over the same TCP connection, the responses arrive as a single stream of bytes:

As shown in the diagram, reads and parses the status line and headers from the byte stream to populate , then returns immediately. The response body remains unread on the connection and is consumed only as the caller reads from .

Because responses are sent back-to-back on the same stream, can only find the start of the next response after the current response body has been read to the very end (as determined by the or header).

Now look back at our example program, where we never read :

func getStatus(url string) (int, error) {
    resp, err := http.Get(url)
    if err != nil {
        return 0, err
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    return resp.StatusCode, nil
}

Through Go 1.26, when is called, sees that there is still an unread response body. Realizing that it cannot reuse the connection, it abandons the existing connection and creates new connections for its next requests, causing it to repeatedly incur the cost of establishing new connections.

(HTTP/2 does not have this problem. Because it multiplexes streams of frames over a single connection rather than sending responses strictly back-to-back, an unread response body on one stream does not block other requests from sharing the connection.)

Where failed connection reuse hurts

This subtlety of HTTP/1 connection reuse can cause silent performance degradation in seemingly innocuous code.

As in our opening example, a client might only care about an API response’s status code. However, the API endpoint it is talking to might send bodies that provide more detailed but ultimately unused information, such as {"success": true, "message": "update processed"}. This will unfortunately cause connection reuse to fail.

Even programs that do read the response body can run into this issue if they stop just short of the end of the body. For example, stops reading as soon as it sees the closing of a JSON object. If a server sends a JSON response terminated with a newline, decoding the JSON object will leave the newline still unread. The connection cannot be reused for a new request until that newline is consumed. Thus, a healthy connection might end up being abandoned, even though it was only a single byte away from being reusable.

The unread body problem has been a long-standing sharp edge. Over the years, many Go developers came up with their own workarounds. Most commonly, this is done by draining the response body prior to closing it:

func getStatus(url string) (int, error) {
    resp, err := http.Get(url)
    if err != nil {
        return 0, err
    }
    drainAndCloseBody(resp.Body)
    return resp.StatusCode, nil
}

func drainAndCloseBody(body io.ReadCloser) {
    io.Copy(io.Discard, body) // Drain the response body before closing it.
    body.Close()
}

While this works for small responses, if the unread body is large, establishing a new TCP connection can be faster than downloading and discarding the rest of the body. A better approach is to cap the number of bytes we are willing to drain:

func drainAndCloseBody(body io.ReadCloser) {
    io.CopyN(io.Discard, body, 256<<10) // Only drain up to 256 KB.
    body.Close()
}

However, a server might send a response body that trickles in slowly, so we also need to cap the time we spend draining:

func drainAndCloseBody(body io.ReadCloser) {
    drainDone := make(chan struct{}, 1)
    go func() {
        io.CopyN(io.Discard, body, 256<<10) // Only drain up to 256 KB.
        drainDone <- struct{}{}
    }()
    // Only spend at most 50 ms trying to drain the response body.
    select {
    case <-drainDone:
    case <-time.After(50 * time.Millisecond):
        // If we reach the 50 ms timeout, body.Close will run and interrupt the
        // io.CopyN, preventing goroutine leaks.
    }
    body.Close()
}

Of course, we also do not want to block for up to 50 milliseconds when closing a response body. Instead, we can drain the body asynchronously in the background and let it race against subsequent requests:

func drainAndCloseBody(body io.ReadCloser) {
    drainDone := make(chan struct{}, 1)
    go func() {
        io.CopyN(io.Discard, body, 256<<10) // Only drain up to 256 KB.
        drainDone <- struct{}{}
    }()
    go func() {
        // Only spend at most 50 ms trying to drain the response body.
        select {
        case <-drainDone:
            // If the drain can finish before a new request is sent, the
            // connection will be reused; otherwise, a new connection is
            // created, and the current connection will be put in a pool of
            // idle connections, potentially being reused for another future
            // request.
        case <-time.After(50 * time.Millisecond):
            // If we reach the 50 ms timeout, body.Close will run and interrupt
            // the io.CopyN, preventing goroutine leaks.
        }
        body.Close()
    }()
}

As we can see, draining response bodies safely is surprisingly tricky and cumbersome. Worse, as the practice of draining response bodies spread, some nuances were often lost. This has led to misunderstandings such as attempting to drain response bodies for HTTP/2 connections, when doing so is unnecessary.

The current state and conclusion

Starting in Go 1.27, automatically does everything we have implemented in the code above: it will asynchronously drain an unread HTTP/1 response body for up to 50 ms or 256 KB. It also implements additional optimizations; for example, when a response contains the header, draining the body is guaranteed to be wasted work, and it therefore skips doing so. Note that this behavior might evolve in future versions of Go, as other possible enhancements become apparent.

As a general best practice, we now recommend that users simply close their HTTP bodies once they no longer need them, like in our original example:

func getStatus(url string) (int, error) {
    resp, err := http.Get(url)
    if err != nil {
        return 0, err
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    return resp.StatusCode, nil
}

Go is all about simplicity. Let your code stay clean and simple, and let deal with the complexities on your behalf.

items.title: ICE Planning $100M 'Nightmare' Domestic Spy Program
items.author: bhrlady
items.content:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement is fast-tracking a $100 million domestic surveillance program to put 142 intelligence agents in more than two dozen cities and the District of Columbia, in what contracting and surveillance experts said would be a significant expansion of the agency’s ability to reach into private lives.

The new program is called the Enforcement and Removal Operations Overwatch and National Security Enforcement, or ERO ONE, described in documents posted last month on federal procurement websites.

Under the program, agents would analyze classified and unclassified information to identify “trends, patterns, relationships, threats, and intelligence gaps,” and provide ICE with briefings for Enforcement and Removal Operation missions, according to a statement of work published on September 18. A forecasting document published a week earlier said that the solicitation will likely be released on December 10. Intelligence contracting experts said the timeline suggests ICE will award the contract around February.

“It looks dangerously like the construction of an internal spying agency,” said Jay Stanley, senior policy analyst with the American Civil Liberties Union’s Speech, Privacy, and Technology Project, who has written extensively on immigration agencies’ mass surveillance. “It’s a nightmare in the making.”

It’s also a weapon that the government will likely use against not only undocumented immigrants, but everyone else, too. That includes political enemies, intelligence experts said. Speaking with the on Monday as news broke that the Trump regime had raided progressive Minnesota Rep. Ilhan Omar’s D.C. home, former military intelligence analyst Michael Wriston said that “you’d expect to see more of this” under ERO ONE.

“Not just necessarily sitting members of Congress, but anyone, and especially members of the immigrant community,” Wriston said. “No one is safe. No one.”

THE PLAN DOES NOT SPECIFY WHAT OR WHOM ICE is looking for with this increased spying capability. But one of the components that caused former intelligence contractors’ concern was that ERO ONE agents will analyze both classified and nonclassified information to produce “network, link and relationship” analyses. That type of analysis involves researching not only a target, but also every other person to whom they’re connected, including household members, family members, friends, acquaintances, or the person with whom they carpool to work.

According to the statement of work, contractors will be tasked with conducting analytical research “to identify and assess relationships among individuals, organizations, locations, events, activities, data points, and other entities.” They will review information to identify “known, reported, or potential relationships; recurring patterns; organizational structures; associations; areas of convergence; temporal or geographic connections; and other linkages relevant to the assigned intelligence requirement.” Contractors will then “evaluate the significance and reliability” of the relationships and “prepare link charts, network diagrams, timelines, analytical summaries, written assessments, or other related products” for ICE to use.

Military intelligence agents compile the same type of research, Wriston said. He knows because he did that job.

“We’ve seen this time and time again. It’s the imperial boomerang,” said Wriston, who is also a data journalist and the founder of ICE watchdog group Project Salt Box, where he reported on ERO ONE the day the first document went live and has written about it since. “These are the kinds of things that happened in Afghanistan, Iraq, Yemen, Syria, for years. Now that methodology is being brought into the ICE space.”

Federal documents likewise do not detail the specific sources of information agents will analyze, only that all agents must possess previously awarded active top secret clearance, with eligibility to access Sensitive Compartmented Information. That’s a type of information that must be accessed through certain formal control systems managed by the Director of National Intelligence, a position held by Trump ally Jay Clayton. The agents will not make any decisions about what to do with the information they compile.

Wriston said that except for the fact that ICE officials are trying to make immigration a matter of national security, it’s unclear why they need this program when they already have the Homeland Security Investigations unit, which conducted the raid on Omar’s house, to research targets. His immediate worry, he said, is that the program will make it easier for the government to find terrified immigrants hiding at home because they think they’ll be safe there.

ICE PLANS TO SEND THE 142 AGENTS, plus two project managers, to locations in Atlanta, Boston, Buffalo, Chicago, Dallas, D.C., Denver, Detroit, El Paso, Harlingen (Texas), Houston, Laguna Niguel (California), Los Angeles, Miami, New Orleans, New York, Newark, Philadelphia, Phoenix, Salt Lake City, San Antonio, San Diego, San Francisco, Seattle, St. Paul, and Williston (Vermont), according to the statement of work.

Details in the document, and the rapid timeline, show that the Trump administration intends to use the program immediately, said Brian Murphy, a government contractor who worked for 25 years with ICE parent agency DHS. It’s rare for the government to only want workers with top secret clearance, he said.

“I’ve only seen it when there is an imminent need to work on something right now,” he told the . “Trump has two years in office. He can’t wait … they want to get rolling on this immediately.”

The program description is so broad that Murphy said he thinks the goal goes beyond targeting immigrants. “I think it’s darker than that,” because the agency could use the intelligence to attack people with identities and views the Trump regime doesn’t like. “The question for DHS is, what is the threat they’re trying to go after?”

The federal government can easily change who qualifies as a threat and produce data that backs up the reasoning, Murphy said, and used as an example annual Homeland Threat Assessments. In 2020, Secretary of Homeland Security Chad Wolf identified white supremacist extremists as “the most persistent and lethal threat in the Homeland.” But by last year, that threat had disappeared from the report, except to appear once in a glossary of terms. The rest of the report focused heavily on Trump administration priorities as national security threats, including immigrants crossing the border with Mexico and transnational criminal organizations.

In addition, the murders of Renee Good and Alex Pretti have shown how the government views protesters against ICE abductions as an abiding threat. In a national security directive known as NSPM-7, President Trump identified anti-fascist protesters as domestic terrorists and proposed an architecture to disrupt and counter dissent.

“If you want to draw a narrative that the real threat to America is whatever you want it to be, you can very easily do that. You just stop gathering intel on militias,” Murphy said. “It’s like any other police state. If you ask it to find something to make my opponents the enemy, well, you can do that.”

Legal liability should be a major concern for anyone who bids on the ERO ONE contract, Murphy said, because it’s unclear whether the information they’d be charged with accessing had been gathered legally. He added, “It’s very, very concerning that they’re fast-tracking this.”

ICE already knows its potential bidders for ERO ONE, said Diana Brozi, the procurement specialist listed on the document. She told the it was unlikely the agency would hold an industry day and declined to provide further information.

DHS did not respond to a request for information or comment on the claim that the program could be used to spy on political enemies.

items.title: Submarine cable resilience
items.author: speckx
items.content:
The Matsu Islands are an archipelago of 36 islands in the East China Sea, alongside the southeastern coast of mainland China. The islands have been administered since 1949 by Taiwan, part of a larger set of outlying islands administered by Taiwan, which includes the Kinmen and Penghu Islands, which all lie in the Taiwan Strait.

The Matsu Islands are connected to Taiwan’s main island by two submarine cables — Taima No.2, Taima No.3, and soon Taima No.4. The Taiwan Strait is a shallow body of water, with an average depth of 70m. The submarine cables that lie on this seafloor are vulnerable to damage from ship-based activity, like being snagged by fishing equipment or anchors. But these particular cables have been remarkably unlucky. Between 2018 and 2022, the submarine cables between Taiwan and the Matsu Islands were cut 27 times, and there have been four major outages in the three years from 2023 to 2025.

That’s not the only location where submarine cables have suffered many faults. The Baltic Sea is a shallow sea that has a dozen or so submarine communications cables, and undersea electricity and gas pipelines. There have been 11 disruptions to these submarine systems since 2023. Again, a very unlucky track record.

There are an estimated total of 1.5Mkilometres of subsea communications cables, used by 607 in-service submarine cable systems (Figure 1) that are critical to the world’s telecommunications services. If they are put out of service for any reason, our satellite systems simply could not replace them. In such a catastrophic scenario, some communities would be totally isolated, with severe logistical and economic ramifications.

We regard this collection of submarine cable systems as critical infrastructure for global communication services, and we take care to make them as resilient as possible. Modern warfare can deliberately disrupt communications systems, which adds another source of potential damage to the list of geological and accidental risks facing subsea cables.

On the night of 4 August 1914, days after Britain declared war against Germany, the British cable ship HMTS Alert sailed from Dover into the English Channel. The vessel dragged grappling hooks along the seabed, hauled up five German transatlantic and European telegraph cables, and cut them. This severed Germany’s direct, secure submarine cable links to the Americas, Africa, Spain, and the rest of Europe. Germany was forced to rely on wireless radio transmissions, where British intelligence could readily eavesdrop. If the German cryptography used to protect these wireless communications was broken, then it allowed the British to track military movements and capture critical messages, such as the Zimmermann Telegram.

This same action to deliberately sever undersea cables was repeated by the British in September 1939, cutting German cables to Lisbon and New York.

These thin polyester-coated cables at the bottom of the ocean are vulnerable, including to:

  • Geology in the form of submarine earthquakes or landslips
  • Being snagged by dragging ship anchors or fishing equipment along the seafloor
  • Deliberate attacks on the cables with grapnels and cutting equipment

How can cables defend against such risks? The inner core of the fibre optic cables and its copper conductor sheath can be wrapped in additional layers of steel cable jacketing as a form of armour (Figure 2). This is mostly used to reduce its vulnerability to shipping accidents.

Figure 2 is somewhat misleading. What is depicted here is a cross-section of submarine cable used in the segments of the cable that lead to the surface cable station. The cable segments that are laid on the deep-sea floor use just the inner components: Optical fibre and a single thin steel thread wrapped in a silicone gel, surrounded by a copper sheath (used to power the cable repeaters), and wrapped in polyethylene. There are no external armour elements. These deep-sea cable segments are around 20mm in diameter, or the size of a garden hose.

The cable surfaces at a cable landing station. These landing stations are typically plain, secured facilities with reliable power. The preferred location is a coastal point with a low volume of fishing or other maritime traffic, and a steep rise from the deep-sea floor. Cables are at their greatest risk from coastal shipping activity, so the shorter the distance from the deep-sea floor to the cable station on dry land, the better.

Many jurisdictions also declare ‘Cable Protection Zones’ as a warning to marine vessel operators that there are cables on the seafloor in this area, and ships should refrain from fishing activity and anchoring in these areas.

Cable routing is also important in terms of resilience. There are several objectives in a cable route, and not all of them can be optimized at the same time.

The cable route should be as short as possible, as additional cable length raises capital costs and increases end-to-end signal delay.

Cables should avoid areas of active geological activity where possible, such as tectonic plate boundaries and mid-plate rifts. Deeper is better, but within reason. Cables on the floor of a deep ocean section are less vulnerable to shipping activity and hostile efforts to disrupt the cable, but with extreme depths it’s more challenging to locate and raise the cable when undertaking a repair. 

Sometimes there are geographic ‘choke points’ through which many cables are routed. The Bab al-Mandab Strait is not just a choke point for surface vessels passing between the Indian Ocean and the Red Sea, but it is also the conduit through which 16 cables pass (Figure 4). In September 2025, several cables were severed in the Bab al-Mandab Strait, disrupting an estimated 25% of cable capacity between Asia, Europe, and the Middle East. Houthi-controlled waters remain effectively ungovernable for cable protection.

There is also the Singapore Strait, a major junction for 35 cable systems (Figure 5). This is a shallow water strait that also hosts a significant volume of surface shipping.

Further north, between Taiwan and the Philippines is the Luzon Strait, where 18 cables pass (Figure 6). This was the location of an earthquake and a subsequent set of submarine landslides in December 2006 that not only severed all the cables running through this strait, but also buried many of them under deep layers of sediment. It took 11 repair vessels 49 days to bring all the cable systems back into operation.

The Black Sea is an area with geopolitical risk and regulatory gaps. While mine risk is confirmed, no cable faults have been directly documented in the war in Ukraine. Russia’s continued presence and the conflict make this region functionally inaccessible for routine cable maintenance.

Geopolitics also plays a role in cable routing. Cable owners will prefer to avoid routes through politically unstable territorial waters if suitable alternative routes exist. There are also political considerations. If a cable lands in US territory, then the cable is subject to several Federal Communications Commission (FCC) constraints, including banning equipment or services from companies the FCC see as a threat to US national security. The FCC has also refused to permit the landing of a cable on US territory if the cable also lands in a territory that the US deems to be a foreign adversary.

Land routes are avoided in general, but there are some circumstances where a land route is the preferred option. Connectivity between Asia and Europe would normally run through the Bab al-Mandab Strait, landing in Egypt in the Gulf of Suez, then overland through Egypt to get to the Mediterranean Sea. There is an alternative route through the Persian Gulf, Iraq and Türkiye, although this entails a segment that transits the Strait of Hormuz, or a second overland segment through Oman and the United Arab Emirates.

Around 200 submarine cable faults are reported worldwide each year, a figure that the International Cable Protection Committee notes has stayed broadly steady in recent years even as the total cable inventory increases. The cables themselves are remarkably reliable. It is the maritime traffic above them that is the cause of most of the problems. 86% of cable faults are likely due to fishing activity or anchoring, and fishing activity is around twice as prevalent as anchoring incidents.

Geological events, such as submarine landslides and seabed movement, account for about 7% of cable faults, cable abrasion for 4%, and component failure (in repeaters) for only 4%.

With the high correlation of faults and maritime activity, it is not surprising that just under one half of cable faults occur in territorial waters, and most of the remainder occur in exclusive economic zones. Just 2% occur on the high seas. Cables are most vulnerable close to shore, in shallow water, where fishing is concentrated, where ships anchor, and where the cable must come ashore at a landing station alongside every other cable serving that coast. The deep ocean, where there is little seabed fishing activity and few ships anchoring, is the safest location for a cable.

National jurisdictions do not stop at the low tide mark of a territory, they extend out into the sea and the seafloor. The 1982 United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (PDF) defined sovereign territorial waters as a 12-mile zone extending out from an economy’s coast. Every coastal economy has exclusive rights to the oil, gas, and other resources in the seabed up to 200 nautical miles from shore or to the outer edge of the continental margin, whichever is the further, subject to an overall limit of 350 nautical miles (650km) from the coast or 100 nautical miles (185km) beyond the 2,500-metre isobath (a line connecting equal points of water depth).

What does this mean for submarine cables? From the point where the cable enters territorial waters, any physical activity related to the cable requires the permission of the authorities. All cable construction and repair operations carried out in these sovereign areas also require the permission of the economy that has exclusive rights to the sea and seafloor.

Locating a cable break is straightforward. An optical pulse will be reflected at the point of a cable break, which can provide the distance to the fault from the start of the cable with considerable precision. At that point, it becomes a marine operation.

A specialist cable repair ship must be engaged, which, in turn, must obtain the relevant government’s permission to work at the location of the cable fault (don’t forget that only 2% of outages occur in international waters). Once at the break location, the repair vessel drags a grapnel along the seabed to hook the cable, cuts it, recovers one end, buoys it off, then recovers the other end. A new section is spliced into the cable aboard the ship in a jointing cabin, the fibre fusion-spliced and tested, the joint rebuilt and sealed against pressure, and the repaired cable laid back down with enough slack to reach the seabed.

The cost of a repair can vary greatly, depending on the location and depth of the fault, the nature of the contracted arrangements for cable repair, the amount of time the cable operator is willing to wait for a repair vessel and crew, and the weather. USD 500k to USD 1M is a representative cost of a single cable repair.

While the number of cables has grown, the time taken to obtain permission to operate repairs in territorial waters has generally increased. Industry data indicates repair response times have more than doubled over the past decade, and the longest single repair recorded in 2023 took 947 days, many of which were spent waiting for permission to undertake the repair.

There is also the issue of repair vessels. The industry has roughly 60 ships capable of repairing a submarine cable, operated under maintenance agreements that pool the cost of running this fleet across cable owners in each geographic region. These collective Submarine Cable Maintenance and Repair Agreements are used in the Atlantic Ocean, the North American Western Coastal region, the Mediterranean, South East Asia and the Indian Ocean, and Yokohama in the North Pacific (Figure 7).

Analysis by TeleGeography and Infra-Analytics has found that around two-thirds of cable maintenance vessels will reach the end of their service lives by 2040, while total cable kilometres are projected to grow by about 48% over the same period. Closing that gap would take USD 3B and require fifteen replacement ships plus five additional vessels simply to hold current service levels as the submarine cable network expands. The immediate problem is that nobody obviously owns this bill. Cable maintenance is funded through shared agreements that have been optimized for decades to be as cheap as possible, which worked when the fleet was young and is precisely the wrong structure for financing a fleet renewal.

This is the core of the cable resilience problem. Adding cable routes is comparatively easy, because today’s hyperscale cloud companies fund much of the new construction themselves and have strong commercial reasons to do so. However, no individual cable is so critical that it can sustain a business case to operate a dedicated repair fleet. The industry uses pooled resources, which suffer from under-investment.

Investigating cable outages

A rundown of recent cable outages includes:

  • Subsea cables were damaged in October 2023 by the anchor of the Hong Kong-flagged Newnew Polar Bear operating in the Baltic Sea.
  • Three cables in the Red Sea were cut in February 2024 by the drifting Rubymar vessel after it was struck by a missile.
  • The C-Lion1 and the BCS East-West Interlink cables were cut in the Baltic Sea in November 2024 with the Chinese bulk carrier Yi Peng 3 nearby.
  • Four cables were damaged in December 2024, with anchor drag marks on the Baltic seabed and the Cook Islands-registered tanker Eagle S detained.
  • Three major cables, including SEA-ME-WE 4 and IMEWE, were cut in the Red Sea in September 2025.
  • Finland and Estonia lost connections again in December 2025, with anchor drag confirmed by March 2026 on Baltic cables.
  • In August 2026, the Indigo West and Indigo Central cables off Perth were damaged, with a UAE-managed tanker under investigation by Australian Federal Police.

The outcomes are much less uniform than this list suggests. Swedish authorities found no conclusive evidence of wrongdoing in the Yi Peng 3 case and ruled the January 2025 Latvia-to-Gotland damage accidental. A Finnish court dismissed the case against the Eagle S captain in October 2025. United States and European officials concluded that several of the Baltic incidents were accidental. The captain of the Hong Tai 58 was convicted in Taiwan and sentenced to three years over the Taiwan to Penghu No. 3 cable, and the Newnew Polar Bear captain faced criminal damage charges in Hong Kong. The April 2026 Matsu fault turned out to have been caused by the wreck of a stranded fishing boat shifting onto the cable.

Anchor dragging is a common occurrence, particularly among poorly maintained merchant vessels in bad weather, accounting for a large share of ordinary faults every year. This may explain why investigators keep reaching inconclusive findings in good faith.

Who is responsible for cable resilience?

Cable systems have changed in recent decades.

The old telephone system regarded each cable as a self-contained system. The cable owner was responsible for its own resilience, independent of any other cables that may exist on similar routes. The telephone’s data carriage system typically used a ring architecture, where any outage in the ring caused the traffic to flow along the other half of the ring. If the ring used diverse paths, then any individual outage in the ring could be repaired immediately.

However, the implication of this design was that the actual capacity of the system was double the usable capacity. The cost of using such a cable reflected this 50% carriage efficiency.

In their search for cheaper services, Internet Service Providers (ISPs) wanted to purchase non-backed-up cable capacity, at a price that reflected this greater efficiency of cable use. They purchased this cheaper form of cable capacity on multiple cable systems. Individual outages caused a break in that cable’s service, but the ISP could reroute their traffic to use capacity that had been purchased on other cable systems which were not affected by the outage. For Internet traffic, this failover function is readily achieved in the routing system.

The overall outcome was that the responsibility for resilience shifted from the individual cable operator to the network operator. Cable outages would still cause a drop in available capacity. But as most Internet traffic is elastic, the drop in capacity would cause a drop in performance but not cause a complete shutdown.

Resilience and critical infrastructure considerations

Submarine cable systems are built by private consortia, repaired by private contracts that collectively fund a commercial repair fleet, regulated by coastal states individually, and governed internationally by international conventions drafted long before the Internet existed.

It would be good if permissions to repair submarine cables were granted in a streamlined manner so that repairs were not stalled for months awaiting a government’s approval to operate in their waters. It would be even better if emergency procedures were agreed in advance rather than negotiated during an outage.

Collectively, the industry needs to invest in repair capacity to upgrade an ageing repair fleet. Who undertakes this investment and how the repair capability is managed as a common asset is proving to be a difficult issue. In the worst case, it will be back to every cable for itself, and the inevitable outcome of higher costs and potentially slower repairs.

Geographic choke points will persist, geology will not stop, extreme weather and changing sediment conditions will continue to pose a threat to these cables. Route diversity is an effective response to these challenges, but economic clustering works against cable route diversity. Each cable would like to run through the shortest and cheapest route, and no cable operator is specifically motivated to spend additional sums to take a diverse route to the other existing cables.

None of this is technologically difficult, but it can be institutionally and economically difficult, which is harder.

The telephone company consortium model that funded and operated almost all the world’s subsea cables 30 years ago has come to an end. The service life of the entire inventory of cables and service vessels that they operated is also coming to an end.

Approximately a quarter of the world’s current subsea cable kilometres are projected to be decommissioned and retired by 2030. This massive retirement of capacity amounts to 845,000 kilometres of subsea fibre-optic cables at the end-of-life cycle for submarine infrastructure laid during the massive Internet boom of the late 1990s and early 2000s. Specifically, TAT-8 and TAT-14 in the Atlantic Ocean are being decommissioned, SEA-ME-WE-3, linking Europe and Asia, has been retired, and Japan-US and China-US have ended operations. In addition, more than half of the current repair vessel fleet will have reached their retirement point by 2040.

In their place are cable projects that are either fully funded or partially funded by the current US digital giants. This raises sovereign risk eyebrows in many economies, where the only communications conduits for an economy are owned and operated by a foreign entity. It also raises the question of sovereign control over the submarine repair vessel fleet and the existing maintenance pooling arrangements through submarine cable maintenance zones.

By 2028, Google will own the largest set of cables, measured by kilometres, in the Pacific, Atlantic and Indian Oceans, and based on current plans it will have more than 50% of the entire cable inventory under its control in the Indo-Pacific region. Similar centralization scenarios are playing out in the Atlantic Ocean as well. At this point, the sovereign risk eyebrows should be hitting the ceiling, as such a dominant position gives this single company unilateral control over the maintenance arrangements and associated repair vessel operations for the entire world’s communications network.

This is a serious issue for us, both as individuals and societally as we try to preserve the integrity and utility of our common communications infrastructure. The stability and productivity of our societies rely on our ability to communicate with each other seamlessly, efficiently and privately.

Passing the investment and operational costs of the public telecommunications services from public to private hands in the latter part of the 20th century was seen as a smart move. The move used private finance to fund the reinvigoration of national telecommunications infrastructure as it shifted from time-based voice switching to a far larger packet switching architecture to support computer-mediated communications and service provision.

However, we may see more uncomfortable outcomes looming in the near future. It was thought that the discipline of competition would rein in the potential abuses by private operators of the privileged position of operating a public communications service. That is not what happened.

Not only are public telecommunications systems now largely in private hands, but we are also seeing consolidation of the global telecommunications system to a few private entities, with no competition. Their accountability is not to the public or users of the service. Their accountability is to their institutional investors to continually improve their value and profitability. Nothing else.

So where does this leave the submarine cable system and efforts to maintain its critical function with the appropriate levels of resilience that reflect their critical role in global communications? Outside the US, few individual economies, if any, have the resources to meaningfully respond to this challenge. The European Union (EU) has taken some action to contribute to funding a fleet of repair vessels and taken measures to improve surveillance on submarine cables as a matter of regional security, but no other economies appear to be following this lead. It would certainly be ironic if this EU money were to end up simply funding the maintenance of Google’s submarine cable assets!

Back to the topic of cable resilience, viewed at a global level: Communications resilience is largely an ocean infrastructure question. Answers to this question rely on:

  • Detailed and current seabed surveys
  • Shipping controls to prevent anchoring and seabed fishing in declared subsea cable protection zones
  • A distributed repair fleet and crews trained to perform repair tasks
  • Rapid clearance to operate in territorial waters

Some coordination of action is necessary to open diverse cable routes and avoid single points of vulnerability and potential failure. The global cloud, for all its connotations of weightless air, firmly rests on the solidity of the seabed, and it can be no more reliable than conventions that we collectively adopt to look after it.

items.title: Passkeys are not a trap
items.author: speckx
items.content:
A post called Passkeys are a trap. Do not use them. has been doing the rounds over the last few days, making it pretty high on Hacker News, and I've had it sent to me many times with an 'is this true?' kind of vibe. It's written for "non-technical citizens of the web", and the headline advice is to stop using passkeys and go back to TOTP codes and passwords.

The post makes what appears to be one central claim: Passkeys support something called attestation, which lets a website ask for cryptographic proof of what made the passkey.

The author calls this a "hidden dial" and argues that sites will slowly turn it up, until you're only allowed to log in with approved software on an approved operating system, with no modifications, no LineageOS and no sharing your Netflix password. Throw in uBlock Origin, the FIDO Alliance membership list and the UK's image-scanning proposals, and the conclusion is that passkeys are "not designed to prioritize your interests". <that-escalated-quickly.gif>

It's a compelling story. It just doesn't match how any of this actually works...

Your Passkeys Don't Attest

The passkeys most people use are synced passkeys, stored in iCloud Keychain, Google Password Manager, 1Password, Bitwarden or whatever other software of your choosing. These passkeys don't give websites an attestation statement at all, and though a site can ask, what comes back is . I know this because I wrote an opensource passkeys library and made it available to everyone.

If a consumer website decided tomorrow that it would only accept attested passkeys, it would lock out almost all of its own users, instantly. What website is going to do that? Besides, the guidance for consumer sites has been to not even request attestation for now.

Attestation Isn't What You Think It Is

The post describes attestation as proving "that an approved passkey manager, operating system, and firmware are in use" which is simply not true.

When it is present, WebAuthn attestation tells the site the make and model of the authenticator, identified by its , with a certificate chain from the vendor to back it up. It says nothing about your OS, your browser, your extensions, whether your phone is rooted or jailbroken, your firmware version, or even what colour it is.

This is the part that surprised me the most. For people who want stronger security, the post recommends a hardware security key like a YubiKey, because it "avoids OS-wide attestation".

YubiKeys are the authenticators that attestation. Every one of them ships with a Yubico-issued attestation certificate, and enterprise attestation exists specifically so organisations can require approved hardware keys. I'd still recommend a YubiKey to anyone who wants one, they're excellent and I use them, but if attestation is the thing you're worried about, the post's own recommendation pushes you towards attestation rather than away from it!

The post holds up TOTP as "already" a great solution. TOTP is better than a password alone, absolutely, but it has one big weakness: you can type the code into the wrong website, just ask my good friend Troy Hunt. Phishing kits like Evilginx sit in the middle, relay your password and code to the real site in real time, and walk away with your session. This isn't theoretical, it's how a huge number of account takeovers happen today and we have the evidence to prove it.

This is the problem that passkeys solve. A passkey is bound to the domain it was created for, so your browser simply won't use your passkey on . There's no code to read out and nothing for the user to get wrong. The author even concedes this in the addendum, saying that passkeys are domain-bound and resist man-in-the-middle attacks, but still tells readers to avoid them. Swapping a phishing-resistant credential for a phishable one is a really bad trade...

Keep using passkeys! Wherever a site offers one, take it, and store it in a password/passkey manager you trust. If you want to be able to move your credentials around, pick a provider that supports that. If you're worried about attestation creeping into consumer logins, then that's worth pushing back on, loudly (if it ever happens). But it hasn't happened, the biggest providers don't support it, and avoiding passkeys today while you wait for it won't protect you from anything, it just leaves you open to phishing.

I have some experience in this area:

I think most of all that it's important to say I use passkeys everywhere I can because they're currently the best thing we have available to protect our accounts. And they're not a trap.
