items.title: How to engineer an AI harness for game development
items.author: kkukshtel
items.content:
I gave a 45 minute presentation entitledYour Game Is A Harness” as part of Indie Rodeo in Calgary on 9/12/26. After speaking with a lot of people after my talk, I thought it would be good to more broadly share the ideas I presented there in a form that could be enjoyed by people beyond just those who attended the conference.

Also, because I talk about a lot on this blog, people assume I use to write. This is not true! Everything below is 100% human authored, with me writing the post with basically only the slides I presented as a reference (this is not a transcription). As much as I enjoy using to write code and tools, I get a similar enjoyment out of writingthe old way”, especially as I have no reason to try and make any part of this process more efficient.

So with that all out of the way, I present to you my first ever blogification of a talk I gave. Enjoy!

[I give a small introduction to myself and my own work, that I’m omitting here, as you’re on my website]

I want to talk about using LLMs in game development. Not one-shot type demos that look cool on Twitter, but like development. Where you’re working eight hours a day, 5 days a week, etc.

And before I get into it, I think it’s useful to level set about LLMs. Or at least get into some basics so the rest of what I talk about here makes sense. I recognize that for a lot of this people this will be review, so if you just want to get into the dev-loop stuff, scroll down to the next section.

My journey into using LLMs for dev work started with a moodboarding site I made called mood.site. This was preagentic” anything, but I wanted to test and see if ChatGPT at the time could actually code anything. The process was a lot of me just blindly copy/pasting code into ChatGPT’s web interface. The process sucked, but I was surprised at the results. I built the site! It worked! I still needed to verify a fair amount of stuff myself, but it was enough to convert me. If I didn’t have access to an I wouldn’t have been able to make that site happen in near the amount of time it ended up taking me (~2-3 weeks of nights, probably like 20 hours total). I’d probably still be working on building the first version today.

Since then, mood has become something of a testbed for me moving through stuff (and a mildly successful project on its own!), and has inspired me to kick up lots of other projects that use similar stacks. Additionally, LLMs have gotten better, especially with things like Claude Code and later Claude models. From my own experience, I feel like now there is very little, if anything, I think an do when it comes to a web-based stack.

It could be easy to then say LLMs can do , as so much of software is web software. But whenever I tried to use an on building a non-web game , it was this resounding takeaway:

Any time I tried to use an for a game-y thing, it would fall over. Maybe this is my own bias. I’ve been a game programmer for nearly 15 years, I think I know how things work. I can sniff outbad” game code a mile away. But when it comes to Svelte web-apps, I’m decidedly less well versed and am inclined to think that whatever code the produces isgood”. Maybe it’s garbage. But there reason to believe the Svelte and web-stack stuff quality, in part due to the fact that there are of high quality web projects with their source available online. Comparatively for games, I imagine there are orders of magnitude less data to train on.

Not only this, but games have a lot of in them that isn’t code. Games aren’t just about putting static images and text in a layout. There are of things in games that aren’t easily representable by code. then on top of that there is all the same text layout stuff of web, but only as a subset of the 100 other systems a game needs to handle.

This is part of the reason why a lot of people have been making games in Three.js — they can easily represent assets as plain boxy primitives and skip a lot of the asset generation/conforming work and processing normally required for games. As a result, a lot of that stuff is slop because it lacks any real authorial voice outside of whatever the median is.

However, maybe they have a point.

A key idea of the one-shot Three.JS workflow (as well as LLMs proficiency at building web apps) is that is code. By having as code, it’s very easy for an to be able to reason about it, make changes, etc.

However for traditional games, this is not the case. Or at least the full story. Games obviously have code, but there is a lot of other stuff that is code. This means that there are key components of games that are effectively opaque to an . If your game then relies on the effective puppeting and transforming of that opaque stuff, then an is going to fall over when trying to work on your game.

I think a lot of the gamedev community maybe gave LLMs a go a bit ago and ran directly into this. TheLLMs are bad/not useful/etc.” sentiment (massive caveat here, just talking about capability specifically and not potential society-ending implications) came from running headfirst into these limitations.

This is to say that, structurally, LLMs are bad at reading games. At least in their default state.

Let’s talk more about why, and what we can do about it.

Any call/prompt to any service breaks down into three basic components. A system prompt, an assistant prompt, and a user prompt:

This is kind of a sidecar prompt section meant to help guide the in terms of what it is responding to. You can think of it basically as the model’s basicinteraction” vector with your prompt, and represents something like the model’sresponse” to the user based on some input. You usually do not have to think about this.

: This is really The Thing. Most any input you put into any tool goes here. Any submitted chat, code, etc. gets dumped into this section. When people talk aboutcontext”, they are largely talking abouthow many tokens are stored in the user (and assistant) portion of a prompt”.

It may be easy to think that each chat is afresh” version of the above, but what actually happens is that, as you work with a model in a given session (the bounds ofsession” vary based on what service you are using — this can be a single Claude Code session before closing it, achat” accessible in the side panel of a web hosted model, etc.), every prior message you sent to the model is re-submitted time you send a message. It’s kind of like playing the old playground game where, on your turn, you have to say everyone else’s thing before then adding your own thing for the next person to have to add on.

Context and Context Pollution

As you do this over and over, you build up thecontext” of the session you’re working in.

This is all well and good, but a key thing to notice here is that you only really are able to address thelatest” thing in your context (i.e., you submit a new message). Things from previous messages get submitted over and over again to the model. Hence, you want to make sure what’s in your context isgood”, otherwise you can find yourself in degenerate scenarios where your context becomes polluted due tobad” things earlier continually informing new work.

Managing context then is a key thing in working with LLMs, and a new engineering practice calledcontext engineering” has emerged in light of these constraints. Context engineering askshow can we get the information into the context, with as little pollution as possible”.

Context Engineering itself is a really big topic that is outside the scope of this talk/blog, but we will be using some of the tenets of it here to explore how to help LLMs do a better job working with games.

Said differently, getting LLMs to work well with games is a problem, not something that is intrinsically linked to how games or LLMsare” (oraren’t”!).

The complicating factor here though is, games are . Or at least: we have no real template to build a game. We have game engines, but there is effectively 0 standardized tooling for anything, in part because every game manifests its own needs differently from one another.

This is acutely unique to games (imo), but it manifests enough in other technological domains that a new concept has emerged in order to get agents to effectivelywork” with whatever your work product is: Harnesses.

Some Description of the Idea of a Harness

The general idea of a Harness is that it’s some set patterns of actions an agent is meant to take in response to some well (or loosely) defined expected input. You’re probably already using a harness like Claude Code, but these can be augmented, extended, distilled, abstracted, etc. to better support the work you are trying to do. There’s also been a of action in this space recently, with many harnesses being built for developing all sorts of things:

The key things these are all pointing to is:how can I better understand I’m building, and guide that process as it is developed”. Harnesses can tie in things like iterating with a browser, telemetry, profiling, and even full work like making tickets, documents, etc.

However, the thing of these do well is actually talk your game. Your game is a bit of a black box, and most of what’s visible to an is only the code-as-written, which as we talked about before, isn’t really enough. We know LLMs are already good at working with code, so it’s not like some harness itself solves thatgames aren’t just code” issue we ran into in the first place.

What really needs to happen here is that we can take all the in games, and try to turn it something the is able to work with. We need to crack open the black box of your game and make more of it addressable directly by an .

During the talk version of this I had this Very Funny Slide that said that the arrow here was the actual content of this talk. The joke hits nowhere near as hard in blog form but I’m leaving it here for posterity:

So let’s talk about what we can do.

Here’s some very tangible, actionable things you can do for your game to make it more legible and by an .

As a brief aside before getting started, it’s also worth noting here that a lot of these tips are good for game development . They get supercharged a bit with , but doing any of this will likely make working on your own games generally just .

A running theme through this whole talk/post is the concept of . Basically, how accurately can you reproduce a very specific state in your game. The general goal is that it should be very easy, and very exact. Doing this at the very end of your production will be hard to do, and would likely require fundamental changes to your game in the 11th hour.

Instead, if you assume this constraint before you write your first line of code, and stick to it as a goal, you’ll be paving the path to a much more productive end game and not find yourself fighting off entropy and spaghetti code.

Starting off here is pretty easy. At the start of your game, create a single source of randomness. Make sure any call to anything non-deterministic uses this source of randomness. This means that your game will be able to deterministically recreate almost any state in the game. If your code calls Random.Float or whatever in 30 places to determine some gameplay behavior, you know that the 30th call will be the same every time. Easy.

Why have reproducible states? Many reasons, but for an agent, imagine you’re iterating many times on trying to correct something. It’s important for the agent to be able to get to the same state from scratch over and over again without needing to churn through state replication failures.

And once you get there, how do you know? How can you evaluate those changes?

Well for one, screenshots! Most engines have some built in screenshot or functionality:

I also recommended adding in the ability to easily toggle layers, gameplay layers, etc. on/off that way you can reduce visual clutter that distracts the from the layer you’re trying to address (ie, dont have gameplay under a if you’re trying to fix some style thing).

Taking a before and after picture of your game between agent changes is a nice way for an agent to be able to understand what changed.

When you take two screenshots (Before/After) a change, the , even if it’s multi-modal (ie, has vision capabilities), will likely have a hard time not only understanding what the change is, but understanding if the change it made moved it closer to its own end goal.

This noise from image data is its own form of context rot: naiively throwing screenshots at models can muddy their own sense of progress, leaving both them and you confused.

A visual example can help here: Imagine you take a screenshot of the home page of this conference:

You ask the model toMake the skeleton a pirate”. Assuming if (and with text LLMs, unlikely) this can be applied as an annotation to the image (Google Stitch does this), your image will be passed to the model provider with your tag, but then also all the stuff you aren’t trying to address (in green below).

This means that everything in green is something akin tocontext pollution”. It is data the is processing as well as your requested change, but it’s not just thinking about what you requested, but is thinking about the image.

You need to get the to think about what needs to change. How do you judge what has changed?

If you take two images anddiff” them, like you do with code changes, you can easily see what has changed. Combined with clever uses of cropping, you can have an understand, with a quantitative measure, how closely some output post-change is close to your provided input/target image.

Given two different images, odiff finds thedifference” between the two, and can output that difference as adiff” image:

odiff also can give you a quantitative difference value like85% similar”, that an is very good at reading, and can then use that as a stable baseline of eval across each agent turn as it strives to reduce the difference/increase the similarity.

Said differently, as you are working, these agent screenshot -> progress diff check become the basis for continual agent evaluation towards whatever your task is:

However, this obviously isn’t all. Games are much more than just their visual elements.Progress” here breaks down into it’s own little inner loop:

This inner-loop is likely the place where an agent will spend most of its time, doing multiple turns on its own before going back to the screenshot comp/diff (assuming that your change has some visual implication).

The goal here is to be able to make every change be the amount of change required for a desired outcome, and have those changes able to be quickly verified. You want an incredibly stable,boring” baseline that can be evaluated in near-isolation to ensure that anything built on top of it doesn’t produce wide ranging technical debt (aka, spaghetti). So let’s talk more about deterministic state.

The rest of the items in the above graph also deal in some part with deterministic state, but I want to talk about specific strategies and techniques for achieving it, as they will be essential for everything else.

There’s a simple question to ask to understand/know how close you are to deterministic state: how easily can you save and load an exact state in your game? Or said differently, the most important part of state reproduction is having a strategy for efficiently saving and loading your game .

Saving/Loading is usually something amateur developers will put off to the end of a game, but this is a grave mistake, as many more seasoned developers will tell you. It’s easy to think of saving/loading as afeature” that you can add at some point during a game’s development, but saving and loading, when leveraged at the start of a game and programmed in conjunction , can be a development superpower that has a near innumerable list of benefits.

Let’s talk about one strategy for doing this, and why it makes of development easier.

We’re going to take a small jaunt here into CS-style programming theory. Most people that spend extensive time with object-oriented type architectures for games will find that, near the end of their project, something like the above statementA Tree is a Dog” is true. They look at their code, and what things actually do in a game, and realize that, these two seemingly very different objects with separate hierarchies are, at the end of the day, actually more or less the same kind ofthing” from the perspective of the code.

A tree is an object that has a mesh and a collider. A dog is an object that has a mesh, collider, and can move.Movement” is not an intrinsicallydog” thing (other things in the game may move), and hence a tree and a dog are basically just compositions of components that have some game-representation. From the code’s perspective, they are effectively the same.

This can be counter-intuitive at first, as it wrong, but there is a chakra-unlocking insight here that, when you hold on to, starts to make game programming much easier and not a constant uphill battle against a wall of abstraction that occurs when you try to maintain a strong OOP-style object model in your game.

Instead, if you take the idea I’m proposing and run with it, you can assume from the very start of your game that everything is actually the same thing (maybe even use the type ). If you were to define Thing in code, you’d have something that looks like this:

You can see a Thing has some stat-type values on it as well as a shared idea ofliveness” from the isAlive flag. Otherwise, thetypes” of thing is just an enum value, and based on that type the implementing code can take some action.

And as It turns out, likes this.

With this type of architecture, there is a for your object model. If instead you have 100 classes of 100 different types of objects, an will need to likely understand of those (and their relationships) to take action. This fills up your context, and makes reasoning about how to fit into that pattern messy — should I (the ) extend some class? Morph the type of a class to better capture this new thing? Make a new class? It’s hard to say!

With a single object type, there is no ambiguity. knows exactly where to make changes, time.

Not only this, but (getting back to saving/loading), having a single object type makes saving and loading easier:

When you have one object type, deserializing/serializing is trivial — it’s a single type, so there is one way in/one way out. With multiple different types (and potential trees of inheritance), you will likely find yourself in weird race condition deserialization paths, needing to link up objects and trees of children in strange ways and grappling with concepts likepolymorphic deserialization. It is well and good to know about these things and use them when required, but for games There Be Dragons here.

A game then is just a giant list of Things. Saving is saving all those things through one path, and loading is the same, but in reverse. Any casing you need to do can happen on the deserialized enum type value. It’s nice!

I’m also far from the first person to ever talk about this, so if you want to hear more about this I highly recommend some of the episodes of Wookash podcast where he talks with some of the creators of Dreams about a very similar system:

By working with a system like this, reproducing state immediately is quite easy and you skirt all the difficulties of saving and loading. There is more complexity here, and I do recommend the above talk for further reading, but the fundamental idea is the same — capture everything as a single object type. State itself is then easily captured by the same system. Nothing is stopping you from have a Turn Number field on every structure as well, and a Type that is GameManager. Make this object do literally everything. And no, it’s not memory expensive like you may think it is.

Once you have a system like this, it makes other parts of the game easier as well.

If you have one type of object, it’s very easy to capture changes to state, because change in your game presumably targets single object type. You may want to change these values directly, but with thisfat struct” approach you can very easily implement something called theCommand Pattern for even more benefit:

The idea of the command pattern is that you capture changes to an object itself not as a loose function call, but instead as an (ideally serializable) object. These commands then get passed through some processing class, which makes the changes to the objects themselves instead of you directly. This level of indirection can again seem strange at first, but bear with me.

Imagine you have some starting state. The player makes some actions that alter state, which manifest as commands. This results in some end state, where a bug occurs.

Now lets say you want to try to reproduce this. One version of this is you trying to communicate with the player to figure out what they did and try to do the same thing in your copy of the game.

, you can take the starting state, andplayback” the serialized commands, which capture what the player did. And notably, this doesn’t have to be you literally playing the game or writing bespoke function calls to change state: you just playback the commands. Or not even you, but an agent can also run them back as it continually tries to assess how its changes affect state.

Taking this a step further, you may notice that these commands also don’t actually have to be authored from the game itself. You can easily string together commands in a text editor (or authored by the ), and then have them played back on a running instance of the game, no compiling required!

Commands give the (and you), a typed interface to interact with your game, effectively making itpuppet-able” and not requiring every change or attempt to work with your game need some bespoke processing logic or reflection (and then compiling those changes). likes this!

To linger on no-compile changes for a bit: the more you can drive your game to be able to make changes without compiling, the better. Not just as some badge of honor, but especially for agentic loops — the more it can test without needing to wait for compile time means it’s able to act more quickly and make/validate changes in a tighter loop.

When I saydata”, I’m talking about the static, operational data your game uses to describe how things . In the example above, I’d consider Type, attackDamage, walkSpeed, and boatSpeed alldata”. These are characteristics of the object that do not change. Things can modify these and work with these, and players may never see literally these numbers, but they describe the baseline shape of some Things existence in the game.

If you were making things for your game, you may write out a lot of your structs directly, setting their properties based on what you know they are. Those changes then get compiled into the game. If you want to change something’s walk speed, you need to either make the change and recompile, or write some function binding that assigns the value and is externally callable (think console commands).

All of these options introduce churn to the agent. Especially in the scenarios where you’re compiling, you’re putting testing basic value changes behind a compilation.

The better way to do this is to have all your data to your game instead of represented as code. Assigning this data is just a matter of deserializing the data, applying it to the correct objects, and done! So changing data is just a matter changing in your data source of choice, setting up some basic deserialization in your game, and combine it with object creation. Done! This also allows you (or an agent, or other team member, etc.) to be able to iterate on your game with a ! They don’t even necessarily need editor access.

Team members made changes in Depot, and the game build handled deserialized changes so they would work in a loop without needing me to cut new builds. Depot is my tool of choice here, but other teams use things like Google Sheets, or their own custom tools.

agents can be taught to use your own tools, and then can, like other team members, test out data changes on their own without needing to rebuild the game constantly. The tighter you can make the agentic loops, the better! It’s all about trying to remove cycle bottlenecks.

This leads into another core idea. It’s a bit of a rabbit hole, so bear with me.

Standalone Simulation / Blackbox

When developing a game, either in an engine or on your own with some custom tooling, it’s usually the case that the logic of the game itself is intermingled with visual state transitions, calls, etc. This is by no fault of anyone, but it makes sense as a default model: some action happens, you update the , maybe change some visuals, etc.

However, in putting all of this together, especially in engine, you start to realize that to start trying to test anything or reproduce someone’s bug, you need to have the game running and doing its thing. Models have to be loaded, sounds setup, scenes loaded, etc. The of your game necessitates havingthe whole game”. When things start to break, it becomes hard to disambiguate between what is breaking and why: is it the simulation? The models? The scene design?

A better way to work here is that the of your game sits of the actual operating logic of the engine. And by outside, I mean literally as its own DLL/library. The game consumes the simulation and its outcomes, but doesn’t itselfown” the simulation.

Instead, the engine communicates with the simulation throughcommands”, not dissimilar from how clients and servers work in web programming.

These commands can (and should!) take the form of the previous idea of commands we introduced earlier:

As the engine pipes commands to the simulation core, the simulation responds with the updated states passed back to the engine. The engine then interprets the updated states (or diff’d state from the last received state) and acts on it.

This sounds a bit abstract, so here’s a more specific example:

Imagine something is moving in your game. That movement is likely a few different things — animation, models, sound effects, and logic around movement start, continuing, stopping, with maybe intermediate updates for things like vision as the object moves. However, what movement fundamentallyis” is something going from point A to point B in response to some player input.

The idea is that the engine sends in a movement request for some Thing (fat structs remember!), and the simulation independently decides if that’s a valid movement target (the engine can also filter for this specifically before submitting the command). The simulation then resolves the movement, and gives back to the engine an updated state object that shows the object has indeed moved. The engine can understand that the movement happened by diffing against the previous state, or other ways that are too complex to fully get into here (recording buffered commands and acting on them if the simulation accepts them, etc.). The key though is that the engine isdumb” — it just acts on what it gets from the simulation and doesn’t question it. The simulation is the source of truth: if the simulation says something moved, the engine then moves the object, no questions asked.

This level of indirection can seem like too much abstraction, but when you have your simulation core separate from your engine, it means that can send commands at your core:

The biggest immediate win here is that network programming becomes easier — because your game is setup to just consume states/diffs, where they are actually coming from doesn’t matter. They can come from the network, , whatever!

There are even simpler use cases. Testing in game development is often a bit of a bear to tackle, but I’d argue the reason for a lot of that is because state/logic/data are often coupled so tightly that it’s very hard to test the game because it requires so much scaffolding.

However, leveraging an architecture like this allows you to test a game’s simulation, without needing an engine at all. You can rip through tests with pure C# projects, using standard C# tooling, and not need any engine running your code. likes this!

This idea broadly is calledBlackbox Game Architecture”. Versions of it have existed before, but this talk by Brian Cronin as part of Roguelike Celebration a few years ago goes into technical detail about he leveraged the technique for Monster Train:

When you leverage something like this, it becomes a gamedev superpower. You can start really working with your game as a technical object that is abstracted from the actual player experience of it. You can run simulations, hypothesis, tests, etc., directly on the simulation itself and can skirt all the questions of state that usually plague related efforts that don’t use some architecture strategy like this.

Going back to our chart above, we’ve made out way to the near end of our flywheel. We set some deterministic input parameters, have ways to modify that state in structured ways that can avoid compilation, and can then verify our own changes in a vacuum.

However, how do we actually know those changes then affect the actual game how we want? This is the idea ofimpact assessment”.

I’m going to focus on a somewhat narrow set of options here, but there are more tools a studio could deploy in this arena that are more specific to their own game. Things like tests fall into general areas here, but also running things like fixed gameplay scenarios to figure out balance impact, etc. These all matter, but are game specific and as such hard to directly extract in the scope of this post.

However, one thing that all games share is a concern for performance. Traditionally, performance profiling has been a relatively manual effort, and required developers to work with profiling tools, with ones built into editors like Unity/Unreal or through tooling like dotMemory:

These tools are designed for consumption — they expect you to dig into the call stacks and graphs and such to find whatever bottlenecks you are looking for. Perhaps unsurprisingly then, it turns out doesn’t really like using tools like this: they aren’t legible to the agent (though worth saying Unity doing a lot of work here to make the profiler better able to be read by agents!).

What really likes it to work with text (and lots of it), so profiling tools that are able to dump out raw captures as text help to accelerate iteration. There are a few options here, but the one I’ve grown to like the most is the (free!) tool samply:

Samply can be hooked up to easily run against your own project, and dump capture output to console. An agent knows how to read the samply source and docs to help it figure out how to eval its own changes here, so the capture and iterate loop can be performed effectively autonomously. likes this!

As we combine all these tools and technique together, something like this comes into view (and this is just one version!):

With the data-oriented, binary-isolated, no-compile-needed version of development I’m sketching here, an agentic turn can run through this loop in . It makes iteration significantly faster than a baseline naiive approach, and at every step helps the to better understand your game and what you’re trying to do. Because the whole loop is efficient and fast, it can be run against change, and not saved for only when itmatters”.

Reframing this a big, you can see what a game-driven harness looks like:

Spoilers: it’s your game! Any game is capable of all of this, meaning any game can easily be its own harness. Or, as we’ve said at the start:

It’s been interesting to write this after having presented it. I stand by a lot of what I’ve said, but am in the process of shipping a project where I’ve also used none of this. I think the scale I’m targeting here is really projects. The thing I’m shipping is very small, so I really didn’t need to do much for it in terms of any harness stuff.

However, as I pick up work on a larger game that I’m cooking, a lot of this is definitely relevant and I’m very thankful for all these tools.

If you apply strategies like the above to your own games, I’d love to hear about your experience and what worked/didn’t work! I’m really thinking about a lot in this space (obviously) as I continue to make games and tools, so am excited to hear what other people are doing.

Again, thanks for reading and talk next time!

items.title: Your C is not standard C
items.author: dverlaeckt80
items.content:
this is an incomplete list of some incompatibilities between c as it's written in the standard and c as it exists in the real world for people who use gcc/clang + glibc/musl.

by default, gcc and clang recognize the keyword as an extension. this is not strictly conformant, because in standard c, is a valid non-reserved identifier. so code which conforms to the standard may not compile with gcc/clang with their default settings.

and like, whatever, that's fine, that's why exists, but 1. it's notable that compilers aren't conformant , and 2. why doesn't the standard just make a reserved word? c++ does that; i'm not sure why c doesn't.

the standard specifies the macro in as follows:

notably, the standard requires that the value dynamically changes with the runtime floating environment. gcc, however, always defines to 1 (rounds to nearest), regardless of the runtime rounding mode: 

/* Addition rounds to 0: zero, 1: nearest, 2: +inf, 3: -inf, -1: unknown.  */
/* ??? This is supposed to change with calls to fesetround in <fenv.h>.  */
#undef FLT_ROUNDS
#define FLT_ROUNDS 1

clang defines a builtin for this (), but gcc doesn't, for some reason.

at some point in the future i'm gonna make an entire blog post dedicated to just this, because i kinda find it fascinating. but the super duper short version is this:

the c standard specifies five standard pragmas to control the behavior of floating point arithmetic: 

// added in c99:
// switch can be ON, OFF, or DEFAULT
#pragma STDC FP_CONTACT ON
#pragma STDC FENV_ACCESS ON
#pragma STDC CX_LIMITED_RANGE ON

// added in c23:
// direction can be FE_DYNAMIC, FE_DOWNWARD, FE_TONEAREST,
// FE_TONEARESTFROMZERO, FE_TOWARDZERO, FE_UPWARD, or some
// other implementation-defined value
#pragma STDC FENV_ROUND FE_DYNAMIC
#pragma STDC FENV_DEC_ROUND FE_DYNAMIC

some (but not all) of the functionality can be replicated with command-line flags, but those operate on the entire translation unit, whereas the pragmas can apply to individual functions and blocks.

clang mostly supports the c99 pragmas, but still doesn't support the c23 pragmas.

there's actually more to say about these. i be writing more about them at some point, but rn i don't really have the motivation cuz it's such a big thing lol

qualifiers in function return types

the standard requires that qualifiers in function return types are discarded:

If, in the declaration "", has the form 
D (  ) attribute-specifier-sequence
and the type specified for in the declaration "" is "derived-declarator-type-list ", then the type specified for is "derived-declarator-type-list function returning the unqualified, non-atomic version of ". The optional attribute specifier appertains to the function type.

but clang treats them as significant: 

$ 
t.c:2:11: error: conflicting types for 'f'
    2 | const int f();
      |           ^
t.c:1:5: note: previous declaration is here
    1 | int f();
      |     ^
1 error generated.
the two declarations should be identical, but clang thinks they're incompatible.

        
outdated  definition on musl
for some reason, musl provides its own versions of some headers which the compiler already provides itself. one of these is , which is required to be supported by freestanding implementations and so is virtually guaranteed to already be provided by the compiler. but because it's provided by musl, compilers will use that header instead of the builtin one.

        
this is a problem because musl's header is strictly worse than the builtin header. here's how musl defines :

        
#define va_start(v,l)   __builtin_va_start(v,l)
this definition is incorrect, because c23 allows the second argument to be omitted. it should be defined like this:

        
#if __STDC_VERSION__ >= 202311L
#define va_start(...) __builtin_c23_va_start(__VA_ARGS__)
#else
#define va_start(v,l) __builtin_va_start(v,l)
#endif
the result is that, when compiling for musl, c23's single-argument  can't be used, even if it's supported by the compiler.

items.title: It took me nine years to hack my Xbox 360
items.author: kennedn
items.content:
I purchased a Matrix CoolRunner Rev D back in 2017. This little chip is called a glitcher and it’s a type of modchip. Its sole purpose, the reason it was designed, is to deliver a short pulse of energy (~ 100 nanoseconds) to an Xbox 360 Console.

You might ask yourself, “What’s the point in that?”. The answer is quite interesting.

It boils down to the simple fact that Microsoft learned from the mistakes of their previous console (the original Xbox) and designed security well on their successor.

So well in fact, that it was deemed essentially unhackable by conventional approaches:

tmbinc said it himself, software based approaches of running unsigned code on the 360 mostly don’t work, it was designed to be secure from a software point of view.

The entry point for the system, dubbed 1BL, is physically baked into the silicon of the Xbox 360’s CPU . The job of 1BL is to load the next phase of the bootloader, called CB from flash storage, and verify that it was signed by Microsoft.

So without Microsoft’s signing keys, there was no real way to hijack control of the system during the boot process. And it only becomes harder as the console boots up through its different phases. Additional security features are turned on as it cascades up the boot chain. And they would all need individually circumvented to get any code running on the console that Microsoft haven’t been over with a fine toothed comb.

So if the door to the castle is locked, and the guards, who are wise to equine ploys, are checking ID at the door, how does one get in? Well you don’t use a key. You inform the guard that his shoelaces are untied and hit him over the head with a club.

The point is that if the lock itself is secure, and the procedures surrounding entry are sound, sometimes the weakest link becomes something more fundamental. In our metaphor this is a person, but in the case of the Xbox 360, it is the fact that computation relies on stable energy conditions to behave in a predictable manner.

And this is the idea that fault injection subverts. In the case of the Xbox 360, researchers found that by very quickly toggling a reset signal on the CPU (), a signal that is usually supposed to reinitialise the CPU, something far more interesting happened. Instead of resetting, the CPU executed the current instruction incorrectly.

Graph demonstrating glitching as voltage over time .

This gave the researchers a very useful primitive. They found that an instruction integral to the signature verification process, the (move register) instruction, could be glitched into ignoring a value it was about to move and instead move a 0 into its destination register .

So by simply knowing when, and toggling the lights on and off, they gained arbitrary code execution.

It is astounding to me that this kind of esoteric side channel exists at all. But I think the larger point is that it’s becoming more common.

The sort of trust chains that made the Xbox 360 hard to hack 10 years ago have now become commonplace in the world of computing hardware. Microsoft themselves began enforcing hardware backed secure boot for their Operating Systems back in 2021.

More recently in 2024, the security features of an ESP32 v3 (secure boot and flash encryption) were bypassed using a fault injection attack .

And there are recent examples specifically leveraging the Raspberry Pi Pico Microcontroller to perform similar fault injection attacks

Apple AirTag’s firmware was dumped in 2021 by stacksmashing using a Raspberry Pi Pico and fault injection .

The PicoFly modchip, released in 2023 for the Nintendo Switch, uses fault injection to defeat secure boot on the console .

To me, this suggests that fault injection has become a more attractive attack vector in recent years due to a security ecosystem that has hardened over time. But I think it has in turn also become more accessible than ever, with the advent of cheap and accurate microcontrollers such as the Pi Pico.

The Raspberry Pi Pico microcontroller, released in 2021 for £5 by the Raspberry Pi Foundation .

The Pico itself is versatile because it allows for very precise timing via its PIO blocks. These specialised blocks come with enough primitives to implement many standard protocols and have an effective timing resolution of ~7.5 nanoseconds due to the 133 MHz clock :

$$\frac{1}{133\text{ MHz}} \approx 7.52\text{ns}$$

I have seen this versatility myself first hand when I finally dusted off the Matrix CoolRunner in 2026 and decided to take another crack at modchipping my Xbox 360.

Back in 2017, when I bought the thing, it was quite expensive to modchip an Xbox 360. You needed a number of tools and skills to successfully mod one:

    I tried to save some money by building my own NAND / JTAG programmer using the printer port (LPT port) on a very old PC that I had in reserve for the specific purpose. If I had ever got this working it would have taken over 30 minutes to dump the NAND. I do not recall the reason but I did not manage to pull this off in 2017 and the project was shelved.

    LPT NAND dumper wiring diagram .

    Reattempting this same procedure in 2026 was a breeze by comparison. I was able to flash PicoFlasher onto a Pi Pico and solder it to the correct pads on my Xbox 360. The dump operation then only took a handful of seconds to run.

    Raspberry Pi Pico wired to the NAND interface header on the Xbox 360.

    Raspberry Pi Pico wired to Matrix CoolRunner JTAG interface.

    So, even the most carefully crafted tower can collapse under the weight of its own fundamental assumptions. Like many aspects of computer security, fault injection has become a game of cat and mouse, with increasingly sophisticated defences being met by new tools and methods of circumventing them.

    But I think we have now reached a point where DIY tooling has really begun to shine, making light work of challenges that, just a decade ago, required expensive, specialised equipment.

    And I have seen this first hand, a project that defeated me in 2017 was made trivial in 2026 by a £5 microcontroller.

    Funnily enough, a software-only exploit for the Xbox 360 dropped just last week , rendering my years of effort somewhat moot. Nevertheless, it was a fascinating deep dive into the inner workings of the console and the security mechanisms designed to protect it.

items.title: Wanted to download an ISO, ended up writing a kernel exploit
items.author: 0xdeafbeef
items.content:
Long downloads kept breaking#

In August 2023 I bought a shiny new Wi-Fi 7 access point, a TP-Link EAP770. The connection was a bit janky, a video would occasionally start buffering, but it didn't bother me much.

I mostly worked on a workstation connected over Ethernet. When I needed to go somewhere, I'd rsync my to the laptop over Wi-Fi and take it with me. Those transfers started failing on files larger than a few GiB. SSH was reporting MAC errors, so I spent a while debugging rsync and SSH. Everything else worked, changing rsync options made it better or worse, Wireshark showed zero bad checksums and zero retransmissions, and a single UDP stream of random bytes came through clean. I trusted TCP to deliver the right bytes because that's what the fucking thing is for, so I was sure the problem was in rsync or SSH. I wrote a wrapper around rsync with retries and moved on.

Later I happened to start using Tailscale for traffic inside my home network, and the transfers stopped needing retries. WireGuard drops a packet if its authentication fails, so the TCP connection inside the tunnel sees a lost packet and retransmits it. Since the transfers worked, I stopped digging.

The device is an EAP770(EU) v1.0 with a Qualcomm IPQ9574 running Linux 5.4.164 and firmware 1.0.0 Build 20230605 Rel. 71641. That's the firmware it shipped with, and apparently the last time TP-Link remembered this thing even existed :)

I bought this thing in August 2023, and the Wi-Fi 7 standard was only finalized in September 2024. It has no Wi-Fi Alliance certification, and buying it was stupid of me. PLZ DON'T BUY STUFF UNTIL STANDARDS ARE FINALIZED AND DEVICES ARE CERTIFIED.

In 2025 I noticed that everything else was getting updates while this thing was still on its original firmware. I contacted support in June because the website only had firmware for v2. They couldn't find v1 in their database and asked for photos of the device and box before sending me this:

The EAP770 Version 1 is an End-of-Life product. While it may still be available through some retailers, it is no longer supported with firmware updates.

Tracking down the corruption#

In 2026 I decided to switch to NixOS and found that a 128 MiB file from the Nix binary cache on Fastly would fail over HTTP/2 but downloaded fine over HTTP/1.1. I still don't know why HTTP/1.1 helped; my guess is that HTTP/2 was simply faster. clones also failed, and HTTPS connections died with . In March, downloading a NixOS ISO with died with a TLS error:

I forced HTTP/1.1 and left it alone again.

In September I turned the workstation into a build farm and switched to the laptop, which connects over Wi-Fi. Wi-Fi was also dropping every day around 11:00, right before my daily call. After it had died right before the call several days in a row, I decided to open this Pandora's box again and sat down with Opus 5.5 to trace what was happening. Spoiler alert: the drops turned out to be a separate bug. I covered the laptop's Qualcomm driver in BPF probes and ran on the AP as root. The bug is in the closed-source firmware on the laptop's Wi-Fi card; see the update at the bottom.

I had tried enabling and disabling Wi-Fi 7, turning off GRO on the client, and replacing the MediaTek adapter in my Framework 16 with a Qualcomm one. The new adapter and disabling GRO seemed to help, but none of this stopped the corruption.

I captured a failing HTTPS download with tcpdump and found a 1440-byte TCP segment with 64 wrong bytes in a row and a valid TCP checksum. stayed at zero. TCP accepted the segment and handed it to TLS, which rejected the record with .

The damaged record wouldn't decrypt, so I couldn't inspect the bad bytes against the expected payload. I switched to raw TCP between a wired machine and the Wi-Fi laptop, sending known data that I could compare byte for byte. The corruption only appeared with several TCP streams running at once, in the LAN-to-Wi-Fi direction. The test found three bad 64-byte blocks in 8192 MiB, each starting with zeros.

A valid checksum on a damaged segment meant something had recalculated it after the corruption, so the question became what on the path rewrites TCP headers. The corruption still showed up after swapping the MediaTek card for the Qualcomm one, so it wasn't the laptop. Wired clients were clean and the CCMP MIC on the bad frames was intact, so it wasn't the cable and it wasn't the air. That left the bridge between Ethernet and Wi-Fi inside the AP. 64 bytes is a cache line on the IPQ9574's cores, which points at a cache or DMA bug rather than a flipped bit. The only thing on that path that both accelerates bridged traffic and recalculates checksums is Qualcomm's SFE/PPE offload.

Two writes that need root#

Reading the driver source suggested disabling SFE/PPE with these two settings:

Both sysfs files are writable only by root, but TP-Link's SSH shell runs as with no capabilities. There's no GUI setting for this either.

There's also no v1 firmware image to patch and flash, and the v2 firmware is for different hardware. I tried the sibling EAP773's , and the device rejected it. Newer v2 firmware releases are encrypted. Flashing the chip directly needed a flash clip. I didn't want to hunt one down or brick the fucking AP.

I wasn't going to spend another $200 replacing an AP because TP-Link couldn't be bothered to maintain the one they had already sold me. It's sitting in my house, I know which setting to change, and their software won't let me.

Shout-out to TP-Link though: the system is pretty hardened. I found zero vectors in their own binaries, they use whitelists everywhere and load only the modules they need. So no free ; echo 0 > /sys/sfe/ppe_rfs_feature cheese for me. So the way in had to be the kernel.

With Opus 4.8, I put together a chain using CVE-2022-0185 and pipe-buffer manipulation. CVE-2022-0185 is an integer underflow in , reachable from an unprivileged user namespace, that lets a write overflow a 4 KiB slab object. The pipe-buffer manipulation turns that overflow into an arbitrary write. There were already public write-ups and PoCs for these.

The exploit had to leave the AP running because the broken offload comes back after a reboot. The overflow leaves the 4 KiB slab in a state where a second attempt panics, so there's one shot per boot. I gave Opus guidance on the primitives, then had it iterate until the exploit was stable.

Getting this working took about seventeen hours of token gambling with Opus 4.8, including reading the device's binaries in radare2, checking the enabled protections, and working through the crashes. The AP stayed up, and disabling the offload stopped the corruption.

A DMA cache coherency bug#

Qualcomm's driver reuses packet buffers without synchronizing the CPU cache for the whole receive buffer before handing it back to the NIC. On this hardware, DMA writes directly to DRAM without keeping the CPU caches in sync. A dirty cache line left over from the previous use of a buffer can be written back after the NIC has received a new packet, overwriting part of that packet in memory.

SFE/PPE then recalculates the checksums over the corrupted payload, so the client gets a fresh TCP checksum that is valid for the garbage. TCP accepts it; the end-to-end MACs in TLS and SSH catch the damage, reporting and .

On x86, the hardware keeps DMA coherent with the CPU caches, so the same missing cache maintenance wouldn't corrupt anything. While looking through the kernel sources, I found similar DMA cache maintenance problems in several other drivers too. I don't know how to test those on hardware or who to report them to yet.

Opus 5.5 found the bug and then stopped talking about it#

When I moved from diagnosing the corruption to applying the fix, Opus 5.5 started cutting sessions off roughly every other message. Mentioning something like "local privilege escalation" is enough. I have the Cyber Verification Program enabled on my account, which hasn't helped. Opus 4.8 worked through the exploitation without that problem.

5.5's guards also kill the session when I just ask it to read this article. GPT-6 Astra reads and edits the same article without any cyber verification.

I tested raw TCP transfers between the same two machines with the offload enabled and disabled.

Disabling the offload cost about 8% of the download speed in this test. I have to give up performance to get correct data because TP-Link won't let me properly fix my own fucking device.

With the offload on, I could never download a large file over Wi-Fi in a single stream; only chunked downloads got through. With the offload off, the overnight run came back with zero bad blocks, and large downloads have worked every time since. Uploads from Wi-Fi to the LAN were already clean before the fix.

The counter in increases after disabling the offload, as bridged flows take the normal path instead of being accelerated.

The settings reset after a reboot, so a watcher on my NAS polls the AP and reruns the exploit when the offload is back on. If the attempt fails, it reboots the AP through TP-Link's management API and tries again on the next boot, with a hard cap on the number of reboots.

Qualcomm can fix their driver if they want, or host it somewhere more open. OpenWrt doesn't have this bug, and TP-Link won't release new firmware for my AP anyway. The similar DMA bugs I found in Linux deserve a closer look, though. I'll get back to those over the weekend.

Update: tracking down the drops#

The Qualcomm card I put in the Framework 16 is a WCN785x, and every few hours it stopped sending data for 1 to 4 minutes. Since I already had root on the AP, I ran on the EAP770 alongside the BPF probes on the laptop and caught three drops with logs from both sides.

Everything the AP sent to the laptop arrived and got ACKed, so the laptop's radio was transmitting and the AP's receiver worked. Only data frames from the laptop stopped going out.

On the laptop, packets kept going into and the queue grew to thousands of frames. The firmware confirmed a few frames at a time and eventually returned the rest to the driver with , 10630 out of 26388 in one drop. The driver was otherwise quiet. On the AP, stayed at for most ticks apart from an occasional burst, with zero RX errors and zero retries, so the frames never left the card. Then the card unblocked on its own and sent the whole backlog in two seconds. The AP saw and then , and the laptop saw 7751 ACKed frames.

The signal was -31 to -42 dBm, the drops happened with no scan running, and the IP layer on the laptop was fine during them. I'm already on the latest upstream firmware, WLAN.HMT.1.1.c7-00108 UPSTREAM-3. only gets completion statuses back, and everything about when a frame goes on the air is decided inside Qualcomm's closed-source . That leaves the firmware.

I still don't know why it stops transmitting. The bursts that got through during a drop look like 802.11ax/be uplink scheduling, trigger-based uplink or MU EDCA, but I didn't find those settings on the AP to check.

I switched the AP's 5 GHz radio from Wi-Fi 7 to Wi-Fi 6 (802.11ax) and left a watcher running for 24 hours. If the drops stop, it's a Wi-Fi 7 bug, so I stay on Wi-Fi 6 and send a bug report to . If they don't, the firmware is broken regardless of the mode, and it's either a bug report or an Intel card.

items.title: A Dynamic and Distributed Virtual GPU Cloud Built on Idle Apple Silicon Devices
items.author: acossta
items.content: The increasing demand for GPU-accelerated machine learning inference has exposed limitations in centralized GPU infrastructures, including high cost, limited elasticity, and long wait times under resource constraints. At the same time, modern Apple Silicon–based macOS devices are equipped with powerful GPUs that remain largely idle during normal usage. This paper presents Minions, a dynamic and distributed virtual GPU cloud that aggregates idle Apple Silicon GPUs across macOS devices to execute large-scale machine learning inference workloads. Minions enables teams to leverage existing hardware without requiring additional GPU procurement. The system provides flexible GPU inference task execution, fault tolerance, and efficient resource utilization. Our experience shows that idle macOS devices can be transformed into a practical distributed GPU inference platform in environments where centralized GPU resources are constrained.

items.title: Show HN: Spotatui, a Spotify TUI/GUI without web API rate limits
items.author: LargeModGames
items.content:
About 11 months ago i revived the amazing but unfortunately unmaintained spotify-tui. Since then I have been working on it almost non stop, finding a lot of problems on the way.

One of the main issues I ran into were the Spotify web API rate limits. Third party clients like spotatui are dependent on a developer app made in the Spotify developer dashboard, which get rate limited a lot and Spotify has slowly been deprecating endpoints from it. The workaround for this used to be using a shared client id from ncspot but unfortunately that got rate limited too. This is when i started adding other playback sources, including YouTube, Navidrome/Subsonic, Internet radio with +- 30.000 stations, local files, Qobuz for lossless audio and Apple Music for macOS only where it controls the music app remotely.

I fixed both the deprecated endpoints and the rate limits with one solution. It still uses librespot in the back, my spotatui specific fork, but gets all data from it instead of only playback. The data comes from the internal API of the official clients, that API gives metadata, playlists, the user library, devices, lyrics and audio analysis. For searching it uses Pathfinder, the internal GraphQL API.

There are no web API rate limits because there is no shared app quota. Every user uses their own session as if it was the official client. The only potential problem is that Spotify does not document this API so any change on their side would break it. I intend to fix any of those issues as soon as they pop up.

It all started as a TUI back in 2019 but since then I've added a GUI to it too. The GUI is still a bit behind the TUI in terms of features, it only ships Spotify for now, but full parity between the TUI and GUI is coming soon. After that full parity with the official client is next. That is also why I made the GUI looks almost the same as the official client. That way its easier for me and users to find missing features.

Spotatui also has lua scripting support, a optional Web companion on spotatui.com, and if you have a AI coding agent like ChatGPT codex or Claude Code you can enable the MCP tools, which lets AI become your personal DJ just by talking to it.

Its written in Rust, uses ratatui for the terminal UI and Tauri 2 for the GUI. The Rust core starts a small web server with localhost that only your pc can reach which the GUI then serves. Both frontends share the same playback logic, the same login and the same Spotify code. The only difference is how you interact with it.

Thanks to librespot for making this all possible

items.title: We turned EmbeddingGemma 2 into a speech-to-text model
items.author: amrrs
items.content:
Google's EmbeddingGemma 2 is an embedding model. We turned it into a speech-to-text model: an hour of audio in about 13 seconds on a base MacBook Air, entirely on device.

Can an embedding model transcribe speech?

EmbeddingGemma 2 is a multimodal embedding model: text, images, audio and video in one shared space. Say a word out loud and its audio lands close to the written word.

So we tried reading words straight out of that space.

  1. EmbeddingGemma 2's audio encoder stays exactly as it is.
  2. A small reader moves each short slice of audio into the model's text space.
  3. The closest of ~229,000 English words wins, and the slices become a transcript.
  4. A tiny extra model adds punctuation and capitals.

Only the reader is trained: under two hours on 8×H100, on openly licensed English speech. The base model was never trained for speech-to-text.

Embedding Gemma Transcribebase M3 MacBook Air, 8 GB
IBM Granite Speech 5.0 TurboCTCbase M3 MacBook Air, 8 GB
NVIDIA Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3 (FluidAudio)
NVIDIA Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3 (FluidAudio)
Phonon-2, a Parakeet v3 fine-tune (FluidAudio)

× real time: seconds of audio per second of processing. Rows 1–2: our tests on the same base M3 MacBook Air. Rows 3–5: FluidAudio's published benchmarks on larger, newer Macs and different audio. A rough guide, not a like-for-like ranking.

Its word error rate is about 5% right now, against 2–3% for leading speech models. We believe a better-trained reader can close that gap; that's the next iteration.

Drop in an audio file, or hold Right Option, speak and release to dictate into any app. It runs on the Mac's Neural Engine; your audio never leaves the machine.

items.title: Character.ai Files for Bankruptcy
items.author: yanis_t
items.content:
Character.AI, one of the first breakout startups of the generative AI boom, has filed for bankruptcy and is selling some of its assets to Disney. The company, which builds various online bots for users to chat or roleplay with, has faced mounting scrutiny and lawsuits over the safety of its chatbots, but has continued releasing updates and products in recent months.

In a press release and blog post published Monday, Character said it had filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in the US to facilitate the sale of the company and its assets. “Over the past year, we’ve taken meaningful steps to sustain and improve our business amid significant legal, regulatory, and operational headwinds,” the company said.

In its bankruptcy filing, Character listed estimated liabilities between $50 million and $100 million. As part of the proposed sale, Disney would serve as the lead bidder for Character.AI’s assets, setting a baseline for competing offers. Disney would pay $20 million for certain undisclosed assets, and provide transition support “using former Company employees it has hired.” It would also receive a nonexclusive license to unspecified intellectual property.

Disney’s involvement comes shortly after the entertainment behemoth hired Character.AI’s former CEO Karandeep Anand as chief technology officer, part of its growing push into AI. Anand’s tenure as Character CEO lasted just over a year and during that time he oversaw the company’s move into microdramas. Disney has previously complained that Character was damaging its brand and exploiting its intellectual property by allowing unauthorized chatbots of its characters, including sending cease and desist letters.

Along with Anand, Disney also said it expected “a number of Character.AI’s technical team” to join the company. The move resembles a kind of “acquihire” strategy that has become increasingly common in Silicon Valley as a means of hoovering up startups’ talent that sometimes leaves the original company struggling to survive. Character.AI has survived it once already — Google spent over $2 billion to hire away much of the company’s talent, including co-founders Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas, in 2024.

Character said it expects the sale process to be completed by late November or early December and plans to continue operating its services, including paid subscriptions, in the meantime. However, the company warned that “the platform will be wound down” if a suitable bid does not emerge. “As we navigate this process, maintaining a safe and engaging experience for our community remains a top priority,” it said.

items.title: AWS Lambda Web Functions
items.author: HatchedLake721
items.content:
Today, we’re announcing AWS Lambda Web Functions, a new form factor that lets you run standard HTTP web applications on Lambda without rewriting your code into an event handler. You can take a standard port-listening server built with Express, Hono, Fastify, Next.js, or any Node.js framework, deploy it with a single command, and Lambda automatically handles scaling, multi-region distribution, and active CPU billing. No adapters, no infrastructure to manage, and no framework lock-in.

With this launch, AWS Lambda now offers three distinct form factors, each built on the same Firecracker isolation technology and designed for a different programming model.

are what you already know as Lambda functions. They use the event-driven, single-concurrent handler model with wall-clock billing. We’re introducing the “Event Functions” name to highlight that programming model: your function receives an event, processes it, and returns a response. The event-driven programming model is ideal for event processing, queue consumers, and invocations triggered by other AWS services.

use an HTTP-native programming model with multi-concurrent execution and active CPU billing. Your code listens on a port and handles standard HTTP requests. That programming model is ideal for web applications, API backends, and interactive HTTP workloads where multiple concurrent requests and I/O-heavy processing are the norm.

provide isolated, stateful sandbox environments with customer-managed lifecycles for running untrusted or user-generated code.

The three complement each other. An application might use Event Functions for asynchronous backend processing, Web Functions for the user-facing API and server-side rendering layer, and MicroVMs for interactive code execution features, all within the same AWS account and sharing the same operational model.

Modern web applications need to serve global audiences with fast, consistent response times while giving developers the freedom to use standard frameworks and iterate quickly. Building this today typically requires assembling multiple infrastructure components, configuring multi-region deployments, setting up latency-based routing, and tuning billing models to avoid paying for I/O wait. Developers often find themselves adapting their application code to fit a specific compute model rather than deploying the HTTP server they already have.

Lambda Web Functions removes this complexity. Each execution environment handles multiple requests simultaneously (up to 128 concurrent requests per environment), which means a burst of incoming traffic can share warm environments instead of mapping each request to a new one. Web Functions meter the CPU time your code uses, so time spent waiting on a database query or an API call consumes little CPU. Memory is metered for as long as the execution environment exists. For I/O-heavy web workloads like server-side rendering, API backends, and AI inference endpoints streaming token responses, this can reduce compute costs.

To get started, I wrote a simple Express.js server. This is the same code I run locally with , no Lambda-specific adapters or wrappers required.

import express from 'express';

const app = express();
const [host, port] = process.env.AWS_LAMBDA_HTTP_ENDPOINT.split(':');

app.get('/', (req, res) => {
  res.json({ message: 'Hello from Lambda Web Functions!' });
});

app.listen(port, host, () => {
  console.log(`Server running on port ${port}`);
});

The only difference from running locally is the environment variable, which Lambda sets to the host and port your server must listen on. To run locally, set it yourself, for example AWS_LAMBDA_HTTP_ENDPOINT=127.0.0.1:3000 node index.js.

aws lambda-web deploy --name my-web-app --code ./my-app

One command. No prior resource setup. The CLI bundled my source, created the Web Function, published its first revision, attached a Web Function endpoint, and returned a live HTTPS URL in under a minute.

A revision is an immutable snapshot of the code I deployed. The endpoint is the HTTPS URL that routes traffic to a revision, or splits traffic across revisions. Those are the resources I use to iterate and to control how traffic moves to new code.

$ curl https://<domain-id>.<shard-id>.lambda-web.us-east-1.on.aws/
{"message":"Hello from Lambda Web Functions!"}

Next, I wanted my application to serve users in Europe and Asia with lower latency. I redeployed with multiple regions:

aws lambda-web deploy --name my-web-app --code ./my-app \
    --regions us-east-1,eu-west-1,ap-northeast-1

Lambda Web Functions replicated my code to all three regions and configured latency-based routing automatically. Each request now routes to the Region with the lowest latency for the caller, on a best-effort basis, through one global URL (<domain-id>.lambda-web.global.on.aws).

When I updated my code and ran the same deploy command again, the CLI detected the existing function, uploaded the new revision, and pointed the endpoint at it. Total turnaround from code change to live: seconds.

For production workflows that require a more gradual rollout, I can shift traffic between revisions with a single API call:

aws lambda-web update-web-function-endpoint \
    --function-name my-web-app \
    --endpoint-name dev \
    --auto-deployment-mode Disabled \
    --revision-weights '[{"revisionId": "<current-revision-id>", "weight": 90}, {"revisionId": "<new-revision-id>", "weight": 10}]'

This sends 90% of endpoint traffic to the current revision and 10% to the new one, giving me a canary deployment without additional tooling.

For applications that combine static and dynamic content, Web Functions works well alongside Amazon CloudFront. You can select a Web Function endpoint as the origin for your CloudFront distribution. Static assets are served from the cache while dynamic requests route to your Web Function, giving you CDN performance for static content with serverless compute for the dynamic parts.

Web Functions improves the private-origin experience with CloudFront. With this launch, you attach CloudFront origin access control (OAC) to a Web Function endpoint instead. CloudFront signs requests to the origin, and the endpoint allows only your distribution to invoke it. You get the same private-origin pattern CloudFront already provides for Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), without exposing the endpoint or adding custom authorization to your app.

AWS Lambda Web Functions is available today in US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (Oregon), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), and Europe (Ireland). Web Functions run Node.js 24 (nodejs24.x) on Arm64 at launch and support Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) connectivity, allowing your function to access resources that exist within a VPC.

To get started, deploy your first Web Function in under a minute:

aws lambda-web deploy --name hello-world --hello-world

items.title: Character.ai has initiated voluntary Chapter 11 bankruptcy
items.author: nryoo
items.content:

items.title: Hittite royal archive found in Turkey
items.author: benbreen
items.content:
Archaeologists have uncovered a royal archive of cuneiform tablets in the ancient Hittite city of Samuha, modern-day Sivas, central Turkey. This year’s excavation unearthed 131 cuneiform tablets and fragments which record an epidemic of fever, military logistics, religious practices and events of royal daily life 3,400 years ago. Last year’s excavation uncovered 53 cuneiform tablets and fragments, so this season’s discoveries more than triple the number of texts. It is now the largest, most comprehensive archive of Hittite-language documents found in the 21st century.

The records date to the reign of King Tudhaliya II, and are written in Hittite and Hurrian. One text tells of a fever epidemic that struck the infant daughter of the king. She was still a nursing baby when she became ill. She never recovered from the fever and her health declined precipitously until she passed away. The cuneiform tablet records the funerary ritual that followed.

The health of the princes and princesses, not just babies but even up to adulthood, was an important focus of the records. The children of high-ranking imperial officials were given the same attention. Because illness was considered an expression of divine will, religious leaders performed many rituals to keep an eye on the physical health of the children of kings and government officials.

Another notable document is a letter from Hittite generals in western Anatolia appealing to the king for reinforcements in men, horses and chariots to fend off enemy forces. The generals’ warnings are dire. They plead that without an infusion of strength, the army would be destroyed by the enemy. They have the temerity to disclaim all responsibility for any upcoming failures if the reinforcements don’t come.

It’s a rare glimpse into the realities of military logistics with armies long distances from the king and court. The text also confirms that the king was at Samuha when the letter arrived, underscoring the city’s political importance. It was a royal stronghold for King Tudhaliya during times of military and political upheaval. His successor Suppiluliuma I used it as a launching pad for military campaigns that consolidated and expanded the territory of the Hittite Empire.

Samuha was also a major center of religious administration. Its patron deity was the goddess Sauska, goddess of love and war who was the Hurrian version of Ishtar and the most important goddess in the Hurrian pantheon. The association with the goddess was central to the city’s identity and was reflected in its religious ceremonies.

One tablet records the journeys of bird diviners who left Samuha and traveled through different regions. Their routes, the cities where they stayed and the birds they observed were recorded in a format resembling a diary. The documents also provide previously unknown information about how bird omens were observed, evaluated and interpreted by the Hittites.

The archive includes texts covering divination, correspondence, rituals and prayers, offering researchers new material for studying Hittite religious practices as well as the development of the Hittite language and scribal culture.

items.title: A look at the math that OpenAI claims computes faster Fourier transforms
items.author: mochomocha
items.content:
Hi there, argmin readers! Today’s post looks at part of OpenAI’s math repository that claims to compute faster Fourier transforms. It’s more technical than usual, but I tried to add some tutorial material for people who need a refresher course on signal processing or computational complexity.

The Fast Fourier Transform is one of the most important innovations in digital signal processing and one of my favorite algorithms. The FFT is a fast way to extract the frequency content of signals, letting you rapidly analyze, filter, and manipulate frequencies across different bands of the spectrum.

To make this acceleration concrete, when n is 1,000, n^2 is 1,000,000 and 5 * n log n is around 50,000, a 20-fold speedup. When n is 1,000,000, the speedup is 10,000-fold. These speedups can be the difference between a transform being computable or not given the constraints of a signal processing application.

Well, lo and behold, in the massive paper dump OpenAI took on the mathematics world last week, they claim to have a faster Fourier transform. The main claim from their discriminatively named “main.pdf” is

I was intrigued about what was going on here. The log(n) term, in theory, was a teeny tiny bit smaller than in the standard FFT.

Did I read this paper? Of course not. No one at OpenAI read this paper either, so why should I? I did what every other mathematician in the world does with AI slop mathematics: I fed it back into the slop machine and ran an information retrieval session with a chatbot interface to extract salient facts. Anthropomorphically speaking: I asked ChatGPT what it thinks about its own output. This is how we do mathematical research now. What a world.

Unfortunately, I did not find a faster Fourier transform. Instead, I found the rot that develops inside applied mathematical theory when formalism becomes so detached from reality that a “breakthrough” is nothing more than an artifact of mathematicians not being able to properly specify the rules of their games in natural language.

First, “big-O” notation has been so abused that it has become meaningless. Let’s review the definition, which impressed me as an undergrad. An algorithm has running time T(n) = O(F(n)) if there exists an integer N and a constant C such that

I mean, sure. But given the constants, the algorithm runs faster only when n is impossibly large. Roughly, you need

whatever the hell that number means.

Lipton and Regan argue galactic algorithms are useful because they spur research. Once you show a running time is asymptotically possible, you can spend your time finding an algorithm that practically achieves this provable running time. Maybe you can send your AI agent swarms after it. You do you. Maybe you can get a practical algorithm out, but I don’t know of any legitimate examples where this happened. I’m particularly doubtful here, because the model of “computation” OpenAI uses bears no resemblance to an actual computer.

Jacques Morgenstern provednumericalinstabilities

engaging in illegal hacking

This is because the theory of computer science has a culture that actively discourages running algorithms on a computer. It’s acceptable to write papers in theory conferences that assert an algorithm exists without ever writing it down. The theory of computer science has become a form of mathematics that doesn’t concern itself with computers, and it offers little reward for impact outside those mathematical pursuits. I explained this to a friend who remarked to me that “theory” has the transdisciplinary meaning of “hiding in obscurity of one’s own making.”

AI is really good at automating our worst tendencies. It amplifies the unspoken cultural practices no one likes, but no individual can reasonably deviate from. It exploits the mechanized traditions recalcitrant to collective action. In that vein, AI can now write useless theory papers. But perhaps in the absurdity of the distasteful OpenAI trash dump of proofs, we can all look up and realize together that we should consider doing something else.
