items.title: LittleJS is 2D and 3D now
items.author: dmit
items.content:
LittleJS just got the biggest update since it launched! It is still the small, fast, dependency-free HTML5 game engine it always was. Now it also has a full 3D renderer sharing the canvas with your 2D game, built-in level editors, a library of ready-made particle effects, a much faster core, and new tools for making games with AI.

2D and 3D in the same engine

This is the big one! Meshes and shape builders, terrain and voxel maps with collision, shadow maps, colored lights and spotlights, fog, reflections, particles, trails, cameras, and custom shaders on any object. 3D objects are regular LittleJS objects with the same physics, children and timers as 2D, so the two mix freely: a 2D UI over a 3D scene, or a 2D game inside a 3D world.

Prefer Three.js for rendering? There is a plugin for that too!

2D got plenty as well: a new dynamic lighting system, one-way platforms, swept bullet collision, parallax layers, and improved object collision performance.

, 2D and 3D, built into the engine. Press Escape in a debug build to pause the game, edit the level in place with undo, autosave and prefabs, then play on. The editor guide shows how to make them an editor for your own game. 2D levels load and save as Tiled JSON.

Particle effects library. Fire, smoke, sparks, explosions, rain and more, each one line: particleEffect('fire', pos), in 2D or 3D. Every effect takes scale, hue and saturation, and the particle designer tweaks them or builds new ones. Most games will not need anything else.

 has over 100 short examples, each a single file that explains what it shows and how it works, with live editing and a Share button that puts your edited code in a link. It is the best place to learn the engine.

The rendering core was reworked: batched 2D sprites on WebGL2, instanced 3D drawing, and far less per-draw overhead. To measure it I built a WebGL Engine Bench: the same two scenes, moving sprites and lit cubes, through LittleJS, PixiJS, Three.js, PlayCanvas, Phaser and Babylon.js, reporting how many objects each holds at 60 fps.

On my machine LittleJS matched the fastest paths of the other engines and beat them in several. That is one machine and two workloads, so run it on yours: it works in the browser with nothing to install, and results and scene improvements from other engine maintainers are welcome.

LittleJS has a small, well documented API, with the whole thing in one reference file. That is exactly what coding AIs are good at, and it is the same thing that makes it readable for people. So it is now a first-class goal:

  • The LittleJS AI toolkit: starter templates, helper modules and agent instructions for any coding AI, Claude Code, Copilot, Codex or Cursor.
  • The  installs with two commands. Ask for a game and you get a complete, playable project, engine included, that opens from a file with no server and no npm install. Because the engine already does the rendering, input, physics and audio, the AI’s effort goes into your game.
  • The LittleJS GPT builds games inside ChatGPT with no code at all.
  • The LittleJS Arcade: 50+ small games made this way, all open source, all usable as starters.

LittleJS was always meant to be a general purpose engine, that I could use for all my games. I started it small on purpose, with js13k as the proving ground, because keeping the core tiny and simple from day one is what makes an engine easy to learn and fast to run.

Everything since has built on that core: people wanted to make more and more ambitious things with it, and what they asked for most was 3D and tools. I wanted the 3D side to feel exactly like the 2D side, same objects, same loop, same small API, not a separate framework bolted on.

The other reason is the community. LittleJS is not a one-person project any more: engine fixes, plugins, examples and a lot of games have come from other people, and the best way to push an engine forward is for people to make things with it. The third LittleJS Game Jam is running right now, October 2 to November 2. Come make something!

The new website littlejsengine.com is a demo of all of this: a train ride through every feature, running on the engine.

Thanks for reading! Give us a star oh GitHub if you like the project. 🚂

items.title: AI is a tool and using it well takes skill
items.author: layer8
items.content:
In his October 11, 2026 article, "'AI' is Not a Tool," Rich Hickey argues that LLMs are automation rather than tools because they cannot be wielded. I agree that outsourcing work can cost us opportunities to learn. But his conclusion does not follow. Even by his definition, an LLM can be something a human wields. And using it well takes skill, just as using other tools does.

Picking up a saw does not guarantee a straight cut. Holding a chisel does not make you a sculptor. Tools can amplify poor judgment as readily as good judgment. Their usefulness depends on the operator's ability to direct them, interpret feedback, recognize mistakes, and make corrections. Those requirements also apply to LLMs.

One of my colleagues used to say, "AI is a mirror." I find that insightful: it reflects who you are, including the curiosity, judgment, and habits you bring to it. The questions you ask and the standards you apply to its answers matter.

An LLM's unpredictability is a meaningful limitation. But predictability, reliability, simplicity, and bounded function are qualities by which we evaluate tools, not prerequisites for membership in the category. A tool does not stop being a tool because it is difficult to control or easy to misuse.

Hickey's distinction between tools and automation also creates a false division. Automation can be a feature of a tool. A compiler performs substantial work without the programmer continuously directing each operation. A spreadsheet recalculates results without someone manually carrying out every calculation. We still wield these systems by specifying inputs, examining results, and deciding what to do next. Why should generating text automatically disqualify an instrument from being a tool when translating code or calculating numbers automatically does not?

The claim that LLM use lacks intention, feedback, direction, and expertise is especially difficult to defend. A programmer can ask an LLM to explain unfamiliar code, challenge that explanation, inspect the source, test a proposed change, reject it, and refine the request. That is a feedback loop directed by a human pursuing a purpose. Doing it well requires knowing what to ask, what evidence matters, and when the answer is wrong. Expertise can make the instrument more useful.

Hickey's concern about reading is valid for a particular use: accepting a summary in place of reading a paper can sacrifice much of what reading teaches. But someone can also read the paper and use an LLM to question their interpretation, explore an objection, or identify something to examine more closely. The possibility of avoiding intellectual work does not establish that every use avoids it. The relevant question is what the person actually does.

What disappoints me the most is the reliance on the AI industry's anthropomorphic vocabulary: "go rogue," "escape containment," "conspire." Repeating those expressions risks accepting the framing that makes these systems sound like independent beings. Software can produce unexpected outputs, fail to follow instructions, or cause harm when given access to consequential actions. Those are real engineering problems. Calling them "conspiracy" adds a suggestion of human motives without establishing any.

I would not claim that an LLM always does exactly what a human tells it to do. It plainly can fail. But failure to obey perfectly does not make it cease to be a tool, any more than successful use proves that its operator has surrendered their judgment.

The useful distinction is between wielding an instrument with skill and delegating work without adequate understanding or oversight. That distinction applies to AI, and it gives us something more practical than declaring that an entire class of software cannot be a tool.

items.title: Who is vfmaddrnd231pd?
items.author: pngmangi
items.content:
Hacker News Lobsters

is a unique instruction from the FMA instruction set. Most instructions in that set have mnemonics like , but here means something very specific. The Intel Software Development Manual documents it as:

VFMADDRND231PD – Fused Multiply-Add of Packed Double-Precision Floating-Point Values with rounding control

[…] The immediate byte defines several bit fields that control rounding, DAZ, FTZ, and exception suppression (See Table 5-3).

Most x86 floating-point instructions use the global rounding mode and settings, changing which is pretty slow. But allows the rounding mode to be controlled on a per-instruction basis, and since FMA can emulate addition, subtraction, and multiplication, this mechanism effectively allows any arithmetic to have controllable rounding without AVX-512 – making some algorithms that rely on rounding incredibly faster.

Or so it , if this instruction actually existed. GNU assembler doesn’t recognize it. The Intel C/C++ Compiler intrinsics and that SDM mentions are absent not only from Clang, but from ICC as well. Trying to assemble the instructions by hand from the SDM opcode list reveals another issue:

VEX.DDS.128.66.0F3A.W1 B8 /r /ib

is the VEX prefix, but what is ? This opcode is the only mention of in the SDM, and this SO answer says that is merely used for documentation and was removed from later SDM versions, but the fact that it’s still present here is suspicious. And when you actually run the instruction on a CPU that supports the FMA instruction set, like my Haswell, it raises (“UnDefined instruction”)!

I already found it strange that the SDM only lists and not other variants like using /// or //, which other FMA instructions have, but this confirmed my suspicions. It was at that point that I downloaded a more recent version of the SDM and noticed that this instruction is absent in the 2026 edition of the SDM, despite being present in the 2024 version.

I must say I’m incredibly confused. This instruction doesn’t look like a typo in the documentation, since the docs contain unique tables and pseudocode that isn’t similar to any other instruction. My best hypothesis is that Intel wanted to add the set, then found an issue with it at the last moment and removed it from the CPU, but didn’t quite adjust the SDM correctly. But I have no way to confirm that.

If anyone reading this has a friend at Intel, I’d love to know the answer.

Back in 2023, Intel failed to add AVX-512 support to consumer CPUs due to hardware limitations, but still wanted to add some goodies from AVX-512. That’s how AVX10 was born – a new extension that looked roughly like AVX-512, but had conditional support for 512-bit vector lengths.

AVX-512 uses a strange instruction encoding with the prefix. For compactness, the bits responsible for the static rounding mode are reused for the operation width (128, 256, or 512 bits), so only scalar and 512-bit operations can customize rounding.

This was a problem for AVX10, which didn’t support 512-bit operations: if it interpreted the same instruction as operating on 256-bit values instead of 512-bit ones, different CPUs would behave inconsistently. So AVX10 had to use a different encoding for its own custom rounding modes.

My theory is that originally, Intel decided that the easiest way to do this was to add an immediate byte that controls the rounding, which is how and similar instructions for other arithmetic operations were born. Notice that it uses a prefix, not the AVX-512-specific prefix – this would allow CPUs without 512-bit vectors to avoid handling the prefix at all. Since they added an entire byte, they utilized it in full: 2 bits for the rounding mode, 6 bits for everything else they thought might be useful.

It seems like by 2024, Intel decided that this approach won’t work. And I get it: it’s odd that was more powerful than AVX-512 instructions, but only supported 256-bit vectors. And if it supported 512-bit vectors, the rounding mode control built into AVX-512 would become obsolete for the most part.

So Intel bit the bullet, dedicated the last unused bit in the prefix to enabling rounding modes for 256-bit vectors, and reused the AVX-512 instruction encoding for AVX10. This also allowed them to reuse the AVX-512 assembly syntax and avoid introducing new mnemonics, at which point the mnemonic and others became unnecessary. During this process, someone forgot to remove specifically from the SDM draft.

By 2025, AVX-512 was considered table stakes due to the popularity of Zen 4, and Intel finally decided to make 512-bit support unconditional in AVX10. This made this entire hack unnecessary, so Intel updated the AVX10 whitepaper:

Removed references to 256-bit maximum vector register size, enumeration of vector-length support, and 256-bit instructions supporting embedded rounding.

In this new whitepaper, all the platforms will support 512 bit vector width (previously, E-core is up to 256 bit, leading to hybrid clients and Atom Server 256 bit only). Also, 256 bit rounding is not that useful because we currently have rounding feature directly on E-core now and no need to use 256-bit rounding as somehow a workaround. HW will remove that support.

We can partially confirm this theory by inspecting the patches. One of them is named:

Revert “AVX10.2 ymm rounding: Support vfmadd{132, 231, 213}p{s, d, h} intrins”

…and removes multiple intrinsics, including , which is named very similarly to the documented intrinsic for the ghost instruction, .

At a later point, someone at Intel realized that was still mentioned in the SDM and removed it.

Summing up: I believe that is of AVX10 lineage. I think it was added during the prototyping stage of AVX10, then reworked to use a different instruction encoding, until it finally became unnecessary. Market pressures, timing constraints, and weird tech debt affected the design process enough that things had to be reworked on the fly, and at some point someone slipped up and accidentally documented an instruction that has never existed in released hardware.
